A function that may have no result returns an Option<T>. some(x) holds a value and none holds nothing:

fn rating_of(r: Int) : Option<Int> = some(r) given r > 0 otherwise none
[5, 0, 4] | map(rating_of) | somes

[5, 4]

somes keeps the present values. Option covers the other ways to handle an Option.

docs.title: Generic functions
docs.text:
Some functions work the same way for every element type. The last element of a list is found the same way whether the list holds titles or page counts. A generic function is written once with a type parameter, a capital letter in angle brackets after the name, and each call fills it in:

fn last_of<T>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs[-1]
[last_of(["Dune", "Emma"]), last_of([] | List<String>)]

["Emma", none]

Called with a List<String>, T is String and the result is an Option<String>. Called with a List<Int>, the result is an Option<Int>:

fn last_of<T>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs[-1]
last_of([412, 280])

Option<Int>

docs.title: Bounds
docs.text:
Inside the body, T can be any type, so the body can only do what works for every type. Finding the greatest element needs an order, and not every type has one. The checker rejects the body:

fn longest<T>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs | max
longest([412, 280])

check error[unsatisfied-bound]: `max` needs elements with an order of their own, and T has none; sort with an explicit key first
 --> <expression>:1:47
  |
1 | fn longest<T>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs | max
  |                                               ^^^

A bound restricts the type parameter. T : Orderable says T has an order, so the body may use max, min and sort:

fn longest<T : Orderable>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs | max
longest([412, 280, 310])

412

The bound is now part of the contract, and each call is checked against it. A set has no order of its own, so a list of sets is rejected:

fn longest<T : Orderable>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs | max
longest([{1}, {2}])

check error[type-mismatch]: `longest` needs T : Orderable, and T is Set<Int> here
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | longest([{1}, {2}])
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A bound is a type or a trait. Traits shows how to declare traits and use them as bounds.

docs.title: 4. Functions
docs.text:
Every step in a pipeline takes a function. filter takes the test that keeps an element, map the function that transforms one, sort the key to order by. Functions are the part of an HQL program you write most often, and they are values: a function can be bound to a name, passed to a step, and returned from another function.

A function has a type, written with an arrow: Int -> Int takes an Int and returns an Int. The type is a contract between the function and the code that calls it, and hql checks both sides before the program runs:

fn days(pages: Int, per_day: Int) : Int = (pages + per_day - 1) / per_day
days("412", 40)

check error[type-mismatch]: this argument is String, and parameter `pages` takes Int
 --> <expression>:2:6
  |
2 | days("412", 40)
  |      ^^^^^

fn label(pages: Int) : String = pages
label(412)

check error[type-mismatch]: `label` is declared to return String but its body is Int
 --> <expression>:1:33
  |
1 | fn label(pages: Int) : String = pages
  |                                 ^^^^^

The first program calls days with the wrong argument. The second has a body that does not return what the declaration promises. A function's caller can rely on its declared type, and the body can rely on its parameters.

HQL writes functions in several forms. Each one gives a function value with a type, and each value is used the same way:

docs.title: Lambdas
docs.text:
n => n * 2 is a lambda: a function written in place, with its parameters before => and its body after it. Passed to a step, a lambda takes its parameter type from the step, so n below is an Int:

[412, 280] | map(n => n * 2)

[824, 560]

The checker uses that type to check the body. A body that does not fit the element type is rejected:

[412, 280] | map(n => n.upper())

check error[type-mismatch]: `upper` needs String, not Int
 --> <expression>:1:23
  |
1 | [412, 280] | map(n => n.upper())
  |                       ^^^^^^^^^

A lambda bound to a name has no step to take its type from, so its parameters must be typed:

double = (n: Int) => n * 2
[412, 280] | map(double)

[824, 560]

double = (n: Int) => n * 2
double

Int -> Int

A function of two parameters has the type (Int, Int) -> Int. A lambda's body is a single expression. A function that needs several steps is declared with fn.

docs.title: Calling a function
docs.text:
f(x) calls a function. A pipe calls one too: x | f is f(x), and x | f(y) is f(x, y). The piped value becomes the first argument:

fn days(pages: Int, per_day: Int) : Int = (pages + per_day - 1) / per_day
[days(412, 40), 412 | days(40)]

[11, 11]

This is why steps such as map and filter read left to right: each is a function whose first argument is the value piped into it.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text: Page What it covers Declaring a function fn, typed parameters and result, recursion, functions taken and returned, variadic parameters Function bodies a body as one expression or as a block, and how a block is scoped Generic functions type parameters, and bounds on them Aliases and holes naming a pipeline fragment with :=, and leaving an argument open with _

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 5 moves functions into modules: files that a program imports, with public and private declarations.

docs.title: Calling a module's functions
docs.text:
An import statement decides how a program writes the calls to a module's functions. There are two statements, and they bind different names:

Statement Binds A call is written import club.reading the module's name, reading reading.days(412, 40) from club.reading import days the function's name, days days(412, 40) import club.titles the module's name, and its receivers "Dune".initials()

The rules are the same for every module: one of the program's own, one of the standard library, or one of an installed package.

docs.title: import binds the module's name
docs.text:
import club.reading binds the name reading, and every public function of the module is called through it, as a call or as a pipeline step:

import club.reading

[reading.days(412, 40), 412 | reading.days(40)]

[11, 11]

The function's own name is not bound. A call written without the module's name is a check error, and the error names both ways to write it:

import club.reading

days(412, 40)

check error[unknown-name]: `days` is declared in the module `club.reading`, which is imported qualified: write `reading.days(…)`, or `from club.reading import days`
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | days(412, 40)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: from binds the names it lists
docs.text:
from club.reading import days, days_for_all binds days and days_for_all, and nothing else:

from club.reading import days, days_for_all

[days(412, 40), 412 | days(40), days_for_all([412, 280], 40)]

[11, 11, 18]

from does not bind the module's name. A program that wants both forms writes both statements:

from club.reading import days

reading.days(412, 40)

check error[unknown-name]: `reading` is not bound
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | reading.days(412, 40)
  | ^^^^^^^

as binds a function under another name, and only under that name:

from stats import mean as average_pages

average_pages([412, 280, 310])

334.0

A name the module does not declare, or declares private, is a check error at the import, where it is written:

from club.reading import dayz

1

check error[unknown-name]: the module `club.reading` declares no public `dayz`
 --> <expression>:1:26
  |
1 | from club.reading import dayz
  |                          ^^^^

docs.title: Groups and exceptions
docs.text:
* binds every public function of a module. except leaves names out, one or several in parentheses:

from stats import * except (variance, stdev)

pages = [412, 280, 310]
[mean(pages), median(pages), pages | variance]

[334.0, 310.0, 3192.0]

The variance here is the prelude's, the population variance; the one of stats was left out.

docs.title: Receiver calls
docs.text:
A function whose first parameter is self is a receiver, called as value.f() (Receiver modules). import reaches every receiver of the module:

import club.titles

["The Hobbit".initials(), titles.initials("Mrs Dalloway")]

["TH", "MD"]

from reaches the receivers it selects, and no others. A name it lists is both a function and a receiver:

from club.titles import initials

["The Hobbit".initials(), initials("Mrs Dalloway")]

["TH", "MD"]

docs.title: Receivers selected by type
docs.text:
A type selector selects receivers by the type of their self. String.* selects every receiver over String, and String.initials one of them. Collection.* selects every function of stats whose self is a Collection:

from stats import Collection.*

[412, 280, 310].median()

310.0

The match is exact. A selector selects functions declared over its type, and none declared over a supertype or a subtype of it: List.* selects nothing from stats, whose functions are declared over Collection.

A group selected by type is renamed by a pattern, a name with one * that stands for each function's own name. A pattern with the type keeps the functions receivers:

from club.titles import String.* as String.club_*

["The Hobbit".club_initials(), "Dune".club_shelf_mark(1965)]

["TH", "D-1965"]

The new name is the same function under another name: no new function is made. A pattern or a name without the type binds a function that is not a receiver:

from club.titles import String.initials as initials_of

"Dune".initials_of()

check error[unknown-name]: String has no function `initials_of`
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | "Dune".initials_of()
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A receiver keeps its type, so an alias may not name another one:

from club.titles import String.initials as Int.initials

1

check error[invalid-import]: `String.initials as Int.initials` changes the receiver type from `String` to `Int`; a receiver alias keeps its type: write `String.initials as String.initials`
 --> <expression>:1:25
  |
1 | from club.titles import String.initials as Int.initials
  |                         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Types and constructors
docs.text:
Type names need no import statement to bind them: a type of an imported module is written by its name. A constructor is written with its type's name, so import binds the constructors of the module's types: import logging and then Logger(…) (Logging).

A from statement may name a type, from encoding import Hex. That checks the name against the module and binds nothing else, not even the module's receivers:

from encoding import Hex

"hé".encode(Hex)

check error[unknown-name]: `encode` is declared in the module `encoding`: write `import encoding`
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | "hé".encode(Hex)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Two imports, one name
docs.text:
Two statements that bind one name to two different functions make the name ambiguous. The error is reported where the name is used, not at the imports:

from stats import median
from club.reading import days as median

median([1, 2, 3])

check error[unknown-name]: `median` is imported from `club.reading.days` and `stats.median`, so it is ambiguous; import one of them under another name with `as`, or call it qualified
 --> <expression>:4:1
  |
4 | median([1, 2, 3])
  | ^^^^^^

as resolves it, by binding one of them under another name. Binding the one function twice, through two statements, is not an error. How names resolve has the rules in full.

docs.title: The prelude
docs.text:
The prelude is the list of import statements every unit starts with, lib/std/prelude.hql. For each of its modules it holds both statements:

import string
from string import *
import seq
from seq import *

So a program writes "Dune".upper(), upper("Dune") and string.upper("Dune") with no import line. core and collections are in the list like the rest. A project that sets prelude = false under [modules] in .hql/config.toml starts every unit with no imports at all.

A project may add import statements to every unit with [modules] import. An entry that names a module is import m; an entry may also be a whole from statement:

[modules]
import = ["club.reading", "from stats import mean, median"]

docs.title: 5. Modules
docs.text:
A program of a few lines can keep everything in one file. Once several programs need the same functions, or a team shares them, the functions need a home of their own. A module is that home: a named file of declarations (functions, types, traits and bindings) that programs import.

A module is also a contract. Its public declarations, with their types, are what every importer relies on. The rest is marked private and can change without breaking anyone. The checker checks every use of a module against that contract before the program runs: a call to a function the module does not export, or with the wrong arguments, is a check error.

A program reaches a module's functions in one of two ways. import m binds the module's name, and calls are written through it, reading.days(412, 40). from m import f binds the function's own name, days(412, 40). The rules are the same for every module, whether a program's own or one of the standard library: "Dune".upper() calls a function of the module string, which every program starts with imported.

docs.title: A module is a file under a module root
docs.text:
A project module is an HQL file under a module root. Its name is its path under the root: lib/club/reading.hql is the module club.reading, and lib/club/mod.hql would be club. The roots come from .hql/config.toml:

[modules]
roots = ["lib"]

or from --modules lib on the command line. The reading club's project uses lib/ as its root, and keeps the book's modules there. Roots that apply outside any project come from ~/.hql/modules/, from [modules] roots in ~/.hql/config.toml, and from $HQL_PATH. The execution context lists them all. A module found under two roots is an error.

Every module file starts with its name, and the checker compares the name with the file's path under its root. This is lib/club/reading.hql:

/// Reading plans: how long a book takes at a number of pages a day.
module club.reading

private fn rounded_up(n: Int, d: Int) : Int = (n + d - 1) / d

/// Days to read `pages` at `per_day` pages a day; a part day counts as one.
fn days(pages: Int, per_day: Int) : Int = rounded_up(pages, per_day)

/// Days to read every book of `shelf`, one after another.
fn days_for_all(shelf: List<Int>, per_day: Int) : Int {
    each = shelf | map(pages => days(pages, per_day))
    each | sum
}

A /// line is a doc string. It documents the declaration after it, and hql help club.reading prints it. private keeps rounded_up inside the module; Visibility covers this.

docs.title: Importing a module
docs.text:
import club.reading makes the module visible under its last segment, reading, and its functions are called through that name:

import club.reading

[reading.days(412, 40), reading.days(280, 40), reading.days_for_all([412, 280, 310], 40)]

[11, 7, 26]

import a.b as c makes it visible under c instead:

import club.reading as plan

plan.days(412, 40)

11

A module's function is a value like any other, and can be partially applied:

import club.reading

[412, 280] | map(reading.days(_, 40))

[11, 7]

from club.reading import days binds the function itself, and Calling a module's functions covers that statement:

from club.reading import days

days(412, 40)

11

Imports come first in a file, before its declarations and expressions. Two imports cannot use the same local name:

import club.reading
import club.titles as reading
1

check error[unknown-name]: `reading` already names the module `club.reading` here; import `club.titles` under another name with `as`
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | import club.titles as reading
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A module that is not imported cannot be used:

reading.days(412, 40)

check error[unknown-name]: `reading` is not bound
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | reading.days(412, 40)
  | ^^^^^^^

docs.title: The standard modules
docs.text:
The standard library is made of modules of the same kind. The prelude is the list of import statements every program starts with. It imports string, seq, math, option and result, among others, both ways, so "a,b".split(","), split("a,b", ",") and string.split("a,b", ",") all call the prelude's string.split. Other standard modules are imported by name:

import regex

regex.split("a1b22c", "[0-9]+")

["a", "b", "c"]

The reference has a page per standard module.

docs.text: Page What it covers Calling a module's functions import and from, as and except, receivers selected by type, and the prelude Which variance? one name in two modules, followed through import, from, except and as Receiver modules module m for T, functions taking self, and value.f() calls Visibility public and private declarations, and a module's contract How names resolve import units, a unit's own names, ambiguity, and modules as closures Modules and packages modules, packages, extensions and libraries; builtin and installable packages

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 6 uses functions over collections to ask the questions SQL asks: where, order by, group by, and the aggregates.

docs.title: How names resolve
docs.text:
When a program writes lower("ABC"), the checker must find the one declaration lower refers to. It may be the program's own function, or a function a from statement bound, the prelude's included. The rules are fixed, so a name always resolves to the same declaration, whatever order things are written in.

Every module is an import unit: one scope in which its imports apply and its names resolve. A program is an import unit of its own, the program module. An import makes a module visible in the unit that imports it, and nowhere else.

docs.title: Imports are per unit
docs.text: A module's imports are its own. A module that imports math sees math, and a program that imports the module does not see math through it. The prelude, too, is the implicit import list of each unit separately.

docs.title: A unit's own names win
docs.text:
A declaration the unit writes itself wins over an imported declaration of the same name, in every spelling: an unqualified call, a pipeline step and a receiver call. The imported one stays reachable through its module. This program declares its own lower:

fn lower(s: String) : String = "mine"
[lower("ABC"), "ABC" | lower, string.lower("ABC")]

["mine", "mine", "abc"]

The program's lower takes no self, so the receiver spelling reaches nothing, and the prelude's lower is not reached in its place:

fn lower(s: String) : String = "mine"
"ABC".lower()

check error[unknown-name]: `lower` is this unit's own function, which takes no `self`, so `value.lower(…)` does not reach it and no import's `lower` over String is reached in its place; write `lower(value, …)`, or qualify the import's
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | "ABC".lower()
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Because the unit's own declaration always wins, adding a function to an imported module never changes what an existing program calls. The order in which declarations are written does not matter either.

docs.title: Two imports, one name
docs.text: When two imports bind the same name to two declarations and the unit declares none, the name is ambiguous, and a call that uses it is a check error. Write the module name to choose one, titles.initials(s) or string.split(s, ","), or bind one of them under another name with as. Where the two declarations take inputs of different types, the input's type chooses, and the call is not ambiguous. The order of the imports never decides.

docs.title: A module is a closure
docs.text:
A name in a module resolves through the module's own declarations and its own imports, and nothing else. A module never sees the program that imports it. The bindings hql provides to a program, such as vault, cards, stdin and stdout, are not bound in a module. What a module needs from a program must be passed in, as a parameter:

module club.shelf

fn books(cards: Seq<Card>) : Seq<Card> = cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")

A program calls it with its own cards, shelf.books(cards). A module written this way is checked once, and behaves the same in every program that imports it.

docs.title: Imports form no cycle
docs.text:
Imports cannot form a cycle. An import that would close one is an error, and the error names the modules in the cycle. Two modules that need each other are fixed by moving the shared part into a third module that both import.

Module names form a tree, but the tree is not a dependency graph: club and club.reading see nothing of each other unless one imports the other. A child may import its parent. A parent that imports its child gets a warning.

docs.title: Modules and packages
docs.text: A program imports modules. Modules are distributed and installed in packages. Some functions in a module are declared in HQL but implemented in Rust, by the package's extension. When you only write programs, you deal with modules. Packages matter when you install code someone else wrote.

docs.title: Four units
docs.text:
Term What it is Example module a named unit of declarations, one mod.hql or one file under a module root; what import names regex, io.net, ml.metrics package the unit that is distributed and installed: a module root holding one or more modules, with the extension that implements them std, hmd, ml extension the native code of a package: the implementations of the declarations its modules write without a body std, ml library the compiled file an installed package's extension is loaded from libhql_ext_ml.dylib

A program never names a package. import regex names the module, and the packages installed where the program runs determine which one provides it. Each module has exactly one provider: a package, or HQL itself when every declaration in the module has a body.

A package carries one extension, with the same name as the package. A declaration such as fn trim(self) : String has no body in HQL. The package's extension implements it, and hql checks that every such declaration has an implementation before any program runs.

docs.title: Builtin packages
docs.text:
A builtin package ships inside the hql binary: its modules are bundled with it and its extension is compiled into it. There are two.

Package Modules How a program gets them std, the standard package core, string, seq, math, io, regex, time and the rest the prelude for many, import for the others hmd, HyperMarkdown hmd, hmd.vault, hmd.search, hmd.search.lexical, hmd.search.semantic import hmd, whose prelude imports the rest

"The standard library" is another name for the std package, and Part IV is its guide. hql builtins names the package beside each module, collections (std 0.7.2, prelude) (chapter 13).

docs.title: Installable packages
docs.text:
An installable package is installed separately. Its extension is built into a library on your machine, and hql loads the library when it starts. A program then imports the package's modules the same way it imports a standard one:

hql package install ml

import ml

Dataset([[1.0f], [2.0f], [3.0f]], target = [3.0f, 5.0f, 7.0f]).fit_linear()

hql package install puts the package under the project's .hql/packages/ml/, or with --home under ~/.hql/packages/ml/: its modules, the library, and a record of the hql version it was built for. A library loads only into the hql version it was built for, so after an upgrade hql package rebuild builds it again.

The source of an installable package is a Rust crate named hql-ext-<package>: ml is built from the crate hql-ext-ml. A package provides modules under its own name only, ml and ml.metrics, and never takes a builtin package's or a builtin module's name.

A package is

  • official when its crate lives in the hql-extensions repository, as ml does;
  • known when its crate lives elsewhere and the package registry kept in that repository admits it by name;
  • a path package when it is installed from a directory.

hql package install ml installs an official or a known package by its name, hql package install --path <dir> a path package, and hql package list shows what is installed.

Part V is the whole of this subject: how a declaration without a body is implemented (chapter 32), writing a package (chapter 34), how its library is loaded (chapter 35), the commands (chapter 36) and the registry (chapter 37).

docs.title: Receiver modules
docs.text:
A module that names a type pattern after for, module club.titles for String, is a receiver module. Its functions take self as their first parameter, at the module's pattern, and once the module is imported they resolve as receiver calls, value.f(args), on every value the pattern fits. This is lib/club/titles.hql:

/// Receiver functions over a book's title.
module club.titles for String

/// The first letter of each word, `"The Hobbit".initials()` is `"TH"`.
fn initials(self) : String = self.words().map(w => w.slice(0, 1)).join("")

/// A shelf mark: the initials and the year, `"TH-1937"`.
fn shelf_mark(self, year: Int) : String = fmt("{}-{}", self.initials(), year)

self is written untyped: its type is the module's pattern, String. Inside the module, self.initials() calls the module's own receiver function.

import club.titles

["The Hobbit".initials(), "Dune".shelf_mark(1965), titles.initials("Mrs Dalloway")]

["TH", "D-1965", "MD"]

value.f(args) is module.f(value, args): the value fills self, and titles.initials("Mrs Dalloway") is the same call written with its module. A function declared without self takes no receiver and is called only through its module.

docs.title: Receiver calls throughout the book
docs.text:
The prelude's modules are receiver modules too: string is module string for String, so "Dune".upper() calls string.upper, and [1, 2].size() calls the collection's size. A receiver call is resolved by the value's type among the modules in scope, so two modules may declare one name over different types: "abc".contains("b") is the string's and [1, 2].contains(2) the collection's.

c.title without parentheses is a field read, not a call.

docs.title: A receiver function's body
docs.text:
A receiver function is a function, and its body takes either form. A block over self names its steps as any block does:

module counting for Int

fn twice(self) : Int {
    doubled = self * 2
    doubled
}

A program declares no receiver functions: self belongs to a module's pattern, and a program has none.

fn initials(self: String) : String = "TH"
"The Hobbit".initials()

parse failure[unexpected-token]: a function with a body takes its receiver at the module's pattern: write `self` untyped
 --> <expression>:1:19
  |
1 | fn initials(self: String) : String = "TH"
  |                   ^^^^^^

docs.title: Visibility
docs.text: A declaration inside a module is public unless it is marked private. A module's contract is its public declarations: what an importer reaches, and what the module promises to keep.

docs.title: Public by default
docs.text:
club.reading declares days and days_for_all unmarked, so both are public, and rounded_up marked private:

module club.reading

private fn rounded_up(n: Int, d: Int) : Int = (n + d - 1) / d

fn days(pages: Int, per_day: Int) : Int = rounded_up(pages, per_day)

days calls rounded_up inside the module. An importer reaches days, and rounded_up is not part of the contract:

import club.reading

reading.rounded_up(412, 40)

check error[unknown-name]: the module `reading` has no function `rounded_up`
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | reading.rounded_up(412, 40)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A private declaration is never exported: no importer reaches it qualified, unqualified, as a pipeline step, or — for a private receiver function — as value.f(). A helper marked private is free to change without changing the module's contract.

docs.title: What private marks
docs.text:
private may mark every declaration a module writes: a function, a receiver function, a type, a trait and a module-level binding.

  • A public declaration may not mention a private type or trait in its signature — a parameter, a result, a bound, a field or a supertype. The checker rejects such a declaration, since an importer would receive a value of a type it cannot name.
  • The parser rejects private on an impl. An implementation of a trait holds in every module that sees the type and the trait.

docs.title: A program is public
docs.text:
A program is read by no other unit, so every declaration in it is public, and the parser rejects private there:

private fn double(n: Int) : Int = n * 2

double(21)

parse failure[unexpected-token]: `private` belongs to a module: every declaration of a program is public, since no other unit reads it
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | private fn double(n: Int) : Int = n * 2
  | ^^^^^^^

docs.title: internal is reserved
docs.text:
internal is visibility across the modules of one package: wider than one module, narrower than every importer. It is reserved, and the parser rejects it wherever it is written:

internal fn double(n: Int) : Int = n * 2

double(21)

parse failure[unexpected-token]: `internal` is reserved: visibility across one package is admitted once every module records its package; mark the declaration `private`, or leave it public
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | internal fn double(n: Int) : Int = n * 2
  | ^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Which variance?
docs.text:
Two modules of the standard library declare a function named variance, and they compute different things:

Function Module Computes Over [1, 2, 3, 4] collections.variance collections, in the prelude the population variance 1.25 stats.variance stats, imported where it is used the sample variance 1.6666666666666667

Which one a bare variance calls depends only on the import statements. The programs below differ in those statements alone, and apply the rules of Calling a module's functions and How names resolve.

docs.title: The prelude's variance
docs.text:
Every program starts with the prelude, which runs from collections import *. A bare variance is the population variance:

[1, 2, 3, 4] | variance

1.25

docs.title: import stats changes nothing
docs.text:
import stats binds one name, stats. The functions of the module are reached through it, and none of them is bound by its own name. So the bare variance is still the prelude's, and stats.variance is the sample variance:

import stats

[[1, 2, 3, 4] | variance, [1, 2, 3, 4] | stats.variance]

[1.25, 1.6666666666666667]

Importing a module this way does not change what the program's existing calls mean: the import adds the name stats, and the bare names stay as they were.

docs.title: from stats import * makes it ambiguous
docs.text:
from stats import * binds every function of stats by its own name, variance among them. Now two imports bind variance to two different functions, and both take a List<Int>. The call is a check error, reported where the name is used:

from stats import *

[1, 2, 3, 4] | variance

check error[unknown-name]: `variance` over List<Int> is declared by `collections` and `stats`, so the call is ambiguous; qualify it, `collections.variance(…)`
 --> <expression>:3:16
  |
3 | [1, 2, 3, 4] | variance
  |                ^^^^^^^^

The other functions of stats are not affected. Only a name two imports bind is ambiguous, and only where a call could reach both:

from stats import *

[mean([1, 2, 3, 4]), median([1, 2, 3, 4])]

[2.5, 2.5]

docs.title: Choosing one
docs.text:
There are three ways to say which variance a call means. Writing the module's name always chooses. from does not bind the name stats, so a program that writes both forms imports stats both ways, as the prelude imports its own modules:

import stats
from stats import *

[[1, 2, 3, 4] | collections.variance, [1, 2, 3, 4] | stats.variance]

[1.25, 1.6666666666666667]

except leaves the name out of the star import, so the bare variance is the prelude's again:

from stats import * except variance

[[1, 2, 3, 4] | variance, mean([1, 2, 3, 4])]

[1.25, 2.5]

as binds the sample variance under a name of its own:

from stats import variance as sample_variance

[[1, 2, 3, 4] | variance, [1, 2, 3, 4] | sample_variance]

[1.25, 1.6666666666666667]

docs.title: Where the input chooses
docs.text:
Two functions bound to one name are ambiguous only for an input both accept. The prelude's variance takes Int and Float values, and only the one of stats takes Decimal values. For a list of Decimal values, the input's type chooses, and the bare name is not ambiguous:

from stats import *

[1.5, 2.5] | variance

0.50

docs.title: 6. SQL-like Queries
docs.text:
SQL asks a table questions: which rows, in what order, how many, grouped by what. HQL asks the same questions with pipeline steps. This chapter works through them over one table — the reading club's shelf, written as a list of records.

These examples run locally in hql. Translating their logical steps into SQL for a database engine is a future backend capability, described in Logical steps and physical plans.

docs.title: The table
docs.text:
shelf = [
    {title: "Frankenstein", author: "Mary Shelley", year: 1818, genre: "novel", pages: 280, status: "done", rating: 5},
    {title: "Dune", author: "Frank Herbert", year: 1965, genre: "novel", pages: 412, status: "reading"},
    {title: "The Hobbit", author: "J. R. R. Tolkien", year: 1937, genre: "novel", pages: 310, status: "todo"},
    {title: "Leaves of Grass", author: "Walt Whitman", year: 1855, genre: "poetry", pages: 145, status: "todo"},
    {title: "A Room of One's Own", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1929, genre: "essay", pages: 112, status: "done", rating: 4},
    {title: "The Common Reader", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1925, genre: "essay", pages: 304, status: "todo"},
    {title: "Mrs Dalloway", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1925, genre: "novel", pages: 194, status: "reading"},
]
shelf | size

7

Every program in this chapter begins with these lines; the book shows them once.

docs.title: Select and where
docs.text:
map is SQL's SELECT: it says what to keep of each row. filter is WHERE:

shelf
| filter(b => b.status == "todo")
| map(b => b.title)

["The Hobbit", "Leaves of Grass", "The Common Reader"]

shelf
| filter(b => b.author == "Virginia Woolf")
| map(b => {title: b.title, year: b.year})

[{title: "A Room of One's Own", year: 1929}, {title: "The Common Reader", year: 1925}, {title: "Mrs Dalloway", year: 1925}]

docs.title: Typed views of a record
docs.text:
ORDER BY pages needs pages to be numbers, and a record's leaves have no type of their own. A small function gives a record a typed view — one field, as the type the program means it to be, with what to do when it is missing:

fn title(b: Data) : String = match b.title { some(String t) => t, _ => "" }
fn pages(b: Data) : Int = match b.pages { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }
fn year(b: Data) : Int = match b.year { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }

From here on, the programs begin with the table and these views.

docs.title: Order by and limit
docs.text:
sort(by = key) is ORDER BY, and take(n) is LIMIT. A comparison orders the other way:

shelf
| sort(by = year)
| take(3)
| map(title)

["Frankenstein", "Leaves of Grass", "The Common Reader"]

shelf
| sort((a, b) => compare(pages(b), pages(a)))
| take(2)
| map(b => {title: title(b), pages: pages(b)})

[{pages: 412, title: "Dune"}, {pages: 310, title: "The Hobbit"}]

docs.title: Distinct
docs.text:
A set keeps each value once, so SELECT DISTINCT is the Set constructor:

shelf | map(b => b.genre) | Set

{"novel", "poetry", "essay"}

docs.title: Aggregates
docs.text:
size counts rows. sum, average, min and max work over numbers, so the pages are read through their view first:

lengths = shelf | map(pages)
{books: lengths | size, pages: lengths | sum, longest: lengths | max, average: lengths | average}

{average: 251.0, books: 7, longest: 412, pages: 1757}

Every aggregate is a fold: reduce with a starting value and a way to combine two values. sum is reduce(0, +). max is reduce(max), which starts from the first value and so is an Option: an empty list has none.

lengths = shelf | map(pages)
{total: lengths | reduce(0, +), longest: lengths | reduce(max)}

{longest: 412, total: 1757}

docs.title: Group by
docs.text:
group(by = key) partitions the rows by a key. Each group holds its key and its items, and a map over the groups computes one row per group — SQL's GROUP BY with its aggregates:

shelf
| group(by = b => b.genre)
| map(g => {genre: g.key, books: g.items | size, pages: g.items | map(pages) | sum})

{{books: 4, genre: "novel", pages: 1196}, {books: 1, genre: "poetry", pages: 145}, {books: 2, genre: "essay", pages: 416}}

HAVING is a filter after the group:

shelf
| group(by = b => b.author)
| filter(g => size(g.items) > 1)
| map(g => g.key)

{"Virginia Woolf"}

docs.title: Several answers in one pass
docs.text:
tee names a side branch of a pipeline. The branch reads the same rows, its result is bound to a name, and the main pipeline goes on unchanged. A branch of several steps continues on lines indented past the | before tee:

reading = shelf
| tee unread =
    filter(b => b.status == "todo")
    | size
| tee read =
    filter(b => b.status == "done")
    | size
| filter(b => b.status == "reading")
| map(title)
{unread: unread, read: read, reading: reading}

{read: 2, reading: ["Dune", "Mrs Dalloway"], unread: 3}

docs.title: From SQL to HQL
docs.text: SQL HQL SELECT title map(b => b.title) WHERE status = 'todo' filter(b => b.status == "todo") ORDER BY year sort(by = year) LIMIT 3 take(3) OFFSET 3 drop(3) SELECT DISTINCT genre map(b => b.genre) \| Set COUNT(*), SUM(pages) size, map(pages) \| sum GROUP BY genre group(by = b => b.genre) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 filter(g => size(g.items) > 1)

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: The shelf was written by hand. In chapter 21 the same books are documents in a vault, and the same questions are asked of the documents themselves.

docs.title: 7. Streams that do not end
docs.text: Every collection so far had an end: a size, a last element. A stream is a succession of values whose production need not end — a log, a feed, the natural numbers. HQL types the difference, so a program cannot ask an endless stream a question that needs its end.

docs.title: A function that yields
docs.text:
A fn whose body is a block, in braces, produces its values with yield, in the order each yield is reached. Its result type says whether production ends: Seq<T> promises an end, Stream<T> does not. These are the natural numbers:

fn naturals(from: Int) : Stream<Int> {
    yield from
    for n in naturals(from + 1) {
        yield n
    }
}
naturals(1) | take(5)

[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

for name in collection { … } runs its block once per value. A block that yields is an iterating block: it holds yield, for and bindings, one per line (function bodies).

Calling naturals(1) evaluates nothing. Its value is a recipe for the numbers, and take(5) asks for five of them and then stops asking — which is what makes an endless producer usable.

docs.title: One value at a time
docs.text:
map, filter and drop take a stream and give a stream. Each value passes through the whole pipeline before the next is produced, so only as many are made as the end of the pipeline asks for:

naturals(1)
| filter(n => n % 7 == 0)
| map(n => n * n)
| take(3)

[49, 196, 441]

docs.title: Questions that need the end
docs.text:
sum, size, sort, group and the other whole-input steps need the last value before they can answer. Over a stream there may be none, and the checker says so before anything runs:

fn naturals(from: Int) : Stream<Int> {
    yield from
    for n in naturals(from + 1) {
        yield n
    }
}
naturals(1) | sum

check error[type-mismatch]: `sum` needs a finite input, and Stream<Int> may not end; bound it first with `take(n)`, or batch it with `collect(n)`
 --> <expression>:7:15
  |
7 | naturals(1) | sum
  |               ^^^

A stream becomes finite through take(n), or is answered in pieces through collect(n), which gathers consecutive values into batches of n:

naturals(1)
| collect(3)
| map(batch => batch | sum)
| take(3)

[6, 15, 24]

emit is the inverse of collect: it passes on every member of every batch, in order. flat_map(f) is map(f) | emit.

[[1, 2], [3]] | emit

[1, 2, 3]

docs.title: A sequence over the shelf
docs.text:
A generator that promises an end is a Seq. This one yields the title of each book on the shelf of chapter 6, in title order — a sequence the shelf produces on demand:

shelf = [
    {title: "Frankenstein", pages: 280},
    {title: "Dune", pages: 412},
    {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310},
    {title: "Leaves of Grass", pages: 145},
    {title: "A Room of One's Own", pages: 112},
    {title: "The Common Reader", pages: 304},
    {title: "Mrs Dalloway", pages: 194},
]
fn title(b: Data) : String = match b.title { some(String t) => t, _ => "" }

fn titles() : Seq<String> {
    for b in shelf | sort(by = title) {
        yield title(b)
    }
}
titles() | take(3)

["A Room of One's Own", "Dune", "Frankenstein"]

A list is such a sequence already. So are the documents of a file read with source, in chapter 9, produced as each one is read.

docs.title: Writing a stream
docs.text:
Formatting an endless stream writes it piece by piece as it arrives: a line of text, a JSON value per line, a CSV row. hql flushes each piece, and a reader that stops reading ends the stream:

naturals(1) | map(n => n * n) | json

$ hql eval '…naturals… | map(n => n * n) | json' | head -3
1
4
9

A diagram format describes a whole, so | mermaid over a stream is a type error until take(n) bounds it.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 8 is about every format a value can be written in, and who chooses it.

docs.title: 8. Writing results out
docs.text:
A program's value is computed first, and written second. How it is written is a presentation format — plain text, HQL, Markdown, JSON, YAML, CSV, or a diagram — and each format is a value of type Format. A step that formats a value returns a String that also carries the format it was encoded in.

The programs of this chapter read the shelf of chapter 6, with its typed views, and the book shows these lines once:

shelf = [
    {title: "Frankenstein", author: "Mary Shelley", year: 1818, genre: "novel", pages: 280, status: "done"},
    {title: "Dune", author: "Frank Herbert", year: 1965, genre: "novel", pages: 412, status: "reading"},
    {title: "The Hobbit", author: "J. R. R. Tolkien", year: 1937, genre: "novel", pages: 310, status: "todo"},
    {title: "Leaves of Grass", author: "Walt Whitman", year: 1855, genre: "poetry", pages: 145, status: "todo"},
    {title: "A Room of One's Own", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1929, genre: "essay", pages: 112, status: "done"},
    {title: "The Common Reader", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1925, genre: "essay", pages: 304, status: "todo"},
    {title: "Mrs Dalloway", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1925, genre: "novel", pages: 194, status: "reading"},
]
fn title(b: Data) : String = match b.title { some(String t) => t, _ => "" }
fn pages(b: Data) : Int = match b.pages { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }

docs.title: Formats are a category of their own
docs.text:
Each format is a Format: Text, Lines, Hql, Markdown, Hmd, Json, JsonLines, Yaml, Csv, D2 and Mermaid. A format describes how values are written, not the text itself: a step named for a format encodes any value in it, and what comes out is a String:

shelf | filter(b => b.status == "todo") | map(title) | markdown

- The Hobbit
- Leaves of Grass
- The Common Reader

shelf | filter(b => b.status == "todo") | map(title) | markdown

String

A formatted value is a String that carries its format, and a host writes its text unchanged instead of encoding it again. A later step may read it, and comparing it with a string compares the text:

([1, 2] | json) == "[\n  1,\n  2\n]"

true

docs.title: The longhand, format
docs.text:
markdown is the shorthand for format(Markdown). The longhand takes two options. limit keeps the first n elements and says how many were cut:

shelf
| map(title)
| format(Text, limit = 3)

Frankenstein
Dune
The Hobbit
… 4 more not shown

A list of strings in text is one string per line.

A list of records in Markdown is a bullet list. A table is a value of its own type, Table: Table(xs, columns = [...]) takes one row per record and the columns in the order written, and every format writes it as a table, a pipe table in Markdown:

shelf
| map(b => {title: title(b), pages: pages(b)})
| Table(columns = ["title", "pages"])
| markdown

| title               | pages |
| ------------------- | ----- |
| Frankenstein        | 280   |
| Dune                | 412   |
| The Hobbit          | 310   |
| Leaves of Grass     | 145   |
| A Room of One's Own | 112   |
| The Common Reader   | 304   |
| Mrs Dalloway        | 194   |

The same table in Csv is a header row and one row per record, in Json an array of objects with their keys in column order, and in Text space-aligned columns. renderer names one of a format's encoders for a shape over the project's choice, format(Markdown, renderer = "mermaid") for a graph; a table renderer, such as pipe, writes only a Table.

A format that cannot write a value is a type error, reported before the program runs:

1 | d2

check error[type-mismatch]: no renderer writes Int as D2
 --> <expression>:1:5
  |
1 | 1 | d2
  |     ^^

docs.title: Choosing the format from outside
docs.text:
A program that does not format its result is written as HQL — the literal you would type to get the value back, a string in quotes. --to text writes a string bare instead, and --to names any other format without changing the program:

shelf | filter(b => b.status == "todo") | map(title)

- The Hobbit
- Leaves of Grass
- The Common Reader

--to none evaluates the program and writes nothing. --envelope json wraps the answer for another program to read: the type, the value, and every diagnostic the run wrote:

shelf | filter(b => b.status == "todo") | size

{
  "diagnostics": [],
  "origin": "<expression>",
  "type": "Int",
  "value": 3
}

The order is fixed: a format step in the program wins, then --to, then the host's own — Markdown for a document, HQL for a terminal.

docs.title: A project chooses its renderers
docs.text:
Which renderer writes a type in a format is a project's choice, in the .hql/config.toml of the vault a program runs in (chapter 21), over the built-in defaults. A graph in Markdown is a D2 diagram unless the file says otherwise:

[format.Graph]
markdown = "mermaid"

A renderer or format the binary does not have fails loading the vault, so the mistake is reported before any query runs.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Every value so far was written to the terminal. Chapter 9 reads files, standard input and the network, and writes files and standard output, without leaving the language.

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
An endpoint of bytes needs a format to make its bytes documents. A channel holds values instead. Channel<T>(name) is an endpoint of values of type T, held in memory for one evaluation. It keeps the values' type, so it takes no format. target writes one value to it, sink writes each value of a sequence, and source gives what it holds now:

c = Channel<Int>("nums")
1 | target(c)
[2, 3] | sink(c)
source(c)

[1, 2, 3]

Values are read in the order they were written. Reading does not consume: two reads give the same values.

c = Channel<Int>("n")
[1] | sink(c)
a = source(c)
b = source(c)
[size(a), size(b)]

[1, 1]

tap(c) gives only what is written after it, as a stream:

c = Channel<Int>("n")
[1] | sink(c)
t = tap(c)
[2] | sink(c)
t | take(5)

[2]

docs.title: The element type is checked
docs.text:
A channel's T is checked as any other type is, and a format beside a channel is a type error, since a channel holds values rather than bytes:

c = Channel<Int>("n")
"x" | target(c)

check error[type-mismatch]: Channel<Int> holds Int, not String
 --> <expression>:2:7
  |
2 | "x" | target(c)
  |       ^^^^^^^^^

c = Channel<Int>("n")
source(c, Json)

check error[type-mismatch]: a channel holds values, not bytes, so it takes no format
 --> <expression>:2:8
  |
2 | source(c, Json)
  |        ^

docs.title: One name, one channel
docs.text:
A channel lives for its execution scope: a program run, or one cell of a document. Within a scope one name is one channel, and constructing the same name with another element type is an evaluation failure naming both:

a = Channel<Int>("n")
b = Channel<String>("n")
1

execute failure[invalid-argument]: the channel "n" holds Int, so it is not also a Channel<String>
 --> <expression>:2:5
  |
2 | b = Channel<String>("n")
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A cell of a document being rendered may write a channel, because a channel stays inside the evaluation (effects and what a host allows). A channel of LogEvent values is how a program keeps its own logs as values.

docs.title: hql on the command line
docs.text:
With source and sink, hql is a structured-data tool for the shell. A first argument that names no command is a program, so hql '<program>' is hql eval '<program>', and hql -c '<program>' is the same, as -c is in Python and Bash. A first argument written as a file, report.hql or ./report, runs that file instead (scripts):

$ cat examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql 'source(stdin, Json) | filter(s => s.seen == "morning") | map(s => s.species)'
"wren"
"kingfisher"

The result is a Stream<String>, so the host writes each value as it arrives, in HQL, the format a result is written in unless --to names another (writing results out).

Options of hql come before the program. Every word after the program is the program's own, read with io.env.argv(), as the words after a Python or Bash script are (Scripts).

docs.title: --to and --compact
docs.text:
--to json presents each document of the result pretty-printed, as jq . does, and --compact gives one line each, as jq -c does:

$ head -1 examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql --to json 'source(stdin, Json)'
{
  "seen": "dusk",
  "site": "meadow",
  "species": "barn owl"
}

$ head -2 examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql --to json --compact 'source(stdin, Json)'
{"seen":"dusk","site":"meadow","species":"barn owl"}
{"seen":"morning","site":"hedge","species":"wren"}

Concatenated JSON values are what source(…, Json) reads, so the output of one hql is the input of the next. sink(e, Json) writes one document per line whatever the flags: a program writing a file says what the file is, and --compact is about the terminal.

Converting between formats is a source and a --to:

$ hql --to yaml 'source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | map(s => s.site)'
- meadow
- hedge
- barn
- river

docs.title: --from
docs.text:
--from names the format of standard input once, on the command line, so the program reads stdin without naming one; a format the program names wins:

$ cat examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql --from json 'source(stdin) | map(s => s.site)'
"meadow"
"hedge"
"barn"
"river"

docs.title: Input and output stay in the program
docs.text:
The command line names no input and no output of a program's own. Input is source or tap in the program, output is target or sink in the program, and --to only chooses how the host writes the final result. A program whose result is Step prints nothing:

$ cat examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql 'source(stdin, Json) | filter(s => s.seen == "morning") | map(s => s.species) | sink(stdout, Text)'
wren
kingfisher

hql run - reads the program from standard input, so such a program cannot also read stdin as data, and source(stdin, …) in it is a type error. hql with no program does the same when standard input is not a terminal, and opens the REPL when it is:

$ echo '1 + 1' | hql
2

--log-level sets every logger's threshold (logging).

docs.title: A program in a file
docs.text: hql FILE runs a file, the same as hql run FILE, when the word ends in .hql or contains a /. A file whose first line is #!/usr/bin/env hql runs on its own, and the exit status follows from its result. scripts covers arguments, the exit status, and where a script's relative paths resolve.

docs.title: Endpoints by id
docs.text:
A program that names a file path is tied to one machine's files. A vault declares its endpoints in .hql/config.toml instead, each under an id, and a program names only the id. The field station of the endpoints examples is such a vault, and the programs on this page run with --vault examples/endpoints/station:

[endpoint.journal]
kind = "vault"
root = "journal"

[endpoint.counts]
kind = "csv"
path = "data/counts.csv"

[endpoint.sightings]
kind = "json"
path = "data/sightings.json"

journal = source("journal")
journal.cards | map(c => c.name)

["kite", "owl", "wren"]

A vault is a folder of documents, each a card with a name, the subject of chapter 21; journal.cards is the cards of that one. Here it is one endpoint among others, read by its id like the rest.

docs.title: The kind states the type
docs.text:
source("journal") is a Vault, with its own cards. source("counts") is a Seq<Data>, a row per element, and a json endpoint is the elements of its file's one array:

source("counts")

[{count: "2", species: "wren"}, {count: "1", species: "owl"}, {count: "1", species: "kite"}]

source("sightings") | map(s => s.species)

["wren", "owl", "kite"]

The kinds are vault, csv, json, json_lines, yaml, sqlite, one table of a database file, postgres, one table of a PostgreSQL database, kafka, one Kafka topic, nats, one core NATS subject, nats_jetstream, one subject of a NATS JetStream stream, and spark, one table of a lakehouse. postgres and kafka are the subject of topics and tables, and nats, nats_jetstream and spark of subjects and lakehouse tables. A path resolves against the directory of .hql/config.toml. The type comes from the configuration, so checking a program reads .hql/config.toml and opens nothing else.

An endpoint read as a declared record decodes each element as the record, as a file does, and tap("id") gives a finite endpoint one element at a time, as a Stream:

type Tally {
    species : String
    count   : Int
}

tallies : Seq<Tally> = source("counts")
tallies | map(t => t.count) | sum

4

docs.title: The id is a literal
docs.text:
The type an endpoint is read as is known only from its configuration, so the id is written in the program as a literal, and a connection string is not an id:

id = "counts"
source(id)

check error[type-mismatch]: `source` names a configured endpoint by a literal id, `source("field_notes")`: a computed id would leave its type unknown until evaluation
 --> <expression>:2:8
  |
2 | source(id)
  |        ^^

source("postgres://db/birds")

check error[type-mismatch]: "postgres://db/birds" is not an endpoint id: connection details belong in configuration, `[endpoint.<id>]` in .hql/config.toml, and a program names the id
 --> <expression>:1:8
  |
1 | source("postgres://db/birds")
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

An id the configuration does not declare is a name error that names the nearest one:

source("count")

check error[unknown-name]: no endpoint `count` is configured; did you mean `counts`?
 --> <expression>:1:8
  |
1 | source("count")
  |        ^^^^^^^

docs.title: The schema boundary
docs.text:
The names and types an external system uses are facts about that system, not about the program's types, so they are configured beside the endpoint. The station's ledger is a CSV whose headers are Species Name, Total and Observer. [endpoint.<id>.fields.<field>] maps a field of the record a program reads to its external field, by name for a column or a key, and by a dotted path for a key below the top level of a JSON or YAML document:

[endpoint.ledger]
kind = "csv"
path = "data/ledger.csv"

[endpoint.ledger.fields.species]
name = "Species Name"

[endpoint.ledger.fields.count]
name = "Total"

[endpoint.profiles]
kind = "json"
path = "data/profiles.json"

[endpoint.profiles.fields.id]
name = "user_id"

[endpoint.profiles.fields.name]
path = "profile.display_name"

type Profile {
    id   : String
    name : String
}

profiles : Seq<Profile> = source("profiles")
profiles | map(p => p.name)

["Ada", "Grace"]

A field's table also takes type, the external type where the format's default is not it; absent, the external values read as an absent optional field, an empty cell in CSV unless written; and write = false for a field a write leaves out.

strictness says what a read does with an external field no field of the record reads. It is compatible unless written: the field is passed to the type, so a closed record does not decode a ledger with an Observer column. Under open the field is not read, under warn it is not read and is reported, and under strict it is an error:

type Tally {
    species : String
    count   : Int
}

tallies : Seq<Tally> = source("ledger")
tallies | map(t => t.count) | sum

execute failure[io-failure]: endpoint `ledger`: document 1 does not decode as Tally: field `Observer`: Tally declares no such field
 --> <expression>:6:24
  |
6 | tallies : Seq<Tally> = source("ledger")
  |                        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

[endpoint.ledger_open]
kind = "csv"
path = "data/ledger.csv"
strictness = "open"

[endpoint.ledger_open.fields.species]
name = "Species Name"

[endpoint.ledger_open.fields.count]
name = "Total"

type Tally {
    species : String
    count   : Int
}

tallies : Seq<Tally> = source("ledger_open")
tallies | map(t => t.count) | sum

4

hql boundary <file> <id> --as <Type> prints an endpoint's effective boundary, each property with the layer it comes from, the format's default or the configuration:

$ hql --vault examples/endpoints/station boundary tally.hql ledger --as Tally
endpoint ledger (csv), read as Tally; strictness compatible, mode replace
species : String
  external Species Name    configuration
  type     text            format
  position 1               format
  read     true            format
  write    true            format
  absent   empty, missing  format
count : Int
  external Total           configuration
  type     text            format
  position 2               format
  read     true            format
  write    true            format
  absent   empty, missing  format

docs.title: Writing by id
docs.text:
A configured endpoint is written by its id as well. xs | target("id") writes a Table<R>, or a List<R> or Seq<R>, of a declared record R through the same boundary: each field under its external name, in position order, a field with write = false left out. The kind fixes the format, so a format beside the id is a type error, and a vault is read and never written:

type Tally {
    species : String
    count   : Int
}

tallies : Seq<Tally> = source("counts")
tallies | filter(t => t.count > 1) | target("counts")

Step

source("counts") | target("counts")

check error[type-mismatch]: `target("counts")` writes rows of a declared record, and Data is not one
 --> <expression>:1:20
  |
1 | source("counts") | target("counts")
  |                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

source("counts") | target("counts", Csv)

check error[type-mismatch]: a configured endpoint's format is its kind's, set in its configuration; name none
 --> <expression>:1:20
  |
1 | source("counts") | target("counts", Csv)
  |                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The endpoint's table takes mode, how a write treats what the endpoint already holds. It is replace unless written:

mode A file A SQLite table create written where none exists; an existing file is an evaluation failure created where none exists; an existing table is an evaluation failure append the rows or documents added after the ones held; created where none exists rows inserted; the table created where none exists replace rewritten whole dropped and created again with the rows written

Reading an endpoint the same evaluation has replaced is an evaluation failure, as for a file, and a document being rendered writes nothing (effects and what a host allows).

docs.title: Topics and tables
docs.text:
A postgres endpoint is one table of a PostgreSQL database, and a kafka endpoint is one Kafka topic. The connection string of a database may hold a password, so the configuration names the environment variable that holds it, dsn_env; a topic's brokers are written as brokers or named the same way by brokers_env:

[endpoint.orders]
kind = "postgres"
dsn_env = "DEMO_DSN"
table = "orders"
order = ["id"]

[endpoint.events]
kind = "kafka"
brokers_env = "KAFKA_BROKERS"
topic = "events"
idle_ms = 2000

Checking a program reads this configuration and connects to neither system. The variables are read, and the connections made, when an endpoint is read or written.

A table ends. source("orders") is a Seq of rows, read through the schema boundary as a sqlite table is: the columns are compared with the record before any row is decoded, and only the columns the record reads are selected. A numeric column reads as a Decimal with its digits, a jsonb column as the tree it holds, and a NULL as an absent field:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

events : Seq<Event> = source("orders")
events
| filter(e => e.kind == "order_placed")
| group(by = e => e.customer)
| map(g => {customer: g.key, total: g.items | map(e => e.amount) | sum})

{{customer: "ada", total: 135.75}, {customer: "grace", total: 42.00}, {customer: "linus", total: 7.99}}

target("orders") writes a Seq or a Table of a declared record in one transaction. A table that does not exist is created, a column per field: BIGINT for an Int, DOUBLE PRECISION for a Float, NUMERIC for a Decimal, BOOLEAN for a Bool, JSONB for a list or a record, and TEXT otherwise. Under mode = "replace" the rows the table holds are removed and its definition, indexes and grants are kept.

A topic does not end. tap("events") is a Stream, one JSON document per message, decoded as the element type. source("events") is a type error, since a Seq is a value that ends:

source("events")

check error[type-mismatch]: `events` is a `kafka` endpoint, read by `tap` as a `Stream`, not by `source` as a `Seq`
 --> <expression>:1:8
  |
1 | source("events")
  |        ^^^^^^^^

The stream starts at the earliest message the topic keeps, or at the next one under from = "latest". Without idle_ms it waits for messages without end; with it, the stream ends once no message has arrived for that many milliseconds.

sink writes as values arrive. sink("events") writes each value as one message, and sink("orders") each row as it arrives, committed one at a time. A stream has no last value for target to wait for, so moving a topic into a table is a tap and a sink:

events : Stream<Event> = tap("events")
events | sink("orders")

and moving a table into a topic is a source and a sink:

orders : Seq<Event> = source("orders")
orders | sink("events")

sink takes no format beside an id, and writes to a kafka, nats, nats_jetstream, postgres or spark endpoint only; a file or an SQLite table is written whole by target. A NATS subject and a lakehouse table take the places of the topic and the table on the next page.

docs.title: Files and Standard Endpoints
docs.text:
An endpoint states where bytes are. Constructing one performs no I/O: it opens, stats and resolves nothing, and prints as it was written:

file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")

file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")

Four endpoints are bound by the host, as vault is, and need no configuration: stdin, stdout, stderr and file(path).

docs.title: What an endpoint can do is its type
docs.text:
An endpoint's capabilities are its supertypes. A Readable endpoint is read by source and tap, a Writable one is written by target and sink, and a Replayable endpoint is a Readable one that gives the same bytes on every read within one evaluation. Stdin is Readable, Stdout and Stderr are Writable, and File is Replayable and Writable. Reading an endpoint that is not readable is a type error, reported before the program runs:

source(stdout, Json)

check error[type-mismatch]: `source` needs (Readable | String), not Stdout
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | source(stdout, Json)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The String in the diagnostic is the other form of source, a configured endpoint named by its id (endpoints by id).

docs.title: A file and its end
docs.text:
file(p) is the whole file. file(p).end is a second endpoint, the end of the same file: Readable and Writable, and not Replayable, since what comes after the end is not there yet. Which endpoint a step names decides what the step does, so a file has no open mode:

file(p) file(p).end source every document in the file, as a Seq a type error naming tap tap the documents one at a time, then it ends the documents appended from now on, as tail -f gives them target, sink replace the file append to the file 
source(file("app.log").end, Lines)

check error[type-mismatch]: the end of a file holds nothing yet; follow what is appended there with `tap`
 --> <expression>:1:8
  |
1 | source(file("app.log").end, Lines)
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Where a relative path resolves
docs.text:
A relative path resolves against the source directory of the unit that names it: the document for hql render, the program file for hql run, the module's own directory for a function of a module, and the working directory for hql eval and the REPL, which have no file. A document, program or module reads the same file wherever it is run from or called from. The programs in this chapter run from the repository root, so examples/io/sightings.jsonl is the file in the I/O examples.

The working directory, the directory hql was started in, resolves no path in HQL source. io.fs reads both, as Path values a program composes paths from explicitly:

import io.fs
fs.source_dir().join("data/users.csv")     // beside this file
fs.working_dir().join("out.csv")           // where hql was started

A path with a scheme is a type error naming the network endpoint, since a URL is not a file:

file("https://example.com/x.json")

check error[type-mismatch]: "https://example.com/x.json" is a URL, not a file; a network resource is read with `http`
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | file("https://example.com/x.json")
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The network adds http, websocket and tcp with import net, and a channel is an endpoint of values rather than bytes.

docs.title: Environment and arguments
docs.text: The io.env module reads the invocation that runs a program: its environment variables, its named arguments, the --arg name=value pairs of the command line, and its positional arguments, the words after the program. A program imports it, import io.env, and reaches it as env: env.arg(…). from io.env import * binds arg and the rest without the module's name. Each operation reads a value fixed for the whole evaluation, so a program that reads the same name twice reads the same value.

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
env.arg(name) is the value of the invocation's --arg name=value, an Option<String>: some of the text, or none where no --arg names it. This program runs as hql --arg species=wren eval '…':

import io.env

[env.arg("species"), env.arg("limit")]

["wren", none]

env.args() is every pair of the invocation, a Map<String, String> by name:

import io.env

env.args()

Map {"limit": "20", "species": "wren"}

A name is a lowercase letter or _, then lowercase letters, digits and _; the value is the text after the first =, and may be empty. A malformed name and a name given twice are invocation errors, reported before evaluation starts:

$ hql --arg species=wren --arg species=owl eval '1'
error: --arg species is given twice: each argument is named once

Usage: hql [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>

For more information, try '--help'.

docs.title: Positional arguments
docs.text:
env.argv() is every word after the program, in order, a Seq<String>. This program runs as hql -c '…' 2026 q1:

import io.env

env.argv()

["2026", "q1"]

The words come after a program file, hql report.hql 2026 q1, and after an inline program, hql -c '…' 2026 q1. The program's own path is not among them. scripts puts them to work in a script.

docs.title: Missing values and conversion
docs.text:
An argument the invocation does not pass is none, and the program supplies its default:

import io.env

env.arg("species") | unwrap_or("owl")

"owl"

An argument is text. A program converts it as it converts any text. to_int is none for text that is not an integer, and and_then passes that none on, so one default covers both a missing argument and a malformed one:

import io.env

limit = env.arg("limit") | and_then(s => s.to_int()) | unwrap_or(10)
limit * 2

40

import io.env

env.arg("limit") | and_then(s => s.to_int()) | unwrap_or(10)

10

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
env.var(name) is the value of the environment variable name, an Option<String>, and env.vars() is every variable the program may read, a Map<String, String> by name. A variable that is unset reads as none:

import io.env

env.var("HQL_BOOK_NEVER_SET") | unwrap_or("anonymous")

"anonymous"

env.vars() | get(name) is the same lookup in the map. A variable whose value is not UTF-8 reads as none too, and is absent from vars().

io.env is not in the prelude. Without the import, var is an unknown name, reported before the program runs:

var("HOME")

check error[unknown-name]: `var` is declared in the module `io.env`: write `from io.env import var`
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | var("HOME")
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: What a host grants
docs.text:
Every operation of io.env is effectful, and hql check reports a function that uses one:

import io.env

fn limit() : Int = env.arg("limit") | and_then(s => s.to_int()) | unwrap_or(10)
limit()

limit is Effectful: it uses `arg`
Int

Named and positional arguments are always granted: the invocation wrote them. The environment is read through a grant the host fixes before evaluation:

Host Variables granted hql eval, hql run, hql repl every variable, or the names env = [...] lists in the project's .hql/config.toml hql render none

In .hql/config.toml, env is a list of names and PREFIX_* patterns, a * matching any suffix:

env = ["SHOP_*"]

A variable outside the grant reads as none. A withheld variable and an unset one are indistinguishable, so a program cannot tell which names exist beyond its grant. In that project, with SHOP_REGION set:

$ cat region.hql
import io.env

[env.var("SHOP_REGION"), env.var("HOME")]

$ SHOP_REGION=eu hql run region.hql
["eu", none]

A rendered document reads no variable, so its output depends on nothing in the renderer's environment and discloses nothing of it. It reads its arguments as any program does (effects and what a host allows):

# Notes

```hql
import io.env
[env.var("SHOP_REGION"), env.arg("who")]
```

$ SHOP_REGION=eu hql --arg who=owl render notes.hmd
# Notes

- none
- owl

The reference states each operation of io.env.

docs.title: Files and folders
docs.text:
A file(p) endpoint names one file by a path written in the program. The io.fs module lists what a folder holds, so a program finds its files first and then reads them. A program imports it, import io.fs, and reaches it as fs, or binds its functions, from io.fs import *.

The programs on this page list a small tree in the file-system examples:

examples/fs/tree/
  assets/logo.txt        5 bytes
  assets/style.css      19 bytes
  data/2026/q1.csv      21 bytes
  data/2026-notes.md    17 bytes
  data/birds.csv        28 bytes

docs.title: A path
docs.text:
A Path is a place in a file system, written as text: segments separated by /. It is part of io, so it needs no import. Its operations read the text and never the file system, so they are pure:

p = Path("examples/fs/tree").join("data").join("birds.csv")
[p.text, p.name(), p.stem(), p.extension() | unwrap_or("?"), p.parent() | map(q => q.text) | unwrap_or("?")]

["examples/fs/tree/data/birds.csv", "birds.csv", "birds", "csv", "examples/fs/tree/data"]

parent() is none for a path of one segment, and extension() is none for a last segment with no .:

Path("data").parent()

none

Paths are ordered by their segments, compared in turn, each by its text. 2026/q1.csv sorts before 2026-notes.md, although - sorts before / as text, since the first segments 2026 and 2026-notes.md already differ:

[Path("data/2026-notes.md"), Path("data/2026/q1.csv")] | sort | map(p => p.text)

["data/2026/q1.csv", "data/2026-notes.md"]

This is the order of a sorted walk, and every listing below gives it.

docs.title: A folder
docs.text:
folder(path) is the Folder at a path, a String or a Path. A folder is an endpoint that holds files and folders, as a database holds tables. Constructing one opens, stats and resolves nothing, and a relative path resolves as a file's does (where a relative path resolves):

from io.fs import *

folder("examples/fs/tree")

Folder(path = Path(text = "examples/fs/tree"))

io.fs is not in the prelude. Without the import, folder is an unknown name, reported before the program runs:

folder("examples/fs/tree")

check error[unknown-name]: `folder` is declared in the module `io.fs`: write `from io.fs import folder`
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | folder("examples/fs/tree")
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A folder is not a Seq itself. Three effectful steps list it, each reading the file system once, where it is written, and each giving a Seq<Entry>. entries gives what is directly in the folder, sorted by name, an entry whose name opens with . included:

from io.fs import *

folder("examples/fs/tree/data") | entries | map(e => [e.name, e.kind])

[["2026", "folder"], ["2026-notes.md", "file"], ["birds.csv", "file"]]

walk gives every entry below the folder, the folder itself excluded: depth first, each folder's entries sorted by name, and each folder followed at once by what it holds:

from io.fs import *

folder("examples/fs/tree") | walk | map(e => e.path.text.trim_prefix("examples/fs/tree/"))

["assets", "assets/logo.txt", "assets/style.css", "data", "data/2026", "data/2026/q1.csv", "data/2026-notes.md", "data/birds.csv"]

The order is never the file system's: the same tree walks the same way on every machine. It is also the order a vault reads its cards in; the vault skips entries whose name opens with ., and walk lists them.

docs.title: An entry
docs.text:
An Entry is one thing a folder holds. It has five fields:

Field Type What it holds path Path the listed folder's path joined with the entry's path below it name String the last segment kind String "file", "folder" or "link" size Int, optional a file's length in bytes; absent for a folder or a link modified Instant, optional the time the entry was last modified, a link's own and not its target's; absent where the platform records none 
from io.fs import *

folder("examples/fs/tree")
| walk
| filter(e => e.name == "birds.csv")
| map(e => [e.path.text, e.kind, str(e.size)])

[["examples/fs/tree/data/birds.csv", "file", "28"]]

modified is an Instant, so it compares with an instant the program writes and sorts the entries by time. A listing reads it once, with the rest of the entry, so the files changed since a cut-off are a filter over it:

from io.fs import *

cutoff = Instant("2020-01-01T00:00:00Z")
folder("examples/fs/tree/data")
| entries
| filter(e => e.modified | map(t => t >= cutoff) | unwrap_or(false))
| map(e => e.name)

["2026", "2026-notes.md", "birds.csv"]

The times themselves are the file system's, so they differ from one checkout of a tree to the next; a program that must give the same answer on every machine does not read them.

size is optional, so a sum over it states what a folder counts as:

from io.fs import *

folder("examples/fs/tree")
| walk
| filter(e => e.kind == "file")
| map(e => e.size | unwrap_or(0))
| sum

90

A link is reported with the kind "link" and not followed.

docs.title: A glob
docs.text:
A Glob is a pattern over paths, matched against a path relative to the folder it is applied to. * matches within one segment, ** any number of whole segments, none included, ? one character other than /, [abc] one character of the set and [a-z] one of the range. matches reads the text and never the file system:

from io.fs import *

[
    Glob("data/*.csv").matches(Path("data/birds.csv")),
    Glob("data/*.csv").matches(Path("data/2026/q1.csv")),
    Glob("data/**/*.csv").matches(Path("data/2026/q1.csv")),
]

[true, false, true]

The glob step gives the entries of walk whose path below the folder matches, in walk order:

from io.fs import *

folder("examples/fs/tree") | glob(Glob("**/*.csv")) | map(e => e.path.text)

["examples/fs/tree/data/2026/q1.csv", "examples/fs/tree/data/birds.csv"]

A pattern that does not parse, an unclosed [ or a ** that is not a whole segment, is an evaluation error where Glob constructs it:

from io.fs import *

Glob("data/a**.csv")

execute failure[invalid-argument]: "data/a**.csv" is not a glob: `**` stands for whole segments, alone between `/`
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | Glob("data/a**.csv")
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Reading what was found
docs.text:
An entry's path is one file reads as written, so a listing feeds source (reading with source). Every row of every CSV file directly in data/:

from io.fs import *

folder("examples/fs/tree/data")
| glob(Glob("*.csv"))
| flat_map(e => source(file(e.path), Csv))

[{count: "2", species: "heron"}, {count: "1", species: "owl"}]

docs.title: A path that may not be there
docs.text:
Listing a folder that does not exist, or is not a folder, is an evaluation error naming its path:

from io.fs import *

folder("examples/fs/nowhere") | entries

execute failure[io-failure]: examples/fs/nowhere: no folder is there
 --> <expression>:3:33
  |
3 | folder("examples/fs/nowhere") | entries
  |                                 ^^^^^^^

exists and entry test a path without an error. exists is false where nothing is there, and entry is some(Entry) or none:

import io.fs

[
    str(Path("examples/fs/tree/data").exists()),
    str(Path("examples/fs/tree/missing").exists()),
    Path("examples/fs/tree/data").entry() | map(e => e.kind) | unwrap_or("?"),
    str(Path("examples/fs/tree/missing.csv").entry()),
]

["true", "false", "folder", "none"]

docs.title: What a host grants
docs.text:
entries, walk, glob, exists and entry are effectful, and hql check reports a function that uses one:

from io.fs import *

fn csv_files() : Seq<Entry> = folder("examples/fs/tree") | glob(Glob("**/*.csv"))
csv_files() | size

csv_files is Effectful: it uses `glob`
Int

A listing is granted exactly where reading a file at the same path is (effects and what a host allows): anywhere under hql eval, hql run and the REPL, and under hql render only below the document's own directory. The reference states each operation of io.fs.

docs.title: Finite or live
docs.text:
A file is replayable, so reading it gives a Seq: the documents end, and every step in the book applies. Standard input arrives once, as it is written, so reading it gives a Stream. hql check prints each type:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))

Seq<Data>

source(stdin, Json)

Stream<Data>

That is the difference the streams chapter drew. map, filter and take run over standard input one document at a time, as it arrives. A step that needs the whole input is a type error until the stream is bounded with take(n) or batched with collect(n):

source(stdin, Json) | size

check error[type-mismatch]: `size` needs a finite input, and Stream<Data> may not end; bound it first with `take(n)`, or batch it with `collect(n)`
 --> <expression>:1:23
  |
1 | source(stdin, Json) | size
