Data Factory wires activities in JSON, PySpark in a DataFrame API, ksqlDB in SQL over topics, Kafka Streams in Java, dbt in SQL models with a dependency graph around them. Each describes the same four things: where data comes from, what is done to it, where it goes, and when. They differ in where a mistake is found: in a validator before deployment, in a cluster at run time, or in a dashboard the next morning.

HQL's claim is that the wiring is a program like any other in this book. A pipeline is one .hql file. What it reads and writes are endpoint ids that configuration binds to systems. Its types are checked before anything connects. And the same text runs over a subject that never ends and over the archive of what the subject once carried.

Part I was about the steps: what each one takes, what it gives, and the type that joins them. This part is about the pipeline the steps form, and the systems a pipeline connects. This chapter is the frame: what a pipeline is, when it is checked, what a step may and may not do, and what stays outside the file. The five after it follow one shop's orders through every kind of system a pipeline reaches, and chapters 19 and 20 are the shop's two sides, the transactions as they happen and the history they leave.

docs.title: A pipeline language
docs.text:
An HQL program is values flowing through typed steps. | is the operator that forms a step: the value on its left becomes the input of the operation on its right, and the result is the input of the next. A step invokes exactly one operation, filter, sort, map, or one presentation, json, markdown:

[3, 1, 2] | filter(n => n > 1) | sort | map(n => n * 10)

[20, 30]

A dot selects a field or calls a function on a value. s.trim() is a receiver call, and b.title a field read. Inside a pipeline step, these expressions compute the values that its operation uses:

["Dune ", " Emma"] | map(s => s.trim().upper())

["DUNE", "EMMA"]

The pipes describe the logical steps and their data dependencies. The dots express computations within those steps. A planner uses that checked program to choose physical execution stages; several steps may share a stage. The companion Logical steps and physical plans follows this distinction through local, parallel and SQL execution.

docs.title: Three phases
docs.text:
A program is parsed, then checked, then executed, and a diagnostic is headed by the phase that wrote it: parse failure and check error before anything runs, execute failure after (chapter 12). Checking resolves every name, import and module, infers and checks every type, and verifies every trait implementation; a program the checker rejects has no meaning, and no step of it executes. hql check runs the first two phases alone and prints the type the third would produce:

[3, 1, 2] | filter(n => n > 1) | sort | map(n => n * 10)

List<Int>

Execution is a strategy a backend chooses. localhost, the one backend the current release has, evaluates the checked program in process. Finite collections pass through each step in turn; streams produce values on demand. A future backend that compiles a program or runs it over many machines receives the same checked program. For the work it supports, it must compute the value localhost computes, at the same type, with the same failure where localhost fails. Unsupported work is a planning refusal before execution. Backend selection belongs to configuration, and hql config reports it.

docs.title: Logical steps and effects
docs.text:
A step is a logical unit of computation, established before planning. Its operation defines the transformation from input to result. Physical planning chooses how to perform that transformation, subject to its data dependencies, shape and effects.

An effectful operation interacts with state outside the evaluation: source reads, target and sink write, and a logger's info emits a record. Planning preserves the order of effects that the program orders and the scope of each transaction. Repeating an effect requires a delivery or transaction guarantee that permits the repeat. A backend that cannot honor the program's contract refuses it before execution.

A pure step may be rewritten as its shape and dependencies permit, while preserving results, sequence order and failures. A step that processes each value alone, filter, map, may run over separate parts of the input; a step such as sort, group, sum or size needs coordination to produce its complete result. The reading list of chapter 21 has three steps: filter tests each card, sort orders the retained cards, and map turns each card into its title. MapReduce is one possible execution strategy for suitable steps: work on parts, then combine the results. The planner chooses traversals and intermediate storage while preserving the pipeline's result. collect(n) and emit change the shape of what flows, batches of values or their members, and tee branches a pipeline without ending it; each of them is a step like any other, and the type says what the next step may ask.

docs.title: The command line
docs.text: The smallest pipeline is a shell pipe. hql '<program>' reads standard input with source(stdin, Json), writes its result as jq or awk would, and names no input or output of its own: input is source or tap in the program, output is target or sink in the program, or the result, presented by --to. The command-line page of chapter 9 shows each flag; one program there reads a log as it is written, appends its errors to a file and prints every message, with no orchestration around it. The shell connects the processes, and each hql process evaluates its program with the localhost backend.

docs.title: Streaming and batching
docs.text:
A platform's second vocabulary is about how a pipeline runs. A batch job reads an input that is all there, computes over the whole of it, and writes a result; it ends. A streaming job reads values as they arrive, computes over each, and writes as it goes; it does not end. The same transformation is often wanted both ways, and most platforms have two engines, two APIs or two deployment modes for it.

In HQL the difference is the type of the input, and the four steps of chapter 9 carry it. source gives a Seq, which ends; tap gives a Stream, which may not. target writes one completed value; sink writes each value as it arrives. A transformation written over a Seq is a batch job, and over a Stream the same text is a streaming job, and the checker says which steps each allows. The revenue of the shop's orders, over a table that ends:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

orders : Seq<Event> = source("ledger")
orders | filter(o => o.kind == "order_placed") | map(o => o.amount) | sum

185.74

and over a topic that does not:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

events : Stream<Event> = tap("order_events")
events | filter(o => o.kind == "order_placed") | map(o => o.amount) | sum

check error[type-mismatch]: `sum` needs a finite input, and Stream<Decimal> may not end; bound it first with `take(n)`, or batch it with `collect(n)`
  --> <expression>:10:71
   |
10 | events | filter(o => o.kind == "order_placed") | map(o => o.amount) | sum
   |                                                                       ^^^

A sum over a stream has no moment to be complete, so it is refused before the program runs, and the error names the two ways out. take(n) bounds the stream and makes a batch of its first n values. collect(n) keeps the stream and makes it a stream of batches, which is the micro-batch of Spark Structured Streaming: inside each batch every whole-input step applies, and the result is one value per batch, written as each closes:

events : Stream<Event> = tap("events")
events
| collect(4)
| map(batch => batch | filter(o => o.kind == "order_placed") | map(o => o.amount) | sum)
| sink(stdout, Json)

170.49
15.25

tap over the events file gives the six orders as a stream that ends after the last, so this program is the streaming job run against recorded input. That is the other half of the rule: an input that ends can be read either way, source as a batch or tap as a stream, and a program written for the stream is tested over a file and replayed over an archive with no change but the id it reads, which chapter 19 relies on.

The two vocabularies are independent. Streaming and batching say how a pipeline runs, one value at a time or all of them at once. OLTP and OLAP, chapters 19 and 20, say what the data is for, the transactions as they happen or the history they leave. A transactional pipeline is usually streaming and an analytical one usually batch, and the exceptions are everyday: an analytical table filled as events arrive, a transactional table backfilled from an archive. The types let a program say which it is without the platform having a word for the combination.

docs.title: The shop
docs.text:
A small shop sells to three customers, ada, grace and linus. Each thing that happens to an order is an event: placed, shipped, or a payment that failed. On the first day the events are one JSON file, and the shop's whole data platform is a pipeline over it:

source("events")
| filter(e => e.kind == "order_placed")
| map(e => e.customer)
| distinct

["ada", "grace", "linus"]

source("events") names no file. The shop's .hql/config.toml, in examples/pipelines/shop/, declares events as a json endpoint, and the program names the id. That one indirection is what lets the rest of Part II happen without the program changing shape: as the shop grows, the events move into a table, then onto a topic, then onto a subject a stream keeps, then into a lakehouse, and at each move the configuration names the new system and the pipeline keeps its steps.

Chapter The shop's events are in Read by Written by 15. Endpoints anywhere: the model every system shares source, tap target, sink 16. Tables and topics a SQLite table, a PostgreSQL table, a Kafka topic source for a table, tap for a topic target, sink 17. Subjects and the lakehouse NATS subjects, a JetStream stream, Delta tables tap for a subject, source for a table sink, target 18. APIs, webhooks and stores a REST API, a webhook, an object store, as design source, tap target, sink 19. OLTP the transactions as they happen, all of the above in one file tap sink 20. OLAP the history they leave: bronze, silver and gold tables source target

Every system in chapters 16, 17, 19 and 20 is in the current release. The programs that reach a server are checked in this book, against the shop's configuration and with no connection made, and run against real servers in the hql-demo repository, whose output is the output the book shows. A checked program is shown with what hql check prints, the type its result would have, and a pipeline that ends in target or sink has the type Step: its result is nothing, because its work is the writing.

A job is one run of a program's plan. An .hql file defines the program; each invocation starts another run, which may include several pipelines. Its steps describe transformations, reads and writes. Configuration names the environment variables that supply credentials and selects the backend. The schedule determines when the program runs. hql check reads the configuration without connecting to endpoints, so a deployment can check the program before running it.

A job's own settings, the customer a report is for or the day it covers, come from the invocation that runs it. hql --arg customer=ada run report.hql passes one, and the program reads it with env.arg from import io.env, as text, with a default where it is not passed (environment and arguments):

import io.env

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

customer = env.arg("customer") | unwrap_or("grace")
orders : Seq<Event> = source("ledger")
orders
| filter(o => o.kind == "order_placed" and o.customer == customer)
| map(o => o.amount)
| sum

135.75

docs.title: Partitions, schedules and backends
docs.text:
The program can declare logical partitioning. Scheduling and backend selection are configuration around it.

A partition is the logical unit of ownership. partition(by = e => e.customer) is in the current release: it states that the orders of one customer belong together, keeps every value and its type, and on localhost changes nothing else. It names no worker and no Kafka partition. A backend reads it as the statement that a per-customer group may run on separate parts without the parts having to meet.

Design only

The rest of this section describes functionality that is not in the current release. The configuration examples illustrate design direction; names and keys may change before it ships.

A schedule is configuration beside the endpoints, [jobs.report] run = "report.hql" with an at, or a trigger that is itself a source: a subject whose messages each start a run. The program declares no schedule; when it runs is configuration.

A backend supplies an execution strategy for the checked program. Future backends could use parallel workers in one process, translate a supported computation into SQL, or distribute it across a cluster. Each must preserve the result, types, sequence order, failures and effects of local evaluation. The companion Logical steps and physical plans explains the planning handoff, including Spark SQL and CTEs on Databricks.

[execution]
backend = "spark"

This illustrates future execution configuration. The spark endpoint kind in chapter 17 already identifies a table the program reads and writes. Backend selection would additionally choose where pipeline computation runs, while keeping the checked program's meaning.

docs.title: What each of them wires
docs.text:
Sources and sinks Transformations Where a mistake is found Data Factory linked services and datasets, in JSON activities, each a box at validation of the JSON, or in the run's monitor PySpark readers and writers, in code DataFrame operations when the job runs, at the operation that fails ksqlDB topics as streams and tables SQL over them when the statement is submitted, or in the records it skips dbt models over a warehouse SQL, with tests after when the model builds, or when its tests run HQL ids bound in .hql/config.toml the steps of this book when the file is checked, before anything connects

The columns are the same four things. What HQL adds is a type for each arrow: stream against table, finite against live, a declared record against a configured boundary, a contract against what a producer actually sent, each checked where the file is written, so that the file that passed is the file that runs.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 15 looks at what "events" names: an endpoint, the one model behind a file, a table, a topic and a webhook.

docs.title: Logical steps and physical plans
docs.text:
An HQL program describes a computation before choosing how to execute it. Its types, operations, data dependencies and ordered effects form the logical program. Planning turns that checked program into work for a particular backend. The physical plan describes how that work will run: which operations share a traversal, where data moves, and which work can run in parallel.

The same HQL expression should be able to run locally, be pushed down into SQL, or become a distributed Spark plan while keeping the meaning of |. This is the design contract for alternative backends.

Current implementation and design direction

localhost is the only execution backend in the current release. Checking, local planning and hql plan work today. Parallel execution, HQL-to-SQL translation and distributed backends are design direction. Their examples below explain the intended separation; they are not commands for selecting an available backend.

docs.title: Logical steps come before planning
docs.text:
Consider two steps over a list:

[3, 1, 2] | filter(n => n > 1) | map(n => n * 10)

[30, 20]

The head supplies three integers. The filter step retains 3 and 2; the map step multiplies each retained value by ten. The checker establishes the operations and their types before planning begins. The result has type List<Int> and preserves the order of the retained elements.

Each | composes the value on its left with the operation on its right. These two logical steps remain the explanation of the result under every execution strategy. Their source positions identify computation; the planner chooses where that computation runs and how much work to combine.

Term Meaning Established by Step One operation or presentation at one position in a pipeline The program, resolved by the checker Stage A region of planned work with an execution strategy The planner Task One scheduled attempt to execute a stage, over a partition where applicable The backend's scheduler Job One run of the whole program's plan The runtime

The stage belongs to physical planning. The task and job describe execution of the plan. The task and job vocabulary here describes the intended model; the current CLI exposes stage annotations through hql plan.

docs.title: From the checked program to execution
docs.text:
Planning resolves execution choices as far as the selected backend allows. For a local evaluator, it can select in-process evaluation directly. For a SQL backend, it can select a query to submit and delegate the remaining physical decisions to the database engine.

HQL program
    -> checking: typed steps, data dependencies, effects
    -> backend planning and translation
        -> localhost: in-process evaluation
        -> parallel backend: work divided among local workers
        -> SQL backend: SQL -> engine planning -> physical execution
        -> distributed backend: stages -> scheduled tasks on workers

SQL pushdown and distributed execution can be parts of the same route: a Databricks backend could translate HQL to Spark SQL, then let the engine plan and distribute the work. A backend may also refine a plan during a run. The logical program supplies the contract throughout those decisions.

docs.title: Local, parallel and distributed execution
docs.text:
Today, localhost puts all steps of each pipeline in stage 0, marked in process. For the finite list above, it evaluates the filter and then the map. hql plan shows the chosen stages without running the program. For streams, values are consumed on demand, as described in chapter 7.

An alternative parallel backend could divide the list into parts and apply both operations in one traversal of each part. It would assemble the retained results in their original order. A distributed backend could do the same work on several machines, often where the input already resides. Parallel execution describes work that runs concurrently; distributed execution adds placement and communication across machines.

More demanding operations need other plans. A reduction may combine partial results from several workers; grouping may move values so that equal keys reach the same worker. Several logical steps can share a stage, and the work of one logical step may span several stages. Those choices depend on the operation's contract, the data and the backend's capabilities.

docs.title: SQL translation and CTEs
docs.text:
Design direction. A backend for Databricks could translate a supported region of HQL into Spark SQL. A chain of common table expressions (CTEs) is one way to express the intermediate relations in a single SQL statement. For the small expression above, a possible translation is:

WITH input(pos, n) AS (
    VALUES (0, CAST(3 AS BIGINT)),
           (1, CAST(1 AS BIGINT)),
           (2, CAST(2 AS BIGINT))
), filtered AS (
    SELECT pos, n FROM input WHERE n > 1
), mapped AS (
    SELECT pos, n * 10 AS value FROM filtered
)
SELECT value FROM mapped ORDER BY pos;

This is an illustrative translation, written by hand. HQL does not generate it today. The backend would decode the returned column as List<Int>. The explicit position column and final ordering preserve the HQL list's order, producing 30 followed by 20.

A CTE names a result within a SQL statement. CTE dependencies express how the relations build on one another; their number does not prescribe the number of physical stages or tasks. Spark plans the submitted SQL and chooses its physical operators. Its EXPLAIN EXTENDED shows the logical plans and the physical plan separately.

Generating SQL therefore completes HQL's translation for that region while leaving physical planning to the engine. A single submitted statement can involve many scheduled tasks. HQL's job describes the whole program run; the engine may organize that work into its own jobs and stages. The backend integration will need to relate those identities when reporting progress.

docs.title: What every plan must preserve
docs.text:
The reference behavior is localhost's result, including its type, sequence positions and failures. Planning also preserves the order of observable effects and the scope of transactions. Reading, writing and logging carry those constraints into the plan.

Pure operations give a planner room to combine or distribute work when their contracts permit it. Data dependencies and failure behavior still apply: changing the order of two pure functions can change the result. A retry of an effectful task also needs the endpoint's delivery guarantees or a transaction protocol that makes the retry valid.

For SQL translation, matching operation names is only a starting point. The backend must preserve HQL's treatment of missing values, numeric precision, ordering and diagnostics. It must reject unsupported work before execution. Which expressions can be translated, and how SQL and local work could share a plan, remain decisions for a future backend specification.

docs.title: An endpoint and an execution backend
docs.text:
The current spark endpoint connects HQL to a table on Databricks or a Spark Thrift Server. It sends the SQL needed for endpoint operations; the HQL pipeline's filter, map and grouping still run in hql.

A future Spark execution backend would also run translated pipeline computation on the engine. Endpoint configuration identifies the data; execution configuration selects where the checked computation runs. Chapter 17 uses the existing endpoint, and chapter 15 explains how endpoints are configured.

docs.title: 15. Endpoints
docs.text: Every system in Part II is reached the same way. A file, a table, a topic, a subject and a webhook differ in where their data is and whether it ends; to a program each is an endpoint, and four steps read and write all of them. This chapter is that model, told over the shop of chapter 14. The programs run with --project examples/pipelines/shop.

docs.title: One file, two spellings
docs.text:
An endpoint is a value that states where documents are. Constructing one performs no I/O, and a program can reach the shop's events by writing the endpoint itself, file(path):

source(file("examples/pipelines/shop/data/events.json")) | size

1

or by naming the id the shop's .hql/config.toml declares it under:

[endpoint.events]
kind = "json"
path = "data/events.json"

source("events") | size

6

The two answers differ because the two spellings say different things. A .json file read by file is one JSON document, the whole array, so the Seq holds one value. The json kind is a file whose one document is an array of records, and it gives the array's elements. A constructed endpoint states where the bytes are and leaves the rest to the program; a configured endpoint states the system, its documents, and, on the schema boundary, the names and types that system uses.

The rest of Part II uses ids, for the reason the second spelling exists: a program that names an id is not tied to one machine's paths, one server's address, or one system. Moving the events from a file into a table is a change to .hql/config.toml, not to the pipeline.

docs.title: Four steps
docs.text:
Two questions sort every read and write. Does the endpoint end, and does the step take the data whole or one value at a time?

Whole One at a time Read source(e): a Seq, every document, from an endpoint that ends tap(e): a Stream, one document held at a time Write target(e): one completed value, written once sink(e): one document per value, written as each arrives

A table ends, so source reads it. A topic does not, so it is read by tap; source of one is a check error, because a Seq is a value that ends and a topic has no last message:

source("order_events")

check error[type-mismatch]: `order_events` is a `kafka` endpoint, read by `tap` as a `Stream`, not by `source` as a `Seq`
 --> <expression>:1:8
  |
1 | source("order_events")
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The writing side is the mirror. A stream has no last value for target to wait for, so a stream is written with sink:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

events : Stream<Event> = tap("order_events")
events | target("orders")

check error[type-mismatch]: `target("orders")` writes a Table or a sequence of a declared record, not Stream<Event>
  --> <expression>:10:10
   |
10 | events | target("orders")
   |          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

events : Stream<Event> = tap("order_events")
events | sink("orders")

Step

tap reads an endpoint that ends as well: tap("ledger") gives the table's rows one at a time, which is how a table larger than memory is read. The type of each step is fixed before the program runs, so a pipeline that would wait forever, tap("order_events") | size, is a check error and not a process that hangs (finite or live).

docs.title: The kind states the type
docs.text:
source("orders") is a PostgreSQL table, and the program above was checked without a database. Checking reads .hql/config.toml, finds kind = "postgres", and types orders from the kind alone: it ends, source reads it as a Seq of rows, and target writes it in one transaction or sink row by row. No connection is made until the program runs, and hql check never runs it:

source("customer_revenue")

Seq<Data>

customer_revenue is a Delta table in a lakehouse; the shop's configuration names it, and that is all the checker needs. The kinds in the current release, and the chapter each is told in:

Kind What one endpoint is Ends Chapter csv, json, json_lines, yaml a file in that format yes 9 vault a folder of documents yes 20 sqlite one table of a database file yes 16 postgres one table of a PostgreSQL database yes 16 kafka one Kafka topic no 16 nats one core NATS subject no 17 nats_jetstream one subject of a JetStream stream no 17 spark one table of a lakehouse, over Spark SQL yes 17

The id is a literal. A computed id, a connection string in place of an id, and an id the configuration does not declare are each refused at checking, on the endpoints-by-id page of chapter 9.

docs.title: Secrets live in the environment
docs.text:
The shop's .hql/config.toml holds no password. An endpoint whose address may carry a secret names the environment variable that holds it, dsn_env for a database, brokers_env for Kafka, url_env for NATS and the lakehouse, and token_env for a token:

[endpoint.orders]
kind = "postgres"
dsn_env = "SHOP_DSN"
table = "orders"
order = ["id"]

An address with credentials written into the configuration refuses the whole vault, before any program is read:

$ hql --vault shop eval '1'
hql: shop: `[endpoint.x]`: `url` holds credentials; name the environment variable that holds the address, `url_env = "VARIABLE"`

A variable that is not set is found when the endpoint is first read, and the failure names the endpoint and the variable, never its value:

$ hql --project examples/pipelines/shop eval 'source("orders")'
execute failure[io-failure]: endpoint `orders`: the environment variable `SHOP_DSN`, which `dsn_env` names, is not set
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | source("orders")

Every failure past checking has that form: the endpoint by its id, then the system's own words, then the row or message by its position. A row that does not decode stops the evaluation there; chapter 16 routes such rows instead of stopping.

docs.title: Transports
docs.text:
An endpoint that reaches outside the evaluation is a transport. Two properties of a transport matter to a program and to whoever runs it:

  • its locality: Direct, on this machine, such as a file or standard input, or Network, another process over a connection;
  • its carriage: what one read moves, bytes that a format splits into documents, a framed message that is one document, or a row of named columns that needs no format at all.

Sqlite and the two NATS transports are declared with both today. Each is a module of its own, imported by its full path, and its constructor takes the keys its kind takes, so a program reaches a subject without any configuration:

from io.msg.nats_jetstream import *

tap(nats_jetstream("orders.raw", stream = "ORDERS", url_env = "NATS_URL", idle_ms = 2000))

Stream<Data>

A message is one document, so no format is named, and it is Json unless one is. A table is rows of named columns, so it takes no format at all, and naming one is a check error:

from io.db.sqlite import *

source(sqlite("data/shop.db", table = "orders", order = ["id"]))

Seq<Data>

A constructor takes no secret, only the name of the variable that holds one; and a constructed transport has no schema boundary, which only configuration states. A row is read as Data, or as the record an annotation names, each column decoded as its type holds it, and a record is written to a constructed table a column per field, replacing the rows it held. A database file is written whole, by target; sink writes rows to a server's table, not to a file's.

Design only

The rest of this section describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: names and types may change before it ships.

Every kind is a transport with a constructor of its name, and every transport states its locality and carriage:

Transport Locality Carriage File, Stdin, Stdout Direct bytes Sqlite Direct rows Http, Tcp Network bytes WebSocket, Kafka, Nats, NatsJetStream, Rest, Graphql, Webhook Network messages Postgres, Spark Network rows

The carriage settles whether a step takes a format: a byte transport needs one, a message transport may name one and is Json without, and a row transport takes none, so source(postgres(dsn_env = "SHOP_DSN", table = "orders"), Json) is a check error. The locality is what a host grants: a document being rendered reaches no Network transport, constructed or configured, and the check reads that from the type, not from a list of names (effects and what a host allows).

The transports are grouped into modules by the system they reach:

io                     file, stdin, stdout, stderr, source, tap, target, sink
├── net                http, websocket, tcp, rest, graphql, webhook
├── db                 sqlite, postgres, spark, and further databases
├── msg                kafka, nats, nats_jetstream, and further brokers
└── store              s3, azure_blob, gcs, sftp, hdfs

from io.db.postgres import * brings postgres(...) into scope, as from io.db.sqlite import * brings sqlite(...) and from io.msg.nats import * brings nats(...). A configured id needs no import: the configuration names the kind, and the kind names its module. A program that constructs a network transport names its module in its first lines, so what a program may reach is visible before reading it. Chapter 18 is the net and store transports the shop reaches next.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 16 moves the shop's events out of a file: into a SQLite table, then a PostgreSQL table, then onto a Kafka topic and back.

docs.title: 16. Tables and topics
docs.text:
The shop's events outgrow a file. This chapter moves them three times: into a SQLite table on this machine, into a PostgreSQL table on a server, and onto a Kafka topic that the checkout writes to as orders happen. At each move the configuration changes and the pipeline does not. The last section is the move every real pipeline makes sooner or later: a topic carrying messages that are not what the type says.

Every event in the shop is an Event, declared once for the chapter:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

docs.title: A table on this machine
docs.text:
A sqlite endpoint is one table in a database file. The shop's ledger is the table orders in data/shop.db:

[endpoint.ledger]
kind = "sqlite"
path = "data/shop.db"
table = "orders"
order = ["id"]

order names the columns the rows are read in, so two reads give the rows in the same order. Filling the table is a target: the events are read as Events, and each field becomes a column. The program is shown checked rather than run, so that the book's tests do not rewrite the table, and Step is the type of a program whose result is what it wrote:

events : Seq<Event> = source("events")
events | target("ledger")

Step

A table ends, so source reads it whole, as a Seq, and every step of chapter 6 applies. The revenue per customer is a group and a sum, and an amount keeps its digits as a Decimal on the way in and on the way out:

orders : Seq<Event> = source("ledger")
orders
| filter(o => o.kind == "order_placed")
| group(by = o => o.customer)
| map(g => {customer: g.key, total: g.items | map(o => o.amount) | sum})

{{customer: "ada", total: 135.75}, {customer: "grace", total: 42.00}, {customer: "linus", total: 7.99}}

tap("ledger") gives the same rows one at a time, a Stream that ends after the last row, and holds one row in memory:

tap("ledger") | take(2) | map(o => o.id)

[1, 2]

docs.title: The same table on a server
docs.text:
The shop hires a second clerk, and the ledger moves to PostgreSQL, where both can reach it. The configuration names the database by the variable holding its connection string; the table and its order are the same:

[endpoint.orders]
kind = "postgres"
dsn_env = "SHOP_DSN"
table = "orders"
order = ["id"]

The revenue report is the program above with "ledger" replaced by "orders". It checks without a database:

orders : Seq<Event> = source("orders")
orders
| filter(o => o.kind == "order_placed")
| group(by = o => o.customer)
| map(g => {customer: g.key, total: g.items | map(o => o.amount) | sum})

Set<Data>

and run against one, it prints what the SQLite table printed. What changes is what happens at the edges. The table's columns are read before the first row and compared with Event through the schema boundary, so a column Event does not declare, or one of the wrong type, fails before any row is decoded. Only the columns Event reads are selected. A numeric column is a Decimal with its digits, jsonb the tree it holds, and NULL an absent field.

docs.title: A topic
docs.text:
The shop opens a web store. The checkout does not write to the ledger: it publishes each event to a Kafka topic, order_events, and whatever needs to know about orders reads the topic.

[endpoint.order_events]
kind = "kafka"
brokers_env = "KAFKA_BROKERS"
topic = "order_events"
idle_ms = 2000

A topic is a log that does not end. tap("order_events") is a Stream, one JSON document per message, decoded as the element type; the stream starts at the earliest message the topic keeps, or at the next one published under from = "latest":

events : Stream<Event> = tap("order_events")
events
| filter(e => e.kind == "order_placed")
| map(e => {id: e.id, customer: e.customer, amount: e.amount})

{amount: 120.50, customer: "ada", id: 1}
{amount: 42.00, customer: "grace", id: 2}
{amount: 7.99, customer: "linus", id: 4}
{amount: 15.25, customer: "ada", id: 6}

The four lines appear as the messages arrive, and the program ends two seconds after the last one: idle_ms bounds how long the stream waits for the next message. Without it the stream waits without end, which is what a service that reads a topic does.

Moving data between the two is a pipeline of two steps each way. A table's rows onto the topic, one message per row, in the table's order:

orders : Seq<Event> = source("orders")
orders | sink("order_events")

Step

and the topic's messages into the table, one row per message, committed as each arrives:

events : Stream<Event> = tap("order_events")
events | sink("orders")

Step

These are the first two programs of the kafka-postgres case of hql-demo, which seeds the table, moves its rows through the topic into a second table, and compares the second with the first.

docs.title: What a write promises
docs.text:
The four steps say what is written. The kind says when it is safe.

target sink a sqlite or postgres table every row in one transaction: all of them or none each row committed as it arrives a kafka topic one message per element of a completed collection one message per value, as each arrives

mode in the configuration states what a write does with what the table already holds: create refuses an existing table, append adds after its rows, and replace, the default, empties it and keeps its definition, indexes and grants. A table that does not exist is created with a column per field. A topic that does not exist is an evaluation failure: creating a topic is the cluster's business.

A write replaces or extends what a table holds. Changing rows it holds, in place, and several such changes as one transaction, are the statements of chapter 19's transfer page.

Every message one program writes goes to the topic's first partition, so a reader is given them in the order they were written. A read records no position: each run of a program starts where from says, so reading a topic twice gives its messages twice. A reader that resumes where it stopped is a JetStream consumer, in chapter 17.

docs.title: A topic that lies
docs.text:
Not every message on a topic is an Event. The web store has a bug that sends "free" as an amount, an old client leaves out the customer, a refund is negative, and a new service publishes order_cancelled, a kind nobody has agreed on. Reading the topic as Stream<Event> is strict: the first such message stops the evaluation, naming the endpoint and the message.

A pipeline that must keep running reads the messages as Data, so none fails to decode, and states what an order is as a contract (validation as a value):

type EventData : DataContract = {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String

    require amount >= 0 as non_negative
    require ["order_placed", "order_shipped", "payment_failed"] | contains(kind) as known_kind
}

validate(EventData) gives one Result per message: the order, or the message as it arrived with every rule it broke. fork gives every branch the same input, and oks() and errs() keep each side. The producer's eight events are in a file as well, so the policy can be tried on this machine before it meets the topic:

source("raw_events")
| validate(EventData)
| fork {
    clean    = oks()  | map(e => e.id),
    rejected = errs() | map(e => {id: e.value.id, rules: e.violations | map(v => v.rule)}),
}

{clean: [1, 2, 4, 6], rejected: [{id: 3, rules: ["EventData.amount.type"]}, {id: 5, rules: ["EventData.customer.missing"]}, {id: 7, rules: ["EventData.non_negative"]}, {id: 8, rules: ["EventData.known_kind"]}]}

The production pipeline is the same shape over the topic, with each branch ending in a table. The clean side is read into a closed Event, since a table is written from a declared record; the rejected side keeps the message as the producer sent it, so it can be repaired and sent again:

type Rejected {
    id      : Int
    message : Data
    rules   : List<String>
}

tap("order_events_raw")
| validate(EventData)
| fork {
    clean =
        oks()
        | map(e => Event(id = e.id, kind = e.kind, customer = e.customer, amount = e.amount, at = e.at))
        | sink("order_clean"),
    quarantine =
        errs()
        | map(e => Rejected(
            id = match e.value.id { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 },
            message = e.value,
            rules = e.violations | map(v => v.rule)))
        | sink("order_quarantine"),
}

{clean: Step, quarantine: Step}

Each message goes to exactly one branch, in the order the topic holds them, and neither branch ends the other. After a run, the quarantine table holds:

rejected : Seq<Rejected> = source("order_quarantine")
rejected | map(r => {id: r.id, rules: r.rules})

[{id: 3, rules: ["EventData.amount.type"]}, {id: 5, rules: ["EventData.customer.missing"]}, {id: 7, rules: ["EventData.non_negative"]}, {id: 8, rules: ["EventData.known_kind"]}]

Each row's message is the tree the producer sent, {amount: "free", …} for the first, so a repaired message is the same tree with one field changed.

The contract is the policy: what an order is. The shape of the pipeline is what happens to a message that is not one. Changing either is a change to one declaration, and the checker checks both before a message is read.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 17 gives the shop a message bus that keeps its place, and a lakehouse whose tables are files in object storage: the same pipeline, with a subject in place of the topic and Delta tables in place of PostgreSQL.

docs.title: 17. Subjects and the lakehouse
docs.text:
The shop's Kafka topic of chapter 16 carries every order, and three needs have grown around it. The warehouse wants to hear about each shipment as it happens and does not care about the ones it missed. Billing wants every order exactly where it left off yesterday. And the owner wants reports over all of history without anyone's pipeline slowing down to produce them.

This chapter meets the three with NATS and a lakehouse. NATS is two kinds: nats, a subject whose messages nobody keeps, and nats_jetstream, a subject of a stream the server keeps. A lakehouse is tables kept as files in object storage, reached by kind = "spark". Each key of each kind is on the subjects and lakehouse tables page of chapter 9; this chapter is what the shop does with them.

The programs need servers. They are checked here against the shop's configuration, and run in the hql-demo repository, whose nats-core, nats and nats-lakehouse cases start NATS, MinIO and a Spark Thrift Server with Docker Compose. The outputs shown are theirs.

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

docs.title: Notifications nobody keeps
docs.text:
Core NATS delivers a message to whoever is subscribed to its subject when it is published, and keeps nothing. That is what a notification is: the warehouse screen shows what is happening now, and an event from before the screen was switched on is not news.

The shop publishes each event to a subject named for its kind, orders.order_placed, orders.payment_failed, orders.order_shipped. The subject is computed, so the program writes the transport itself, with the constructor of io.msg.nats:

from io.msg.nats import *

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

events : Seq<Event> = source("events")

for_kind = (kind: String) => events | filter(e => e.kind == kind)
subject = (kind: String) => nats("orders." + kind, url_env = "NATS_URL")

for_kind("order_placed") | sink(subject("order_placed"))
for_kind("payment_failed") | sink(subject("payment_failed"))
for_kind("order_shipped") | sink(subject("order_shipped"))

Step

A reader names one subject or a family of them. A subject may hold the wildcards *, one token, and >, every token that follows, so the shop's notifications endpoint reads all three:

[endpoint.notifications]
kind = "nats"
url_env = "NATS_URL"
subject = "orders.>"
idle_ms = 3000

events : Stream<Event> = tap("notifications")
events
| filter(e => e.kind == "order_placed")
| map(e => {id: e.id, customer: e.customer, amount: e.amount})

{amount: 120.50, customer: "ada", id: 1}
{amount: 42.00, customer: "grace", id: 2}
{amount: 7.99, customer: "linus", id: 4}
{amount: 15.25, customer: "ada", id: 6}

The subscription starts when the stream is first traversed, so the nats-core case starts this program before the publisher, and a message published before it would not be there to be given. Nothing confirms a core message: sink ends once the server has the messages, whether or not anyone was listening. A wildcard endpoint is read only, since a message is published to one subject.

docs.title: A log the server keeps
docs.text:
Billing cannot miss an order. JetStream is the part of the NATS server that keeps messages: a stream stores every message published to its subjects, in order, and a nats_jetstream endpoint names the stream and one subject in it. The shop's checkout publishes raw orders to orders.raw, in the stream ORDERS:

[endpoint.orders_raw]
kind = "nats_jetstream"
url_env = "NATS_URL"
stream = "ORDERS"
subject = "orders.raw"
idle_ms = 2000

source("raw_events") | sink("orders_raw")

Step

A message is written once the stream answers that it stored it, so a program that ends without a failure has lost nothing. A subject no stream stores is an evaluation failure rather than a message that disappears.

tap("orders_raw") reads the stream's messages under that subject in the order the stream holds them, from the earliest it keeps, or from the next one published under from = "latest". Like a Kafka read, it records no position: two runs give the same messages twice.

docs.title: Billing's place
docs.text:
A consumer is the server's record of how far one reader has come in a stream, and a durable consumer is one the server keeps under a name. Billing's endpoint is the same subject with a consumer named:

[endpoint.billing]
kind = "nats_jetstream"
url_env = "NATS_URL"
stream = "ORDERS"
subject = "orders.raw"
consumer = "billing"
idle_ms = 2000

The first run through billing reads every message the stream keeps. The next run reads only what was published since; a run with nothing new prints nothing. Another endpoint with another consumer keeps its own place over the same messages, so the warehouse's reports and billing's invoices never move each other's position.

A message is acknowledged once the program asks for the one after it, and the last one when the stream ends. A message is therefore delivered at least once: a program that fails while it holds a message, or stops early, is given that message again by its next run.

tap("billing") | take(2) | map(e => e.id)

[1, 2]

take(2) asked for no third message, so 2 was never acknowledged, and the next run of this program starts with 2. A program that writes what it reads, an invoice per order, writes it so that writing it twice does no harm.

docs.title: The lakehouse
docs.text:
The owner's reports need history, and a broker is not where history is queried. A lakehouse keeps tables as files in object storage, with a transaction log beside them, and answers SQL over them. Databricks is one; Apache Spark with Delta Lake over an S3 bucket is another, built from open-source parts, and the spark kind reaches either, by the URL of a Databricks SQL warehouse or of a Spark Thrift Server:

[endpoint.orders_silver]
kind = "spark"
url_env = "LAKEHOUSE_URL"
table = "default.orders_silver"
order = ["id"]
mode = "append"

[endpoint.orders_silver.fields.amount]
type = "DECIMAL(12,2)"

A lakehouse table ends, so it sits on the table side of the line: read by source through the schema boundary, written by target in commits of up to 500 rows, or by sink as rows arrive. A DECIMAL column states how many digits it holds, so the boundary names the type each amount is written as. The valid orders of the subject above land in this table by the quarantine of chapter 16 with the ids changed, a subject in place of the topic and this table in place of the clean one:

type EventData : DataContract = {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String

    require amount >= 0 as non_negative
    require ["order_placed", "order_shipped", "payment_failed"] | contains(kind) as known_kind
}

type Rejected {
    id      : Int
    message : Data
    rules   : List<String>
}

tap("orders_raw")
| validate(EventData)
| fork {
    silver =
        oks()
        | map(e => Event(id = e.id, kind = e.kind, customer = e.customer, amount = e.amount, at = e.at))
        | sink("orders_silver"),
    rejected =
        errs()
        | map(e => Rejected(
            id = match e.value.id { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 },
            message = e.value,
            rules = e.violations | map(v => v.rule)))
        | sink("orders_rejected"),
}

{silver: Step, rejected: Step}

That table is the shop's first analytical one, and what it is for, the layers a lakehouse is organized in, and what a report built over it needs from it are chapter 20. This chapter's business with it ends at the transport: a subject in, a table out, and what each promises.

docs.title: Where the work runs
docs.text:
The filter and the grouping above run where hql runs. The spark endpoint reaches a table over Spark SQL and sends the statements needed to read or write it. The surrounding HQL pipeline is evaluated locally.

A future Spark execution backend could translate supported pipeline steps into SQL and let the engine plan their execution on the cluster. The companion Logical steps and physical plans explains that handoff and the requirement to preserve the meaning of |.

What the current release does not do: several programs sharing one consumer to divide its messages, NATS credential files, a lakehouse column holding a list or a record, and a Databricks token other than a personal access token.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 18 is where the shop's data comes from outside: a payment provider calling a webhook, a carrier's REST API, and an archive in object storage. It is design, not yet in the release.

docs.title: 18. APIs, webhooks and stores
docs.text:
Design only

This chapter describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: apart from http, websocket and tcp, which the network page of chapter 9 shows running, these programs do not run against the current binary, and names, keys, types and outputs may change before they ship.

Everything the shop has read so far, it wrote first: its own files, tables, topics and subjects. A business also reads what others publish. The payment provider calls the shop when a payment settles. The carrier answers questions about parcels, a page of answers at a time. The supplier's catalogue is a GraphQL API. And the auditor wants every order kept for seven years, somewhere cheaper than a lakehouse.

Each of those is one more transport, and the model of chapter 15 does not change for any of them: an endpoint by id or by constructor, read by source if it ends and by tap if it does not, written by target or sink, its type known from configuration before anything connects.

docs.title: Three transports over HTTP
docs.text:
http(url) in the current release reads one resource as bytes, with a format to say what the bytes are. Most APIs are more than one resource: a collection split into pages, a query posted to one address, or a server that calls back. Three transports of io.net name those shapes, and each gives messages, one item per document, Json unless a format is named:

Transport What one read is Ends Read by rest(url, items, next) the items of a collection, every page in turn yes source graphql(url, query, variables, items) the nodes one query returns yes source webhook(port, path) the body of each request the host receives no tap

The shapes are the same two as before. A paginated collection and a query result are finite, read once per evaluation and replayable within it. A webhook is live: requests arrive when the sender decides, and the stream is as endless as a topic.

docs.title: The carrier's API
docs.text:
The carrier lists parcels at https://api.carrier.example/parcels. Each response holds a page of them under results, and the Link header names the next page. The shop configures it once, with the token in the environment:

[endpoint.parcels]
kind = "rest"
url = "https://api.carrier.example/parcels"
items = "results"
next = "link"
token_env = "CARRIER_TOKEN"

type Parcel {
    order   : Int
    status  : String
    updated : String
}

parcels : Seq<Parcel> = source("parcels")
parcels
| filter(p => p.status == "delivered")
| map(p => p.order)

source sends a GET for each page in turn until none is named, and gives every item in page order. items is a field path into each response body, "data.results" for one nested deeper; next is "link" for the rel="next" target of the Link header, or a field path to a URL in the body. The token is sent as Authorization: Bearer, and the pages are fetched once per evaluation, so a program that reads parcels twice asks the carrier once.

The parcels are now one more table to the shop. Joining them to the silver orders of chapter 17, each an Event of chapter 16, is a join of two Seqs, which chapter 6 already showed:

orders : Seq<Event> = source("orders_silver")

orders
| filter(o => o.kind == "order_placed")
| left_join(parcels, left = o => o.id, right = p => p.order,
            into = (o, p) => {id: o.id, customer: o.customer, status: p.map(x => x.status).unwrap_or("not sent")})

A rest endpoint is read only. Creating something on the carrier's side is a request by another method, which is a write to an http endpoint.

docs.title: The supplier's catalogue
docs.text:
The supplier answers GraphQL. A graphql endpoint is one query: one POST of the query and its variables, and the items are the array at items below the response's data:

[endpoint.catalogue]
kind = "graphql"
url = "https://supplier.example/graphql"
query = "{ products(inStock: true) { sku name price } }"
items = "products"
token_env = "SUPPLIER_TOKEN"

type Product {
    sku   : String
    name  : String
    price : Decimal
}

products : Seq<Product> = source("catalogue")
products | filter(p => p.price < 50.00) | map(p => p.name)

A response whose errors is not empty is an evaluation failure naming the URL and the first error's message: a GraphQL server answers 200 for a query it could not run, and the endpoint does not mistake that for an empty catalogue.

docs.title: The payment provider's webhook
docs.text:
The payment provider does not wait to be asked. When a payment settles or fails, it sends a POST to an address the shop gave it. A webhook endpoint is that address, and tap over it is a Stream of request bodies:

[endpoint.payments]
kind = "webhook"
port = 8080
path = "/payments"
token_env = "PAYMENTS_TOKEN"

type Payment {
    order  : Int
    status : String
    amount : Decimal
}

payments : Stream<Payment> = tap("payments")
payments
| filter(p => p.status == "failed")
| map(p => {id: p.order, kind: "payment_failed", amount: p.amount})
| sink("orders_raw")

The program listens from the first traversal until it ends, and each accepted body is one value. The sender is answered as HTTP has it: 202 once the body is read and decoded, 400 for a body that does not decode, 401 for a request without the token, 404 for another path. A body that does not decode is answered and dropped; the stream goes on, because the sender, not the shop, made the mistake.

A webhook listens on the loopback address unless host says otherwise, so a program on a developer's machine is not reachable from outside by accident. It is the one transport that accepts connections, and like every Network transport it is refused in a document being rendered.

The failed payments go onto the shop's own raw subject, where the bronze pipeline of chapter 17 validates them with every other order. The webhook is an edge; what comes through it joins the flow the shop already has.

docs.title: The archive
docs.text:
The auditor wants every raw order kept for seven years, as files, in object storage. An object store is a transport whose documents are objects under keys, and its module is in the io.store family: s3, which also reaches MinIO and Ceph, azure_blob, adls, gcs, sftp and hdfs.

[endpoint.archive]
kind = "s3"
bucket = "shop-archive"
prefix = "orders/raw/"
region = "eu-central-1"
format = "json_lines"
credentials_env = "ARCHIVE_CREDENTIALS"

tap("orders_raw") | collect(1000) | sink("archive")

collect(1000) turns the stream into batches, and sink writes each batch as one object under the prefix, so the archive is files of a thousand orders each rather than a million files of one. Read back, the prefix is a finite set of objects, and source("archive") is a Seq of every order in it: a replay of last year is a pipeline over the archive instead of over the subject, as chapter 19 shows.

A format says what the bytes of one object are. Beside the text formats of chapter 9, binary formats decode bytes to values with a schema of their own: Parquet for columns of a table, Avro and Protobuf for records on a wire. An archive written as Parquet is smaller and is read by every analytics tool there is:

import io.store.s3

orders : Seq<Event> = source("orders_silver")
orders | target(s3("shop-archive", key = "orders/2026.parquet", credentials_env = "ARCHIVE_CREDENTIALS"), Parquet)

A table format is one level up: Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg keep a table as Parquet objects and a transaction log in a store. Where the spark kind of chapter 17 asks a SQL server for a table's rows, a delta or iceberg kind reads the log and the objects itself, through the store's transport, so a table in a bucket is readable with no server running at all.

docs.title: Further brokers and databases
docs.text:
The families have room for the systems a shop meets next, each a module named for its system, each a transport with a constructor and a kind:

Family Systems io.msg rabbitmq, pulsar, mqtt, redis_streams, sqs, azure_service_bus, artemis, rocketmq, nsq, zeromq io.db duckdb, clickhouse, mongodb, couchdb, cassandra, opensearch, redis, neo4j io.net grpc, feed io.store s3, azure_blob, adls, gcs, sftp, hdfs

A queue such as RabbitMQ or SQS is a tap and a sink, as a topic is; a document database is a source and a target, as a table is. Whether a new system ends is the one fact about it a program depends on, and the kind states it.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 19 puts every system of Part II into one file: the shop's whole day as a pipeline, checked before it runs, and where that pipeline may run.

docs.title: 19. OLTP
docs.text:
The shop's systems so far are its OLTP side: online transaction processing, the side where things happen. An order is placed and a row is committed; a payment fails and a message is published; the warehouse reads the next shipment and acknowledges it. Each fact is one row or one message, written once as it occurs, and what the system holds is the current state of the business: these orders, these customers, this stock. The PostgreSQL table, the Kafka topic and the JetStream subject of chapters 16 and 17 are all of this kind, and so is the first lakehouse table the raw orders land in.

The pipelines of this side share a shape. They read one value at a time, tap, and write one value at a time, sink, as each arrives; they decide each value on its own, validate, filter, map, and keep nothing between two values; and they run for as long as values arrive. The guarantees they rest on are the ones of chapter 16 and chapter 17: a row committed as it is written, a message stored before the write ends, a message delivered at least once and so written so that twice does no harm.

This chapter is the shop's whole transactional day as one file, and what follows from its being a file. The other side, the history those transactions leave and the questions a report asks of it, is chapter 20.

docs.title: The pages
docs.text: Page What it covers The shop's day in one file one pipeline from the raw subject to an archive, a silver table, an alert subject and a dead-letter subject, checked against the configuration with nothing connected When a mistake is found the phase each broken binding is found in, and what is said A replay is the same file the pipeline as a function of its input: a test over a file, a replay over the archive, production over the subject, and a stream bounded into a batch Streams against tables enrichment of a stream by a lookup table, and windows, as design A transfer is one transaction insert, update and delete changing rows in place, and with transaction making several of them one transaction, with its rollback, its retries and its failure as data

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 20 turns from the transactions to what they leave behind: bronze, silver and gold tables, the grain of a row, duplicates and how they are removed, and a table kept up to date by key.

docs.title: When a mistake is found
docs.text:
A binding can break, and it breaks at the earliest phase that can see it. Checking sees the configuration; evaluation sees the systems:

What is wrong Found What is said tap("order_event") checking check error[unknown-name]: no endpoint order_event is configured; did you mean order_events? source("order_events") checking check error[type-mismatch]: order_events is a kafka endpoint, read by tap as a Stream, not by source as a Seq a stream written by target("orders") checking check error[type-mismatch]: target("orders") writes a Table or a sequence of a declared record, not Stream<Event> sink("ledger") checking check error[type-mismatch]: endpoint ledger is a sqlite endpoint, which sink does not write; write it whole with target a password in .hql/config.toml loading the vault url holds credentials; name the environment variable that holds the address, url_env = "VARIABLE" SHOP_DSN not set evaluation, before the first row execute failure[io-failure]: endpoint orders: the environment variable SHOP_DSN, which dsn_env names, is not set a raw order read as Event evaluation, at that order execute failure[io-failure]: endpoint raw_events, field amount: "free" is not a decimal number a write to a wildcard subject evaluation, at the write execute failure[io-failure]: subject orders.> holds a wildcard, which reads many subjects and writes none; a message is published to one subject

A secret is named by the variable that holds it and never printed. A failure at evaluation names the endpoint by its id and the value by its field; what it never does is continue past a value it could not read and count it later as missing. A pipeline that must continue says so in its shape, as day.hql does with validate and fork: the order that would have stopped it is a row in the dead-letter subject instead.

docs.title: A replay is the same file
docs.text:
The pipeline names one input. Bound to a function, it takes any stream of Data, and the input is chosen where it is called:

type EventData : DataContract = {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String

    require amount >= 0 as non_negative
    require ["order_placed", "order_shipped", "payment_failed"] | contains(kind) as known_kind
}

route = (raw: Stream<Data>) => raw
| validate(EventData)
| fork {
    clean    = oks()  | map(e => fmt("ok   {}", e.id)) | sink(stdout, Text),
    rejected = errs() | map(e => fmt("err  {} {}", e.value.id, e.violations | map(v => v.rule))) | sink(stdout, Text),
}

tap("raw_events") | route

ok   1
ok   2
ok   4
ok   6
err  3 ["EventData.amount.type"]
err  5 ["EventData.customer.missing"]
err  7 ["EventData.non_negative"]
err  8 ["EventData.known_kind"]
{clean: (), rejected: ()}

tap over a file is a Stream that ends after the file's last order, so the routing written for a subject runs over a file of recorded messages, with no broker at all. That is a test. The archive day.hql writes is such a file, so the same call over tap(file("archive/orders.jsonl")) is a replay: last week's orders through this week's rules. And the call over tap("orders_raw") is production. The platform words, test, replay, backfill, name three inputs to one pipeline, not three pipelines.

The other direction is as short. A stream becomes something finite by bounding it: take(n) for a count, collect(n) for batches of a size, each batch a List every whole-input step of chapter 6 applies to:

tap("orders_raw") | take(100) | size

Int

A snapshot is the first hundred, or the first day, of a stream written whole by target; a micro-batch is collect(n) and one write per batch.

docs.title: Streams against tables
docs.text:
Design only

This section describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: these programs do not run, and names and types may change before they ship.

The commonest enrichment is a stream against a lookup: each order joined to its customer's record in a table. The finite side is read whole; the live side passes through one value at a time, and no value waits for another, so join takes a Stream on the left and a Seq on the right:

type Customer { customer : String, region : String, vip : Bool }

customers : Seq<Customer> = source("customers")

tap("orders_raw")
| Event
| join(customers, left = o => o.customer, right = c => c.customer,
       into = (o, c) => {id: o.id, region: c.region, vip: c.vip, amount: o.amount})
| filter(x => x.vip)
| sink("vip_orders")

Two streams joined would wait for each other without end, and the checker says so: join over two Streams is refused until one of them is bounded. A window is collect by time instead of by count, a Stream<List<T>> whose batches close when the span does:

tap("orders_silver_changes")
| window(1d, by = e => e.at)
| map(day => day
    | group(by = e => e.customer)
    | map(g => Revenue(customer = g.key, orders = g.items | size, total = g.items | map(e => e.amount) | sum)))
| emit
| sink("daily_revenue")

Inside a window every whole-input step applies, which is how a daily total is a group and a sum over an input that never ends.

docs.title: The shop's day in one file
docs.text:
Orders arrive on the JetStream subject orders.raw. Each is appended to an archive file as it arrived. Each is validated: the valid ones land in the silver Delta table, and a placed order of 100 or more is also published as an alert to a core NATS subject; the invalid ones go to the dead-letter subject with the rules they broke. The configuration is the shop's .hql/config.toml; the pipeline, day.hql, is this:

type EventData : DataContract = {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String

    require amount >= 0 as non_negative
    require ["order_placed", "order_shipped", "payment_failed"] | contains(kind) as known_kind
}

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

type Rejected {
    id      : Int
    message : Data
    rules   : List<String>
}

tap("orders_raw")
| tee archived = sink(file("archive/orders.jsonl").end, Json)
| validate(EventData)
| fork {
    silver =
        oks()
        | map(e => Event(id = e.id, kind = e.kind, customer = e.customer, amount = e.amount, at = e.at))
        | tee large =
            filter(e => e.kind == "order_placed" and e.amount >= 100)
            | map(e => {customer: e.customer, amount: e.amount, text: fmt("large order from {}", e.customer)})
            | sink("alerts")
        | sink("orders_silver"),
    rejected =
        errs()
        | map(e => Rejected(
            id = match e.value.id { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 },
            message = e.value,
            rules = e.violations | map(v => v.rule)))
        | sink("orders_rejected"),
}

{silver: Step, rejected: Step}

Read top to bottom, it is the dataflow diagram a platform would draw:

orders.raw ──┬──▶ archive/orders.jsonl
             │
             └──▶ validate ──ok──┬──▶ orders_silver
                     │           └──▶ alerts.orders   (≥ 100, placed)
                     └──err─────────▶ orders.rejected

One input, three kinds of fan-out, four outputs. tee branches a pipeline without ending it: the archive receives every order before validation, and the alert branch receives each valid order before the silver table does. fork sends every value to every branch, and oks() and errs() keep one side each. A branch of either is typed like the trunk, so a branch that ended in target over this stream would be refused, as any target of a stream is.

There is no orchestration around the file: no activity names, no cluster, no connection strings. hql check day.hql reads .hql/config.toml, resolves every id to its kind and every kind to a type, checks the whole file, and opens no connection; the result above is what it prints. Every system in the file is in the current release, and the nats-lakehouse case of hql-demo runs the same shape against NATS and a lakehouse.

The gold report of chapter 17 is the second file, and the subject of chapter 20: it reads the silver table whole when a report is wanted, and replaces the gold table in one commit. The two share no state but the silver table.

docs.title: A transfer is one transaction
docs.text:
The shop pays its suppliers from a ledger: an accounts table and a transfers table in the one PostgreSQL database of chapter 16. A transfer of 100 from one account to another changes two rows and adds one, and the three changes hold together or not at all. target cannot say that: it rewrites a table whole, and three writes are three commits. This page is the statements that change rows in place, and the scope that makes several of them one transaction (HQL-0051).

Every program here is checked, not run: the book's tests connect to nothing. The two records are declared once:

type Account { id : Int, owner : String, balance : Decimal }

type Transfer { id : Int, from_id : Int, to_id : Int, amount : Decimal }

The configuration names each table's record, element = "Account", beside its connection:

[endpoint.accounts]
kind = "postgres"
dsn_env = "SHOP_DSN"
table = "accounts"
order = ["id"]
element = "Account"

[endpoint.transfers]
kind = "postgres"
dsn_env = "SHOP_DSN"
table = "transfers"
order = ["id"]
element = "Transfer"

docs.title: Changing rows in place
docs.text:
configured("accounts") is the table itself as a value, where source("accounts") is its rows. Three statements change what a table holds. update selects rows with the filter of every pipeline and set gives the fields that change; its value is the number of rows changed:

accounts = configured("accounts")

update accounts
| filter(a => a.id == 1)
| set(a => {balance: a.balance - 100.00})

Int

The lambdas are not run row by row. The statement runs on the database as one UPDATE … SET … WHERE …, so a lambda holds only what translates: a field of the row, a literal, a value bound outside the lambda, comparisons, and, or, not, arithmetic, contains of a bound collection, and is_none or is_some of a field. Anything else is a check error that says to compute it in HQL and bind it. insert adds a row or a collection of them, and delete removes the rows it selects:

transfers = configured("transfers")

added = insert transfers Transfer(id = 1, from_id = 1, to_id = 2, amount = 100.00)
gone  = delete transfers | filter(t => t.amount == 0.00)

[added, gone]

List<Int>

A filter that matches no row is no failure: the statement changes nothing and its value is 0. A program that needs the row to exist reads the count. A statement outside a transaction is its own transaction, committed when it ends, as target of a table is. The checker refuses a statement over an endpoint that cannot take it: a Kafka topic is not Updatable, a CSV file is not Deletable. A sqlite or postgres table is all three, and a spark table too, where the table's format allows it.

docs.title: Two updates and an insert, or none
docs.text:
A transaction scope runs its block as one unit over its participants, a set of endpoints in one database, and commits when the block ends:

accounts = configured("accounts")
transfers = configured("transfers")
ledger = {accounts, transfers}

with transaction(isolation = Serializable) tx on ledger {
    sender = source(accounts) | filter(a => a.id == 1) | one
    tx.rollback("insufficient balance") given sender.balance < 100.00

    debited = update accounts | filter(a => a.id == 1) | set(a => {balance: a.balance - 100.00})
    credited = update accounts | filter(a => a.id == 2) | set(a => {balance: a.balance + 100.00})
    tx.rollback("no such account") given debited != 1 or credited != 1

    insert transfers Transfer(id = 1, from_id = 1, to_id = 2, amount = 100.00)
}

Result<Int, TransactionFailure>

Inside the block every read and write of a participant runs on the scope's own connection: a source after an update sees the update, and a sink commits no row of its own. one gives the one element of a sequence of exactly one, and fails otherwise. Each update is bound so that its count is read: a credit to an account that does not exist changes no row, and without the check the scope would commit the debit alone.

isolation = Serializable is what keeps the balance check true when two transfers run at once. Under it, two scopes that both read a balance of 150 and both debit 100 cannot both commit: the database refuses one of them as a conflict. PostgreSQL's default level, ReadCommitted, does not refuse it: the second debit waits for the first, then subtracts from the committed 50, and the balance ends at -50. SQLite has no other level.

The handle tx ends the attempt early: tx.rollback(reason) undoes it and gives the reason back, tx.commit(value) commits before the end, and tx.retry() runs the block again. Each is written as a statement of the block or as an arm of a given … otherwise or a match that is one, and tx goes nowhere else: not into a lambda, not into a function.

The scope's value is a Result: ok with the block's final value, here the rows the insert added, and err with a TransactionFailure saying why the scope did not commit. A rollback by the program's own rule, a constraint the database enforced and a conflict that outlasted the attempts are all data, matched like any other:

accounts = configured("accounts")
transfers = configured("transfers")

outcome =
    with transaction(attempts = 3, isolation = Serializable) tx on {accounts, transfers} {
        sender = source(accounts) | filter(a => a.id == 1) | one
        tx.rollback("insufficient balance") given sender.balance < 100.00
        debited = update accounts | filter(a => a.id == 1) | set(a => {balance: a.balance - 100.00})
        credited = update accounts | filter(a => a.id == 2) | set(a => {balance: a.balance + 100.00})
        tx.rollback("no such account") given debited != 1 or credited != 1
        insert transfers Transfer(id = 1, from_id = 1, to_id = 2, amount = 100.00)
    }

match outcome {
    ok(n) => "transferred",
    err(f) => f.kind + ": " + f.reason,
}

String

A scope is observed when it is bound, as outcome is here, or when it is the program's last statement, whose value is the program's result. A scope written as a statement before the last one has a value nothing reads, and the checker warns, kind effect: this transaction's `Result` is neither bound, nor the program's result, nor matched: its failure would be observed by nothing. The program still runs; a rollback in that scope goes unnoticed.

attempts = 3 runs the block again, on a fresh transaction, when the database refuses an attempt because of a concurrent one: in PostgreSQL a serialization failure under isolation = Serializable or a deadlock, in SQLite a database file another transaction is writing. The attempt is retried with no delay, whether a statement or the commit was refused, and after the last one the scope is err with kind = "conflict". A retried attempt reads the balance again, so a transfer that lost the race to another one meets the balance that one left, and rolls back by its own rule where it no longer holds. HQL's own tests run that race over SQLite: two of these transfers of 100 start together from a balance of 150, both pass the balance check, one commits, and the other rolls back on the balance after a retry or ends conflict, with no half of it left. A constraint violation is never retried, since the same rows would be refused again.

A retried attempt undoes what it wrote to a participant and nothing else. A write to an endpoint outside the set, a target or sink to a file, a channel or a topic, or a log call, runs on every attempt and is rolled back by none. Where attempts is written as a number above 1, the checker warns of each such write, kind effect, naming the endpoint: `sink` to `audit` runs on every attempt of the scope and is not rolled back. A write wanted once per outcome is written after the scope, from its value; a log line per attempt is often what is wanted, and the warning says what it is.

Any other failure inside the block, a division by zero, a lost connection, rolls the attempt back before it is reported, so a program that stops leaves no half-made transfer.

The ledger case of hql-demo runs this transfer against PostgreSQL 17: twice it commits, and the third time it rolls back on the sender's balance.

docs.title: What the kind promises
docs.text:
The statements read the same over every table; what a scope guarantees is the kind's.

Kind One scope holds insert, update, delete postgres every table of one database, at ReadCommitted unless the scope names RepeatableRead or Serializable all three, as one statement each sqlite every table of one database file, at Serializable, the one level it offers all three; a Decimal computed on the server is a float spark, a Delta table one table, and at most one statement that changes it: a Delta table commits one statement of itself all three where the table's format allows it

A set of two kinds, or two databases, is refused where the program is checked: no scope spans them, and nothing runs weaker than it was asked to. Two Delta tables that must change together are two commits, and the scope has no form for it; coordinating them is a later record.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 20 turns from the transactions to what they leave behind, and its merge page is the analytical counterpart of update: a table kept up to date by key, whole.

docs.title: Bronze, silver and gold
docs.text:
A lakehouse keeps tables as files in object storage, with a transaction log beside them, and answers SQL over them. Databricks is one; Apache Spark with Delta Lake over an S3 bucket is another, built from open-source parts, and the spark kind of chapter 17 reaches either. What a lakehouse holds is the shop's analytical side, and data platforms name its layers by their metals.

Bronze is what arrived, as it arrived. Silver is what passed the checks, typed, one row per fact. Gold is what a report reads, already aggregated at the grain the report asks. Each layer has a load rule, and the rule is what the layer promises:

Layer Holds Load Promise bronze every message, raw append only, never changed nothing is lost; a silver load can be run again from here silver every valid fact, typed, once append the new, deduplicated by key one row per fact; a sum over it is right gold one row per report grain replaced whole by each run what a reader sees is one run's answer

In the shop, bronze is the JetStream subject itself, kept by the stream; silver and gold are Delta tables:
