checkout ──▶ orders.raw ──▶ validate ──ok──▶ orders_silver ──▶ customer_revenue
             (bronze)          │             (silver)          (gold)
                               └──err──▶ orders.rejected
                                         (dead letters)

[endpoint.orders_silver]
kind = "spark"
url_env = "LAKEHOUSE_URL"
table = "default.orders_silver"
order = ["id"]
mode = "append"

[endpoint.orders_silver.fields.amount]
type = "DECIMAL(12,2)"

[endpoint.customer_revenue]
kind = "spark"
url_env = "LAKEHOUSE_URL"
table = "default.customer_revenue"
order = ["customer"]
mode = "replace"

[endpoint.customer_revenue.fields.total]
type = "DECIMAL(12,2)"

A DECIMAL column states how many digits it holds, so the boundary names the type each amount is written as, and the amounts read back with two decimal places.

docs.title: Bronze to silver
docs.text:
The load is the quarantine of chapter 16 with four ids changed: the subject in place of the topic, a Delta table in place of the clean table, and a dead-letter subject in place of the quarantine table.

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

type EventData : DataContract = {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String

    require amount >= 0 as non_negative
    require ["order_placed", "order_shipped", "payment_failed"] | contains(kind) as known_kind
}

type Rejected {
    id      : Int
    message : Data
    rules   : List<String>
}

tap("orders_raw")
| validate(EventData)
| fork {
    silver =
        oks()
        | map(e => Event(id = e.id, kind = e.kind, customer = e.customer, amount = e.amount, at = e.at))
        | sink("orders_silver"),
    rejected =
        errs()
        | map(e => Rejected(
            id = match e.value.id { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 },
            message = e.value,
            rules = e.violations | map(v => v.rule)))
        | sink("orders_rejected"),
}

{silver: Step, rejected: Step}

sink("orders_silver") appends rows as they arrive, in statements of up to 500, each one commit to the table's log. The dead letters are a subject a stream keeps, so they are themselves a source another program reads, to repair or to count:

rejected : Stream<Rejected> = tap("orders_rejected")
rejected | map(r => {id: r.id, rules: r.rules})

{id: 3, rules: ["EventData.amount.type"]}
{id: 5, rules: ["EventData.customer.missing"]}
{id: 7, rules: ["EventData.non_negative"]}
{id: 8, rules: ["EventData.known_kind"]}

This load keeps the first half of silver's promise, every valid fact and only those, and not the second: a message the subject delivers twice is appended twice. The next three pages are the second half.

docs.title: Silver to gold
docs.text:
The report reads a table that ends, so it reads it whole, and writes the gold table over the one before it:

type Revenue {
    customer : String
    orders   : Int
    total    : Decimal
}

events : Seq<Event> = source("orders_silver")
events
| filter(e => e.kind == "order_placed")
| group(by = e => e.customer)
| map(g => Revenue(customer = g.key, orders = g.items | size, total = g.items | map(e => e.amount) | sum))
| target("customer_revenue")

Step

Under mode = "replace" the new rows take the place of the old ones in one commit, so a reader of the gold table never sees it empty:

revenue : Seq<Revenue> = source("customer_revenue")
revenue

[{customer: "ada", orders: 1, total: 120.50}, {customer: "grace", orders: 1, total: 42.00}]

Of the eight raw orders, four passed; of those, ada's first and grace's are the placed ones, and linus's only placed order was the one sent as "free".

The two programs share no state but the silver table. The first runs for as long as messages arrive; the second runs when a report is wanted and reads whatever the first has committed by then. Gold is cheap to throw away and rebuild, which is why it is replaced; silver is the one copy of each fact, which is why it is appended to and never replaced; bronze is the record of what was received, which is why it is never touched at all.

docs.title: Deduplication
docs.text:
A sum over the replay is wrong, and the amount it is wrong by is the whole motivation for this page:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows | filter(r => r.kind == "order_placed") | map(r => r.amount) | sum

253.73

The right answer is 188.49: orders 2 and 4 are counted twice, and order 6 is counted at both its amounts. Three kinds of duplicate are in those nine rows, and each has its own step.

docs.title: Exact duplicates
docs.text:
A row delivered twice, identical in every field, is removed by distinct, which keeps each value once at its first position:

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows | distinct | map(r => r.id)

[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 6]

That is what at-least-once delivery produces: the subject of chapter 17 delivers a message again when a reader stopped before acknowledging it, and the message is the same bytes both times. distinct is the whole answer where every copy is exact. It is not the answer for order 6, whose two copies differ.

docs.title: Duplicates by key
docs.text:
Two rows with one key are the same fact, and one of them is the one to keep. Which one is a rule the pipeline states. For a correction, the latest by at:

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | max_by(r => r.at))
| somes
| sort(by = r => r.id)
| map(r => {id: r.id, amount: r.amount, at: r.at})

[{amount: 120.50, at: "2026-11-01T09:15:00Z", id: 1}, {amount: 42.00, at: "2026-11-01T09:20:00Z", id: 2}, {amount: 42.00, at: "2026-11-01T09:21:00Z", id: 3}, {amount: 7.99, at: "2026-11-01T10:02:00Z", id: 4}, {amount: 120.50, at: "2026-11-02T08:00:00Z", id: 5}, {amount: 18.00, at: "2026-11-02T11:50:00Z", id: 6}]

Read step by step: group(by = r => r.id) is one group per key, each holding every row with that key in input order; max_by(r => r.at) picks the row with the latest timestamp out of each group, an Option since a group could be empty; somes unwraps; sort puts the keys in order, since a set of groups has none. Six rows, order 6 at its corrected amount.

In SQL this is the pattern every warehouse carries:

select * from (
  select *, row_number() over (partition by id order by at desc) as n
  from silver_replayed
) where n = 1

partition by id is group(by = r => r.id), order by at desc with n = 1 is max_by(r => r.at), and nothing is numbered, because the row wanted is named by what makes it the one to keep rather than by its position after a sort. Keeping the first version instead, the fact as first reported, is min_by:

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | min_by(r => r.at))
| somes
| filter(r => r.id == 6)
| map(r => r.amount)

{15.25}

max_by and min_by take any Orderable key, so the rule may be a timestamp, a version number, or a comparison of two rows written out. Of two copies equal under the rule, the one earlier in the input is kept. Where they are the same row, as the exact duplicates are, that is no choice at all; where they differ, a rule that ends in a key no two rows share decides between them, and Windows writes one with then. row_number itself is there too, as the step over.

The sum, over the deduplicated rows:

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | max_by(r => r.at))
| somes
| filter(r => r.kind == "order_placed")
| map(r => r.amount)
| sum

188.49

docs.title: Duplicates with no key
docs.text:
A row with no key is identified by its content. Two deliveries of one webhook body carry the same fields, written in another key order or with 42.00 for 42, and differ in when each arrived, so distinct keeps both. The fingerprint of a Data tree is the SHA-256 of its canonical JSON, and two trees equal under HQL equality have one fingerprint. It is the key the rows do not have:

from crypto.digest import *

type Delivery {
    received : String
    body     : Data
}

deliveries = [
    Delivery(received = "2026-11-01T09:15:02Z", body = Data("{\"customer\": \"c-17\", \"sku\": \"tea\", \"amount\": 42.00}", Json)),
    Delivery(received = "2026-11-01T09:15:09Z", body = Data("{\"amount\": 42, \"sku\": \"tea\", \"customer\": \"c-17\"}", Json)),
    Delivery(received = "2026-11-01T09:16:40Z", body = Data("{\"customer\": \"c-21\", \"sku\": \"jam\", \"amount\": 6.50}", Json))
]
deliveries
| group(by = d => fingerprint(d.body))
| map(g => g.items | min_by(d => d.received))
| somes
| sort(by = d => d.received)
| map(d => d.body)

[{amount: 42.00, customer: "c-17", sku: "tea"}, {amount: 6.50, customer: "c-21", sku: "jam"}]

The step is the one of Duplicates by key, with fingerprint(d.body) as the key and the first delivery as the one to keep. A fingerprint is a String, so a load may write it as a column and the merge page match on it as on any key. crypto.digest and canonical JSON are chapter 30.

docs.title: In the load
docs.text:
Deduplication belongs in the load that writes silver, once, at the grain of a fact. A batch load reads the replay whole, deduplicates and writes. It writes to the lakehouse, so it is shown checked: Step is what hql check prints for a pipeline that ends in target, a program whose result is what it wrote:

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | max_by(r => r.at))
| somes
| sort(by = r => r.id)
| target("orders_silver")

Step

A streaming load cannot group a stream that never ends, and the checker refuses it, as chapter 14 showed for a sum. It deduplicates within each micro-batch instead, and sort makes each batch a List of the declared record, which is what sink writes as rows:

events : Stream<Event> = tap("orders_raw")
events
| collect(500)
| map(batch => batch
    | group(by = r => r.id)
    | map(g => g.items | max_by(r => r.at))
    | somes
    | sort(by = r => r.id))
| emit
| sink("orders_silver")

Step

Two copies that land in different batches are not caught by this program, and that is a limit of what a bounded window can know. The merge page is the complement: deduplication against what the table already holds.

docs.title: Grain and keys
docs.text:
Before a row can be a duplicate, it has to be clear what one row stands for. That is the table's grain: the thing in the business that one row describes. The shop's silver table has one row per event; its gold table has one row per customer. A row is a duplicate when the table already holds a row for the same thing, and "the same thing" is decided by the grain, not by the row's contents.

The key is the field, or fields, that name the thing at the table's grain. Two kinds of key are told apart:

  • a primary key names a row and is given by whoever produced it: the event's id, which the checkout assigned. It is unique by construction and means nothing to the business.
  • a business key names the thing in the business's own terms: the customer's name, the order's number on the invoice, the pair of a customer and a day. It is what two systems that never shared an id agree on.

The silver table's key is the primary key id. The gold table's key is the business key customer. A table at the grain of a customer-day has the composite business key of the two.

docs.title: The replay
docs.text:
silver_replayed is the shop's six valid events as a replay of the subject delivered them. Reading it as Events, the rows, the distinct rows, and the distinct ids are three different counts:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
[rows | size, rows | distinct | size, rows | map(r => r.id) | distinct | size]

[9, 7, 6]

Nine rows arrived. Seven are distinct as values: two events were delivered twice, identical to the byte. Six ids are distinct: one event was delivered twice with different contents, a correction. At the grain of an event, the table should hold six rows, and which six is the question of the next page.

The ids that occur more than once, with how often and with which amounts:

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows
| group(by = r => r.id)
| filter(g => (g.items | size) > 1)
| map(g => {id: g.key, copies: g.items | size, amounts: g.items | map(r => r.amount) | distinct})

{{amounts: [42.00], copies: 2, id: 2}, {amounts: [7.99], copies: 2, id: 4}, {amounts: [15.25, 18.00], copies: 2, id: 6}}

Order 6 is the one whose copies disagree: placed for 15.25, then corrected to 18.00 five minutes later.

docs.title: Another grain
docs.text:
The same rows at another grain are a different table with a different key. One row per customer per day, keyed by both:

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows
| group(by = r => {customer: r.customer, day: r.at.slice(0, 10)})
| map(g => {customer: g.key.customer, day: g.key.day, events: g.items | size})

{{customer: "ada", day: "2026-11-01", events: 1}, {customer: "grace", day: "2026-11-01", events: 3}, {customer: "linus", day: "2026-11-01", events: 2}, {customer: "ada", day: "2026-11-02", events: 3}}

The counts are wrong, because they were taken over the replay and not over the deduplicated events: grace has two events on the first day, not three. A gold table is only as right as the silver table it is built from, which is why deduplication is silver's job and is done once, at the grain of a fact, before any report is built at any other grain.

docs.title: What a key is to the checker
docs.text: A declared record has no field marked as its key, and the configuration of a table has none yet either. The key is stated where it is used: in the by of a group, in the left and right of a join, in the key of a to_map, which refuses two values under one key as an evaluation error, and, as design, in the key of a write mode on the merge page.

docs.title: Incremental loads
docs.text: A load that reads everything every time is simple and, past a certain size, impossible. An incremental load reads only what is new since the last one. There are two places the pipeline can learn where "new" starts: from the table it writes, or from the system it reads.

docs.title: A watermark the table holds
docs.text:
If every fact carries a timestamp, the latest one in the table is the watermark: everything after it is new. The load reads the watermark, filters the incoming rows by it, and appends:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

current  : Seq<Event> = source("ledger")
incoming : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")

watermark = current | map(o => o.at) | max

incoming
| filter(o => o.at > watermark.unwrap_or(""))
| map(o => {id: o.id, at: o.at})

[{at: "2026-11-02T11:50:00Z", id: 6}]

The ledger holds the six orders as first reported, so its watermark is order 6's first timestamp, and the only row after it is the correction. max over an empty table is none, and unwrap_or("") makes the first load a full one.

A watermark is only as good as the timestamp: a row that arrives late, with an at before the watermark, is never loaded. The replay has one, the second copy of order 4, which here is harmless because it is an exact duplicate of a row the table holds, and in general is the reason a watermark load is paired with the merge of the previous page, or replaced by a position the reading side keeps.

docs.title: A position the server keeps
docs.text:
The durable consumer of chapter 17 is an incremental load with no watermark in the program at all. The server records how far the consumer has read, so each run of the load is given only what was published since the run before, and the program is the plain append:

events : Stream<Event> = tap("billing")
events | sink("orders_silver")

Step

A message is acknowledged once the program asks for the next one, so a run that fails is given its last message again, and the silver table it appends to needs the deduplication of this chapter exactly once: at that message. A late message is no problem, because the position is in the stream's order, not the message's timestamp.

The two mechanisms suit the two sides. A watermark is what an analytical table can offer a batch load over another table, where no server keeps a position for it. A consumer is what a transactional system offers a streaming load, and it is the better of the two whenever it is there.

docs.title: The three loads together
docs.text:
Load Reads Writes Guards against full the whole source replace nothing; it starts over incremental by watermark rows after the table's latest timestamp append reading what is already held incremental by consumer messages after the server's position append or sink reading what is already held, and late arrival

None of them guards against a duplicate on its own; that is the deduplication in the load, or the merge mode of the table. Bronze is loaded in full and never again; silver is loaded incrementally and merged; gold is rebuilt in full from silver. The layers of the first page are the three loads, one each.

docs.title: 20. OLAP
docs.text:
Chapter 19 was the shop's transactions as they happen. This chapter is what they leave behind. The owner does not ask the order topic a question; the owner asks how much each customer spent this month, which day of the week sells most, and whether refunds are rising. Those are questions over history, over every order rather than the next one, and the tables they are asked of are the shop's OLAP side: online analytical processing, the warehouse, the lakehouse, the place a report reads.

The two sides differ in almost every way that matters to a pipeline, and a platform that serves both, as Databricks does, keeps them apart on purpose:

OLTP OLAP What a row is one fact as it happened: an order, a payment one fact at a chosen grain: an order, a customer-day, a customer What the table holds the current state the history How it is written one row at a time, as the fact occurs in batches, by a load that runs on a schedule or as a stream lands How it is read one row, by key many rows, by scan, aggregated The shape of its pipeline tap, decide each value, sink source whole, group and sum, target What goes wrong a row that does not decode a row that arrives twice, late, or corrected

The last line is the subject of most of this chapter. A transactional pipeline delivers each message at least once, and a message delivered twice into a transactional table is a duplicate row to be found later. In an analytical table a duplicate is a wrong total in a report, and the pipeline that loads the table is where it is removed. Every load of an analytical table therefore answers three questions: what a row stands for, which rows are the same row, and which of the same rows is the one to keep.

In the terms of chapter 14, an analytical load is usually a batch: a source that ends, whole-input steps over it, a target that replaces or appends. It need not be. The silver table of chapter 17 is an analytical table filled by a stream, and the pages here show the same deduplication over a batch and over micro-batches. The side a table is on says what its rows mean; whether it is loaded by a batch or by a stream is the type of the input.

docs.title: The pages
docs.text:
Page What it covers Bronze, silver and gold the three layers of a lakehouse, what each promises, and the load rule of each Grain and keys what one row stands for, the key that names it, and a duplicate at each grain Deduplication exact duplicates with distinct, duplicates by key with group and max_by, and a replayed stream as their source Windows one value per row from its place in its partition: over, ranks, neighbours and frames, and a total order with then Merge a table kept up to date by key: insert or update, today as a pipeline and as design as a write mode Incremental loads loading only what is new: a watermark the table holds, and a position the server keeps

The pages run against the shop's vault, --project examples/pipelines/shop. A program that writes to the lakehouse is shown checked, with the type hql check prints; a pipeline that ends in target or sink is Step, the type of a program whose result is what it wrote. The file silver_replayed is the shop's six valid events as a replay delivered them: two delivered twice, one corrected after the fact, and one delivered late.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Part III reads a different kind of data. Chapter 21 opens a folder of documents and asks it the questions chapter 6 asked a table.

docs.title: Merge
docs.text: The write modes of chapter 16 are create, append and replace, and each is about the table as a whole. An analytical table that is kept up to date needs a fourth, about rows: a row whose key the table does not hold is inserted, and a row whose key it does hold is updated. Warehouses call it upsert or merge, and Delta Lake calls the statement MERGE INTO.

docs.title: Merge as a pipeline
docs.text:
Merge is deduplication by key over the union of what the table holds and what arrives. The current rows and the incoming rows are read, concatenated, and deduplicated with the same rule as the previous page, and the result replaces the table:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

current  : Seq<Event> = source("ledger")
incoming : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")

current
| concat(incoming)
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | max_by(r => r.at))
| somes
| sort(by = r => r.id)
| map(r => {id: r.id, amount: r.amount})

[{amount: 120.50, id: 1}, {amount: 42.00, id: 2}, {amount: 42.00, id: 3}, {amount: 7.99, id: 4}, {amount: 120.50, id: 5}, {amount: 18.00, id: 6}]

The ledger held six orders; the replay brought nine rows; the result is six rows, with order 6 updated to its corrected amount and the other five unchanged. An incoming row with a new id would be inserted by the same steps, since a group of one keeps its one row. Written back under mode = "replace", the table is the merge, in one transaction:

current  : Seq<Event> = source("orders_silver")
incoming : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")

current
| concat(incoming)
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | max_by(r => r.at))
| somes
| sort(by = r => r.id)
| target("orders_silver")

Step

The merge rule, which copy wins, is the max_by and nothing else. A rule that prefers the row already held is min_by over the same key; a rule that prefers the incoming row whatever its timestamp is last over each group, since concat put the current rows first.

This reads and rewrites the whole table, which is right for a table of thousands of rows and wrong for one of billions. The cost is the point of having a write mode for it. A row changed in place, one at a time as a transaction does it, is update of the transfer page; a merge is the whole table kept up to date by key.

docs.title: Merge as a write mode
docs.text:
Design only

This section describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: names and keys may change before it ships.

A table's key is a fact about the table, so it is configured beside it, and mode = "merge" makes the key the rule of every write:

[endpoint.orders_silver]
kind = "spark"
url_env = "LAKEHOUSE_URL"
table = "default.orders_silver"
order = ["id"]
mode = "merge"
key = ["id"]

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | max_by(r => r.at))
| somes
| sort(by = r => r.id)
| target("orders_silver")

target sends only the deduplicated rows, and the system does the rest: a row whose key the table holds replaces that row, and a row whose key it does not hold is inserted, in one commit. A lakehouse runs it as MERGE INTO, a PostgreSQL table as INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, a SQLite table as INSERT OR REPLACE. The program is the one above, and which statement the kind runs is the kind's business, as a transaction is today.

Two rules follow. A write under mode = "merge" to an endpoint with no key is a check error naming the key. And the rows a target sends must themselves be unique by the key, so the deduplication stays in the program: a merge is told which row to keep among the incoming ones by the pipeline, and which to keep between an incoming row and a held one by the mode.

sink under mode = "merge" writes each row as it arrives, inserting or updating one at a time, which is the streaming load of the previous page without its blind spot: a copy that lands in a later batch updates the row the earlier one inserted.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text: group makes one group of the rows with one key, and a step after it reduces each group to one value. Some questions keep every row and add a value that depends on the row's neighbours: the position of an order among its customer's orders, the balance after each ledger entry, the change from the previous revision. In SQL those are window functions, written OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...). In HQL they are the step over.

docs.title: One value per row
docs.text:
over(by, order, into) partitions a sequence by the key by gives each row, orders each partition by order, and calls into once per row, with the row and its Window: the row's place in its ordered partition. The result is a List holding what into gave for each row, at the row's input position. No row is merged or dropped.

row_number is the row's position in its partition, from 1. Ranking the replay's rows within each id, latest first, and keeping the first of each is the deduplication of the previous page in its SQL form, row_number() over (partition by id order by at desc) = 1:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows
| over(by = r => r.id, order = (a, b) => compare(b.at, a.at),
       into = (r, w) => {row: r, n: w | row_number})
| filter(x => x.n == 1)
| map(x => {id: x.row.id, amount: x.row.amount})

[{amount: 120.50, id: 1}, {amount: 42.00, id: 2}, {amount: 42.00, id: 3}, {amount: 7.99, id: 4}, {amount: 120.50, id: 5}, {amount: 18.00, id: 6}]

order = (a, b) => compare(b.at, a.at) is a comparison of two rows, here reversed for latest first; order may also be a key, r => r.at, for ascending order. The kept rows are in input order, each at its own row's position. Without by, every row is in one partition.

group with max_by gives the same six rows, and is the shorter program when one row per key is all a step wants. over is the step when a row's position is itself the value, or when every row stays.

docs.title: Ranks
docs.text:
Rows equal under order keep their input order, so row_number never gives two rows one position. rank gives rows equal under the order one rank and skips the positions they share; dense_rank does not skip:

type Score {
    name  : String
    score : Int
}

scores = [
    Score(name = "a", score = 9),
    Score(name = "b", score = 7),
    Score(name = "c", score = 9),
    Score(name = "d", score = 5),
]
scores
| over(order = (x, y) => compare(y.score, x.score),
       into = (s, w) => [w | row_number, w | rank, w | dense_rank])

[[1, 1, 1], [3, 3, 2], [2, 1, 1], [4, 4, 3]]

a and c tie at 9. a is first in the input, so its row_number is 1 and c's is 2; both have rank 1. b has rank 3 and dense rank 2.

docs.title: A total order
docs.text:
A row kept by its position among equals is kept by where it happened to arrive. Two revisions of one order written in the same second are equal by at, and max_by, like row_number, keeps the earlier in the input:

type Revision {
    id     : Int
    at     : String
    seq    : Int
    amount : Int
}

rows = [
    Revision(id = 6, at = "2026-11-02T11:50:00Z", seq = 1, amount = 15),
    Revision(id = 6, at = "2026-11-02T11:50:00Z", seq = 2, amount = 18),
]
rows
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | max_by(r => r.at))
| somes
| map(r => r.amount)

{15}

With the rows in the other order the result is 18. then composes two comparisons, the second deciding where the first is Equal; a comparison that ends in a key no two rows share, here the change sequence seq, is a total order, and the row kept no longer depends on input order:

rows = [
    Revision(id = 6, at = "2026-11-02T11:50:00Z", seq = 1, amount = 15),
    Revision(id = 6, at = "2026-11-02T11:50:00Z", seq = 2, amount = 18),
]
rows
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | max_by((a, b) => compare(a.at, b.at) | then(compare(a.seq, b.seq))))
| somes
| map(r => r.amount)

{18}

docs.title: Neighbours
docs.text:
lag is the row before in the partition and lead the row after, each an Option, none past either end. lag(n) and lead(n) reach n rows:

[1, 4, 9]
| over(order = x => x,
       into = (x, w) => [w | lag | unwrap_or(0), w | lead | unwrap_or(0)])

[[0, 4], [1, 9], [4, 0]]

docs.title: Frames
docs.text:
A frame is a list of rows of the partition, in order. running is the rows from the first up to and including the row, rows(before, after) the rows from before positions before to after after, clipped at the ends, and whole the partition. An aggregate over a frame is an ordinary step over a list. The balance after each ledger entry, per account:

type Posting {
    account : String
    seq     : Int
    amount  : Int
}

ledger = [
    Posting(account = "a", seq = 1, amount = 100),
    Posting(account = "b", seq = 1, amount = 50),
    Posting(account = "a", seq = 2, amount = -30),
    Posting(account = "b", seq = 2, amount = 20),
    Posting(account = "a", seq = 3, amount = 10),
]
ledger
| over(by = t => t.account, order = t => t.seq,
       into = (t, w) => w | running | map(x => x.amount) | sum)

[100, 50, 70, 70, 80]

running counts rows, as SQL's ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW does. SQL's default frame with an ORDER BY also takes in the rows equal to the current one; running does not. A moving sum, and the partition's first, last and size:

[1, 2, 3, 4]
| over(order = x => x,
       into = (x, w) => [w | rows(1, 1) | sum, w | first, w | last, w | size, w | whole | sum])

[[3, 1, 4, 4, 10], [6, 1, 4, 4, 10], [9, 1, 4, 4, 10], [7, 1, 4, 4, 10]]

docs.title: The first n of each key
docs.text:
Keeping the two latest orders of each customer is row_number and a filter. A record literal is Data, whose fields are Option<Data> and not ordered, so into builds a declared record to compare n with <=:

type Order {
    id       : Int
    customer : String
    at       : Int
}

type Ranked {
    id : Int
    n  : Int
}

orders = [
    Order(id = 1, customer = "ada", at = 1),
    Order(id = 2, customer = "ada", at = 3),
    Order(id = 3, customer = "bob", at = 2),
    Order(id = 4, customer = "ada", at = 2),
    Order(id = 5, customer = "bob", at = 1),
    Order(id = 6, customer = "ada", at = 4),
]
orders
| over(by = o => o.customer, order = (a, b) => compare(b.at, a.at),
       into = (o, w) => Ranked(id = o.id, n = w | row_number))
| filter(x => x.n <= 2)
| map(x => x.id)

[2, 3, 5, 6]

docs.title: What over refuses
docs.text: A window is a view of its partition while into runs. into may not give one back, in any type: the checker refuses into = (x, w) => [w]. And over takes a Seq: a partition of a stream is never complete, since a stream may not end, so over of a Stream is refused like group of one. Inside collect(n), over ranks each batch, and a row in one batch is not compared with a row in another.

docs.title: 21. A vault of documents
docs.text: The shelf of chapter 6 was a list written by hand. Here the same books are documents in a folder, and HQL reads the folder. This part of the book is about knowledge: documents, the links between them, their meaning, and the agents that read them.

docs.title: A vault is a folder
docs.text:
A vault is a directory of Markdown and HyperMarkDown documents, marked as one by an .hmd/ directory at its root. The reading-club vault looks like this:

examples/reading-club/
├── authors/
│   ├── frank-herbert.hmd
│   ├── jrr-tolkien.hmd
│   ├── mary-shelley.hmd
│   ├── virginia-woolf.hmd
│   └── walt-whitman.hmd
├── books/
│   ├── a-room-of-ones-own.hmd
│   ├── dune.hmd
│   ├── frankenstein.hmd
│   ├── leaves-of-grass.hmd
│   ├── mrs-dalloway.hmd
│   ├── the-common-reader.hmd
│   └── the-hobbit.hmd
├── club.hmd
├── frankenstein-inspires-dune.hmd
├── librarian.hmd
├── .hmd/config.toml
└── .hql/config.toml

.hmd/ makes the directory a vault. .hql/config.toml makes it an HQL project too, which configures the programs run in it; the two are separate, and a vault need not be a project (chapter 13).

The vault's .hmd/config.toml says where its cards start, with the key wiki: a path against the vault root, doc/wiki when the file does not set it. The reading club keeps its cards at the vault root, so it says so:

wiki = "."

That directory is the namespace root. A document is a card exactly when it lies below it, and a card's path is written from it, so books/dune.hmd above. A file of the vault outside it, a README.md beside .hmd/ in a vault whose wiki is doc/wiki, is not a card. A card is a .hmd file, or a .md or .markdown file whose body is plain Markdown.

Each document is a card. A card has a header of metadata and a body someone wrote:

---
title: Dune
metadata:
  category: book
  author: Frank Herbert
  year: 1965
  genre: novel
  pages: 412
  status: reading
---
# Dune

A novel by [[frank-herbert]]. A desert planet, a spice, and a family that inherits both.

A program run inside a vault reads it: hql takes the nearest directory at or above the program's file that holds .hmd/, or at or above the working directory for an expression or standard input. --vault <directory> names one instead, and --bare runs with none. The cards are read through the builtin package hmd, which the reading-club's project imports for every program ("The vault itself" below):

hql --vault examples/reading-club eval 'cards | size'

cards | size

15

docs.title: cards
docs.text:
cards is every card of the vault, as a sequence. Its order is the order a sorted walk of the folder reaches each document — the entries of each directory by name, depth first — so a program answers the same on every machine:

cards | take(4) | map(c => c.name)

["frank-herbert", "jrr-tolkien", "mary-shelley", "virginia-woolf"]

A card has the fields of a document: its name (the file stem), title, path, format, body, its kind, and metadata, the header's tree.

docs.title: A link is an optional card
docs.text:
@[[name]] refers to a card by name: @ followed by the link a document writes, [[name]]. A link may point at a document nobody has written yet, so its type is Option<Card>, and reading a field through it reads through the option:

@[[dune]].title

"Dune"

@[[nowhere]].title

none

docs.title: Metadata is Data
docs.text:
A card's metadata is the Data of chapter 2, so every question from chapters 2 and 6 applies. The books are the cards whose category says so:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| map(c => c.title)

["A Room of One's Own", "Dune", "Frankenstein", "Leaves of Grass", "Mrs Dalloway", "The Common Reader", "The Hobbit"]

docs.title: The reading list
docs.text:
The club's reading list is the books still to read, by title:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| sort(by = c => c.title)
| map(c => c.title)

["Leaves of Grass", "The Common Reader", "The Hobbit"]

Read it as three steps, each consuming the one before: filter decides each card on its own, sort needs every card before it can place the first, and map turns each card into its title. Nothing is stored in between, and nothing is a loop.

No one maintains this list. Mark a book status: done in its header and the next run of the query no longer lists it.

docs.title: Writing cards
docs.text:
The formats of chapter 8 apply to a card as to any value. A card written as Markdown is its body; a list of cards, a list of links:

cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "author") | markdown

- [[frank-herbert]]
- [[jrr-tolkien]]
- [[mary-shelley]]
- [[virginia-woolf]]
- [[walt-whitman]]

docs.title: Grouping cards
docs.text:
group partitions the books by a header value, as it partitioned the shelf:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| group(by = c => c.metadata.status)
| map(g => {status: g.key, books: g.items | map(c => c.title)})

{{books: ["A Room of One's Own", "Frankenstein"], status: "done"}, {books: ["Dune", "Mrs Dalloway"], status: "reading"}, {books: ["Leaves of Grass", "The Common Reader", "The Hobbit"], status: "todo"}}

A typed view of a card works as the views of chapter 6 did, and the pages per author are a map over each group and a sum — map, then reduce:

fn pages(c: Card) : Int = match c.metadata.pages { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| group(by = c => c.metadata.author)
| map(g => {author: g.key, pages: g.items | map(pages) | sum})

{{author: "Virginia Woolf", pages: 610}, {author: "Frank Herbert", pages: 412}, {author: "Mary Shelley", pages: 280}, {author: "Walt Whitman", pages: 145}, {author: "J. R. R. Tolkien", pages: 310}}

docs.title: Kinds of card
docs.text:
A card whose header declares a relation between two other cards is a RelationCard; every other card is a ConceptCard. of_type keeps the cards of one kind:

cards | of_type(RelationCard) | map(c => c.title)

["Frankenstein inspires Dune"]

Chapter 22 is about what that relation means: cards and the links between them form a graph.

docs.title: The vault itself
docs.text:
cards is a binding of the builtin package hmd, cards = vault.cards, over vault, the value the host seeds when it is given a vault:

[vault.name, vault.cards | size | text]

["reading-club", 15]

A vault is HyperMarkdown's, and so are vault and cards. They are bound while the package hmd is active, and a run that has a vault activates it: the vault found at or above the program, or the one --vault names. A program in a vault writes cards with no import.

A run with no vault activates hmd by importing it: import hmd in the program, --import hmd on the command line, or [modules] import in the project's .hql/config.toml:

[modules]
import = ["hmd"]

With no vault and no import, cards names what is missing:

cards | size

check error[unknown-name]: `cards` is HyperMarkdown's: write `import hmd`, or run with `--import hmd`, to bind it
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | cards | size
  | ^^^^^

With hmd imported and no vault, cards has nothing to read, and the check says so:

import hmd
cards | size

check error[unknown-name]: `cards` needs a vault: run inside one or pass --vault <directory>
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | cards | size
  | ^^^^^

docs.title: A vault is a namespace
docs.text:
A card is a file with a place in a vault, and the place is what makes it addressable by name: [[dune]] names a card because there is one tree to resolve the name in. That tree is a namespace, rooted at the vault's namespace root, and a vault is exactly one namespace. cards holds what a wikilink can reach and nothing else, and a card's path is its place in the vault, relative to the namespace root, so the cards of one folder are a filter on the path:

cards | filter(c => c.path | starts_with("books/")) | size

7

HQL resolves a reference exactly as HyperMarkdown does, through HyperMarkdown's own resolver, so hql and hmd lint always name the same card. A [[name]] in a card is looked up from that card: a path that opens with /, ./ or ../ is followed; otherwise a name the card imports, then the card's own folder and each folder above it, nearest first, then the folders it imports with *, and last a search of the whole vault. A search that finds two cards chooses neither, and the reference has to be qualified, [[books/dune]]. @[[dune]] in a program is resolved as though written at the namespace root. Where dune.hmd and dune.md sit side by side, [[dune]] is the .hmd card and [[dune.md]] the other, whose name keeps its extension.

docs.title: Other vaults
docs.text:
A second vault is a second namespace. It is reached as a configured endpoint of kind vault (endpoints by id), with its own cards and graph, and its cards are never merged into cards: a wikilink in one vault never resolves into another, and a relation between cards of two vaults is a join's result, not a link. The field station of the data sources examples configures two:

journal = source("journal")
archive = source("archive")
[journal.cards | map(c => c.name), archive.cards | map(c => c.name)]

[["kite", "owl", "wren"], ["finch", "heron"]]

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: A document that writes [[frank-herbert]] links to another. Chapter 22 follows the links, and the cards and links together are a graph.

docs.title: 22. Links and graphs
docs.text: A document that writes [[frankenstein]] links to another. The links of a vault make its cards a graph: cards are the nodes, links are the edges. This chapter follows links, builds graphs, and draws them.

docs.title: Following links
docs.text:
An edge goes from the card that wrote the link, its source, to the card it names, its target. uplinks gives the edges leaving a card, and downlinks the edges arriving at it:

@[[mrs-dalloway]] | uplinks

[mrs-dalloway -> virginia-woolf]

@[[virginia-woolf]] | downlinks | map(e => e.source)

["a-room-of-ones-own", "mrs-dalloway", "the-common-reader"]

A link in a body may carry data of its own, written after it in braces: [[bearer-tokens]] {relation: defines}. The edge holds it as e.data.

docs.title: Building a graph
docs.text:
Graph(cards) — or cards | Graph — is the graph of those cards and the links among them:

cards
| filter(c => c.name == "virginia-woolf" or c.metadata.author == "Virginia Woolf")
| Graph
| text

a-room-of-ones-own
  -> virginia-woolf
mrs-dalloway
  -> virginia-woolf
the-common-reader
  -> virginia-woolf
virginia-woolf
  -> a-room-of-ones-own
  -> mrs-dalloway
  -> the-common-reader

A graph is a value with two fields, both sets: its nodes, the cards, and its edges. The vault's whole graph is bound as graph:

{nodes: graph.nodes | size, edges: graph.edges | size}

{edges: 22, nodes: 14}

A graph can also be built from edges alone, Graph(edges), or from cards and edges together, Graph(nodes, edges). Its nodes are the cards given and every edge's endpoints:

@[[virginia-woolf]] | downlinks | Graph | text

a-room-of-ones-own
  -> virginia-woolf
mrs-dalloway
  -> virginia-woolf
the-common-reader
  -> virginia-woolf
virginia-woolf

docs.title: Growing a graph
docs.text:
expand(depth = n) starts from some cards and follows links outwards, n steps, in both directions. Every node it reaches records why it is present — which card it was reached from, and how far away:

@[[mrs-dalloway]] | expand(depth = 1) | text

club  (expanded from mrs-dalloway at depth 1)
  -> mrs-dalloway
mrs-dalloway
  -> virginia-woolf
virginia-woolf  (expanded from mrs-dalloway at depth 1)
  -> mrs-dalloway

direction = "uplinks" or "downlinks" follows links one way only. A graph of matches and their neighbours never claims that the neighbours matched: the reason travels with each node.

docs.title: A relation is an edge
docs.text:
The card frankenstein-inspires-dune declares a relation in its header:

---
title: Frankenstein inspires Dune
metadata:
  category: influence
  knowledge:
    type: Relation
    relation:
      source: frankenstein
      target: dune
---

In a graph such a card is not a node but the edge it declares, between the two cards it names:

cards | of_type(RelationCard) | Graph | text

dune  (expanded from frankenstein-inspires-dune at depth 1)
frankenstein  (expanded from frankenstein-inspires-dune at depth 1)
  -> dune

docs.title: Drawing a graph
docs.text:
A graph is written in a diagram format by the step named for it. mermaid writes a Mermaid diagram and d2 a D2 one; json writes the node-link form a graph library reads:

cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book") | Graph | mermaid

graph LR
  n0["a-room-of-ones-own"]
  n1["dune"]
  n2["frankenstein"]
  n3["leaves-of-grass"]
  n4["mrs-dalloway"]
  n5["the-common-reader"]
  n6["the-hobbit"]
  n2 --> n1

In a Markdown document — chapter 24 — a graph is written as a fenced d2 block, which documentation sites draw.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: expand grew a graph from a starting card. Chapter 23 finds the starting cards for a question in words.

docs.title: 23. Finding cards by meaning
docs.text: filter answers a question with a yes or no per card. Retrieval answers a question in words with a ranking: every card that matches, best first, each with a score. HQL has two retrievals over a vault's cards, both HyperMarkdown's, in the builtin package hmd.

docs.title: Lexical retrieval
docs.text:
lexical matches the words of a query against the words of each card. It needs nothing built in advance:

import hmd
cards | lexical("desert spice") | take(3)

[dune (0.2928), frankenstein-inspires-dune (0.2778), frankenstein (0.2471)]

Both retrievals are modules of the builtin package hmd, hmd.search.lexical and hmd.search.semantic, and hmd's prelude imports them: import hmd makes lexical and semantic steps of the program. The reading-club's project imports hmd for every program, so the import hmd above restates it. Without hmd, the name is not a step, and the error says which import provides it:

["desert spice"] | lexical("desert spice")

check error[unknown-name]: `lexical` is declared in the module `hmd.search.lexical`: write `import hmd`
 --> <expression>:1:20
  |
1 | ["desert spice"] | lexical("desert spice")
  |                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: A ranking holds hits
docs.text:
A ranking is a sequence of hits. A hit holds the card it retrieved, as value, and its score:

import hmd
cards
| lexical("desert spice")
| take(2)
| map(h => {card: h.value.name, score: h.score})

[{card: "dune", score: 0.2927674902397191}, {card: "frankenstein-inspires-dune", score: 0.2777641653663699}]

A score is evidence that a card is relevant to the query, not relevance itself, so every hit carries the retrieval that produced it — the model, the index, the metric, and whether the search was approximate:

import hmd
ranked = cards | lexical("desert")
{model: ranked.retrieval.model, metric: ranked.retrieval.metric, approximate: ranked.retrieval.approximate}

{approximate: false, metric: "cosine", model: "hql.hashbag.v1"}

take keeps a ranking a ranking, in the retrieval's order. Any other order is the program's own: sorting a ranking by another key makes it a plain sequence of hits.

docs.title: Retrieval, then the graph
docs.text:
A ranking is a collection of cards, so every step of the earlier chapters applies. expand grows a graph from the best hits, and the nodes it adds say they were reached, not retrieved:

import hmd
cards
| lexical("a creature and its maker")
| take(2)
| expand(depth = 1)
| text

club  (expanded from frankenstein at depth 1)
  -> dune
  -> frankenstein
  -> leaves-of-grass
dune  (expanded from frankenstein at depth 1)
frankenstein  (retrieved 0.2064)
  -> mary-shelley
  -> dune
leaves-of-grass  (expanded from walt-whitman at depth 1)
  -> walt-whitman
mary-shelley  (expanded from frankenstein at depth 1)
  -> frankenstein
walt-whitman  (retrieved 0.1261)
  -> leaves-of-grass

docs.title: Semantic retrieval
docs.text:
lexical matches spellings: a card that never uses the query's words scores nothing, and a card that uses common ones scores something. semantic scores by meaning, against embeddings a language model computed ahead of time into an index the vault names in .hql/config.toml:

[semantics]
index = ".hmd/index.sqlite"

Asked for a creature and its maker, semantic ranks Frankenstein, the relation card that names it, and Mary Shelley, though none of the three contains the word "creature":

import hmd
cards | semantic("a creature and its maker") | take(3) | map(h => h.value.title)

["Frankenstein", "Frankenstein inspires Dune", "Mary Shelley"]

The same question, by spelling, finds Frankenstein and then two cards that share only its small words:

import hmd
cards | lexical("a creature and its maker") | take(3) | map(h => h.value.title)

["Frankenstein", "Walt Whitman", "Librarian"]

A semantic ranking reports the model that embedded the cards, so two indexes built by two models are never compared by score:

import hmd
ranked = cards | semantic("a creature and its maker")
{model: ranked.retrieval.model, metric: ranked.retrieval.metric, approximate: ranked.retrieval.approximate}

{approximate: false, metric: "cosine", model: "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"}

The binary never loads a model: HyperMarkdown's hmd-semantics embeds the cards and builds the index, and embeds each question the index will be asked, named at build time with --query. The reading-club vault's index holds the three questions this book asks. A question it does not hold is a diagnostic naming the build command, not a ranking of nothing:

import hmd
cards | semantic("night hunting birds") | take(1)

execute failure[invalid-argument]: the index holds no vector for `night hunting birds`, and this binary has no model to make one: rerun `hmd-semantics build --query "night hunting birds"`
 --> <expression>:2:9
  |
2 | cards | semantic("night hunting birds") | take(1)
  |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

hql doctor checks the chain — vault, configuration, index, model, query vectors — and names the first part that is missing.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: A ranking, a graph and a reading list are values a program prints. Chapter 24 writes them into the document that asks for them, and builds the document from its queries.

docs.title: 24. Queries inside documents
docs.text: A document can hold the queries that compute parts of it. hql render runs them and builds the document they describe, so a reading list, an index or a status table is a query, not a list somebody keeps up to date.

docs.title: Cells
docs.text:
A cell is a fenced block whose info string is hql#eval or hql#query. This is examples/notebook/reading-list.hmd:

# The club's reading list

Built from the vault with `hql --vault examples/reading-club render`.

```hql#query id=books
cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
```

## Still to read

```hql#eval id=todo
books
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| sort(by = c => c.title)
| map(c => c.title)
```

## How far along

```hql#eval
{books: books | size, to_read: todo | size}
```

The fence's info string sets what hql render does with the block:

Fence Runs Writes output ```hql#eval yes yes ```hql#query yes no ```hql no no
  • A query cell, ```hql#query, is ```hql#eval hidden. It runs so that other cells can read its value by id, and its output is not written.
  • A fence marked plain ```hql is a code listing, not a cell. It is not checked and does not run, and every render leaves it as it is. An id= on it names nothing, so a cell that reads that name fails with an unknown name.

docs.title: Building the document
docs.text:
hql render runs every cell against the vault and writes the document with each cell replaced by its output, as Markdown:

hql --vault examples/reading-club render examples/notebook/reading-list.hmd

# The club's reading list

Built from the vault with `hql --vault examples/reading-club render`.

## Still to read

- Leaves of Grass
- The Common Reader
- The Hobbit

## How far along

| key     | value |
| ------- | ----- |
| books   | 7     |
| to_read | 3     |

The source is the program; the built document is its result. --write <file> writes the build to a file instead of standard output.

docs.title: Cells share values
docs.text:
A cell's info string carries attributes after its kind:

  • id=<name> exports the cell's value to the other cells of the document, under that name. books and todo above are such names.
  • hidden runs the cell and writes nothing, for a value other cells read. hql#query implies it.
  • replace or after chooses where that one cell's output goes.

Only a cell's value leaves it: a binding inside a cell stays in that cell. The cells form a dependency graph, and run in the order their reads require, not the order they are written in. A cycle or a duplicate id is an error naming the cells, and a cell that reads a failed one is skipped, saying which cell it waited on.

The document is checked as a whole before any cell runs, so a type error in the last cell stops the build before the first one runs.

docs.title: Keeping the cells
docs.text:
--emit after keeps every cell and writes its output after it, between two comments a Markdown preview does not display:

```hql#eval id=todo
books
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| sort(by = c => c.title)
| map(c => c.title)
```
<!-- hql:output id=todo hash=9c9f41e99b94 status=ok -->
- Leaves of Grass
- The Common Reader
- The Hobbit
<!-- /hql:output -->

With --in-place that rewrites the source itself, the way a notebook saves its outputs, and the next render replaces what is between the markers. The opening marker records the cell's id, a hash of its code and of the code of every cell it reads, and its status. An output whose hash differs from the cell's current one is stale, and an editor can say so without running anything.

--cell <id> runs one cell and the cells it reads, and rewrites only its output. --envelope json prints the built document and a record per cell — its id, span, hash, type, status, output and reports — for an editor to read.

docs.title: Cells that maintain a vault
docs.text:
Design only

This section describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: these cells do not run against the current binary, and names, types and outputs may change before they ship.

A vault's upkeep is a set of questions asked of the vault itself: which cards are related to this one, what does each category hold, which card does nothing link to. Each is a cell a card carries, and the hash in its saved output says when the answer is stale, so maintenance is a render, not a chore. A card of a vault's own wiki might end with these:

## Related

```hql#eval id=related
cards | semantic(this.title) | take(3) | map(h => h.value)
```

## Index

```hql#eval id=index
cards
| group(by = c => c.metadata.category)
| map(g => {category: g.key, cards: g.items | map(c => c.name)})
```

## Health

```hql#eval id=orphans
cards | filter(c => (c | downlinks | size) == 0) | map(c => c.name)
```

this is the card the cell is written in, so the related cards are the three nearest in meaning to its title, written below its body as links. A cell marked cached would keep its output until the hash of its code and its inputs changes, so a summary a model wrote (chapter 25) is computed once and read many times. The cell kinds exist today; this, cached and a semantic over a question the index was not built for are design direction.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 25 gives a language model the cards a query selected, runs an agent over them, and keeps the run as a value.

docs.title: 25. Agents and runs
docs.text:
Design only

This chapter describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: these programs do not run against the current binary, and names, types and outputs may change before it ships.

Most of the work around a language model is not the call itself. Choosing evidence, building the context, writing the prompt, giving the model tools, continuing a conversation and keeping what came back are dataflow, and HQL writes them as dataflow. Every stage is a typed value: what reached the model, what it called and what it answered are read the way a card is read.

The constructors in this chapter are pure and need no import. The steps that reach a model need import ai, which is how a program states that it may spend money and send text to a third party.

docs.title: An agent is a card
docs.text:
An agent is behaviour and configuration, written as a card. Its body is its instructions, and its agent header table configures it. This one is the reading-club vault's librarian.hmd:

---
title: Librarian
agent:
  model: default
  tools: [books_by]
  max_turns: 4
---
# Librarian

Answer questions about the club's shelf from the cards you are given and the
tools you have. Name the books you rely on. Say so when the shelf does not
answer the question.

Agent reads one from a card:

librarian = @[[librarian]] | Agent
librarian.tools

["books_by"]

A card is an agent only by saying it is one: Agent refuses a card with no agent table, and an unknown key in it, so a misspelt max_turn does not quietly select the default. model names a key of [ai.models] in the vault's .hql/config.toml, never a provider, so a committed card does not fix a vendor:

[ai]
recordings = ".hql/runs"

[ai.models.default]
api = "messages"
endpoint = "https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages"
model = "claude-sonnet-5-5"
max_tokens = 1024
temperature = 0

docs.title: Context and prompt
docs.text:
Context(label) turns values into what a model reads: one item per element, each written as markdown writes it, with where it came from:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| Context("unread")
| map(i => {label: i.label, source: i.provenance.name})

[{label: "unread", source: "leaves-of-grass"}, {label: "unread", source: "the-common-reader"}, {label: "unread", source: "the-hobbit"}]

A context is a Seq<ContextItem>, so contexts are combined with concat and narrowed with filter, like any other sequence. A ranking from chapter 23 keeps each hit's score and retrieval in its item, so cards | semantic(question) | take(10) | Context("evidence") is evidence that says how it was found.

Prompt(instructions) puts the task in front of the context. Its rendered field is the text exactly as sent:

p = cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| Context("unread")
| Prompt("Which unread book should the club start with?")

p.rendered

Which unread book should the club start with?

## unread

Source: leaves-of-grass

# Leaves of Grass

Poems by [[walt-whitman]], revised and enlarged for the rest of his life.

Source: the-common-reader

# The Common Reader

Essays by [[virginia-woolf]] on reading, written for readers rather than critics.

Source: the-hobbit

# The Hobbit

A novel by [[jrr-tolkien]]. A hobbit is talked into an adventure and comes home changed.

docs.title: Tools are functions
docs.text:
A tool is a named HQL function. Tool records its name, a description and the JSON Schema of its parameters, derived from their types:

fn books_by(author: String) : List<String> =
    cards | filter(c => c.metadata.author == author) | map(c => c.title) | List

Tool(books_by, "The titles on the shelf by one author")

Tool {name: "books_by", description: "The titles on the shelf by one author", parameters: {"properties":{"author":{"type":"string"}},"required":["author"],"type":"object"}}

A tool is pure. While the harness evaluates one for a model, every effectful step is refused, so no path through the function reaches a file, a network or another model. The tools a run is given must be exactly those the agent's card lists: the card is where a reader learns what an agent can do.

docs.title: Running an agent
docs.text:
run(agent, tools = …) executes the agent over a context or a prompt until it stops, and returns a Run. This program is pick.hql:

import ai

fn books_by(author: String) : List<String> =
    cards | filter(c => c.metadata.author == author) | map(c => c.title) | List

librarian = @[[librarian]] | Agent

pick =
    cards
    | filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
    | Context("unread")
    | Prompt("Which unread book should the club start with?")
    | run(librarian, tools = [Tool(books_by, "The titles on the shelf by one author")])

pick.result

"Start with The Common Reader. It is the only unread book by Virginia Woolf, and the club has already read A Room of One's Own and is reading Mrs Dalloway, so it completes the club's Woolf."

The answer is one field among many. The harness never collapses a run into the text the model last wrote:

pick.calls | map(c => {tool: c.tool, status: c.status, output: c.output})

[{output: "[\"A Room of One's Own\",\"Mrs Dalloway\",\"The Common Reader\"]", status: "ok", tool: "books_by"}]

turns is the conversation, stop says why it ended — end, max_tokens, max_turns or refused — and model and usage are what the provider reported, not what configuration asked for. trace puts everything that happened in one order:

pick | trace | map(e => e.kind)

["prompt", "request", "response", "tool_call", "request", "response", "stop"]

docs.title: Continuing and delegating
docs.text:
A Run never changes. ask(message) continues its conversation with the same agent and tools, and returns a new run whose parent is the first:

why = pick | ask("What did you rely on?")
why.result

"The books_by tool listed three Woolf titles, and the card for The Common Reader is the only one marked todo."

delegate(agent, task) starts a fresh conversation for another agent, given the first run's context and its result. An agent named in a card's agents: list is offered to the model as a tool of that name, so a model may delegate by itself; each child run is kept in children, and delegation stops at depth three.

remember(name) writes a run's result, or a string, as a card in the vault's [ai.memory] dir. Memory is cards: writing it is one explicit step, and reading it is a query like any other.

docs.title: Recordings: a run that answers again
docs.text:
A program that reaches a model would answer differently on every evaluation. HQL keeps each response as a recording, keyed by the SHA-256 of the request it answers, under the vault's [ai] recordings directory. --ai chooses what may happen:

Mode What it does replay the default: answers from recordings only, and never reaches a network record sends what is not recorded yet, and records it live always sends

The mode is never read from .hql/config.toml, so spending money is always a choice made on the command line. Record once, and the same program then evaluates offline, byte for byte:

$ hql --vault . --ai record run pick.hql
"Start with The Common Reader. …"
$ hql --vault . run pick.hql
"Start with The Common Reader. …"

A request with no recording is a diagnostic, not an empty answer:

evaluation failure: no recording for this request (5e10ae23…); run with --ai record
  --> pick.hql:13:7

hql check checks the whole program, its type is Run, and no model is reached. Committed recordings make a document that calls a model as reproducible as one that does not.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: A cell is a program, so a cell may run an agent, and the document around it is the prompt. Chapter 26 writes a document whose cells retrieve evidence, run the librarian over the draft they sit in, and save the answer where it was asked.

docs.title: 26. Agents inside documents
docs.text:
Design only

This chapter describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: these programs do not run against the current binary, and names, types and outputs may change before it ships.

Chapter 25 ran an agent from a program. This chapter runs one from inside the document that asks the question. The knowledge, the prompt, the program that assembles the prompt and the answer then sit in one file, each visible, each editable, each a value a later cell can read. The document is examples/notebook/next-meeting.hmd, rendered against the reading-club vault like the reading list of chapter 24.

docs.title: The document is the harness
docs.text:
Two bindings reach a cell from the host. cell is the cell being rendered, whose logs channel the logging page wrote to. this is the card the cell is written in, as it stands when the render starts: its header, its prose, and every output a previous render saved into it.

The prose of a cell's section, from the nearest heading above the cell down to the cell itself, is the default instructions of every Prompt the cell builds. The question is written once, as prose a reader reads, and the cell below it carries only the program that gathers the evidence.

hql render --emit after --in-place writes each cell's output back into the document, between the markers of chapter 24. The opening marker's hash covers the cell's code and the code of every cell it reads; a cell that reads this also covers the document's text, so its output is stale after every edit of the prose around it. That is the loop this chapter is about: edit the draft, render, read the answer, edit again.

docs.title: The document
docs.text:
---
title: Next meeting
---
# Next meeting

Notes for the club's next meeting, built from the shelf with
`hql --vault examples/reading-club render`.

```hql#query id=books
cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
```

## Candidates

The books nobody has finished.

```hql#eval id=unread
books
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| sort(by = c => c.title)
| map(c => c.title)
```

## Evidence

What the shelf holds on the question the club keeps returning to.

```hql#query id=evidence
import hmd
cards | semantic("which unread book suits a reading club") | take(3) | Context("evidence")
```

## What should we read next?

Pick one unread book for the next meeting, and say why. The candidates and
the evidence are in this draft; rely on them and on the shelf.

```hql#eval id=pick
import ai

fn books_by(author: String) : List<String> =
    cards | filter(c => c.metadata.author == author) | map(c => c.title) | List

[this]
| Context("draft")
| concat(evidence)
| run(@[[librarian]] | Agent, tools = [Tool(books_by, "The titles on the shelf by one author")])
```

## What happened

```hql#eval id=trace
pick | trace | map(e => e.kind)
```

## Remembered

```hql#query id=note
pick | remember("next-meeting-pick")
```

```hql#eval
cards | filter(c => c.path | starts_with("memory/")) | map(c => c.title)
```

The first two cells run against the current binary; they are the reading list of chapter 24 again. The rest is the subject of this chapter.

docs.title: Evidence by meaning
docs.text:
The evidence cell is a ranking of chapter 23 turned into a context. Each hit becomes one item, and the item keeps what the hit knew: its score, and the retrieval that produced it, in its provenance. Evidence that reaches a model says how it was found:

evidence | map(i => {source: i.provenance.name, score: i.score})

[{score: 0.3127, source: "the-common-reader"}, {score: 0.2904, source: "club"}, {score: 0.2851, source: "leaves-of-grass"}]

The question is a literal because the vault's index answers the questions it was built for, as chapter 23 explains; a question the index lacks is a diagnostic naming the build command, not an empty context.

docs.title: The agent reads the draft
docs.text:
[this] | Context("draft") is a context of one item: the document as it stands, written as Markdown, with the card's name and path as its provenance. concat(evidence) appends the ranking. The run step builds the prompt from the section's prose and both contexts, and the rendered prompt opens with the question the reader just read:

Pick one unread book for the next meeting, and say why. The candidates and
the evidence are in this draft; rely on them and on the shelf.

## draft

Source: next-meeting

# Next meeting
…

## evidence

Source: the-common-reader
…

The run's result is written after the cell, and the next cell reads the run itself, not its text:

```hql#eval id=pick
…
```
<!-- hql:output id=pick hash=3b91c0e4d2a7 status=ok -->
Start with The Common Reader. It is the only unread book by Virginia Woolf,
the club has read A Room of One's Own and is reading Mrs Dalloway, and the
draft lists it among the candidates.
<!-- /hql:output -->

["prompt", "request", "response", "tool_call", "request", "response", "stop"]

Change the prose above the cell, "say why" to "say why, in one sentence", and the cell's hash no longer matches its saved output. An editor shows the answer as stale without running anything; the next render asks again, with the new instructions and the draft as it now stands, which includes the previous answer. The agent reads what it wrote last time, as a value among the others.

docs.title: Memory is cards
docs.text:
remember(name) writes a run's result as a card in the vault's [ai.memory] directory, here memory/next-meeting-pick.hmd, with the run's id in its header so the card names the run that wrote it. Memory is cards: writing it is one explicit step, and reading it is a query like any other, which is what the last cell does. On the next render, cards holds the memory card and this holds the saved pick, so the document reads what it wrote.

In replay mode, the default, remember succeeds only when the card already holds the same content, so a committed vault renders without writing. Under --ai record or --ai live it writes.

docs.title: The editor loop
docs.text:
A request a run makes can be answered by three answerers, and every answer is a recording under the hash of the request, so a document rendered later reads all three alike. A provider answers over HTTP, as chapter 25 configured. A headless session of an agent host answers when the model entry names one. And under --ai host, a request with no recording is not sent anywhere: it waits, and whoever is driving the program answers it. In an editor that is the agent the user is already chatting with.

$ hql --vault examples/reading-club --ai host render --emit after --in-place examples/notebook/next-meeting.hmd
$ hql --vault examples/reading-club ai pending
5e10ae23…  messages  next-meeting.hmd:31  pick
$ hql --vault examples/reading-club ai answer 5e10ae23… --text "Start with The Common Reader. …"
$ hql --vault examples/reading-club render examples/notebook/next-meeting.hmd

hql ai pending lists each waiting request with its key, the wire format its answer is written in, and the request itself: the agent's instructions, the conversation, and the tools offered with their schemas. hql ai answer writes the answer as a recording marked answered_by: host, so a reader of the document can tell a provider's answer from one a person's chat gave. The second render replays it. Committed recordings make the document a procedure the chat executed once and anyone can read again.

edit the draft ──► render ──► request waits ──► chat answers ──► recording
      ▲                                                             │
      └───────────────── read the saved output ◄────────────────────┘

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Every card in this chapter was in one vault. Chapter 27 asks what the same steps are over a web of them.

docs.title: 27. The hyper web
docs.text:
Design only

This chapter describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: nothing in it runs against the current binary, and names, types and outputs may change before any of it ships. It is the direction the rest of the book points in, stated so that the direction can be read, questioned and changed.

A vault is one namespace: a tree of cards, closed by construction, in which every [[name]] resolves or is reported. The chapters of Part III queried, drew, ranked and ran agents over one such tree. This chapter asks what each of those steps is over many trees, authored and served independently, and what a reader is when the trees are read by programs and agents as much as by people.

docs.title: Namespaces beyond one tree
docs.text:
A reference may name a namespace: [[club:dune]] is the card dune in the namespace bound as club. The binding lives in the vault's configuration, never in a card, so a card cannot reach a namespace by mentioning it, and removing the binding breaks every link that used it, visibly. A prefix is a permission.

[namespaces.club]
root = "../reading-club"

[namespaces.lit]
url = "https://lit.example.org/"

HQL already has the local half of this. source("club") in chapter 21 is a vault bound by configuration, with its own cards and graph, and a relation across the two is a join. A namespace bound to a URL is the same source whose provider is a server; the program is unchanged:

lit = source("lit")
lit.cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book") | size

The rule the design rests on is no silent dereference: rendering, checking and linting make no network call, and a program that reads a remote namespace does so in a step the host sees and may refuse, as it sees and may refuse source(http(…)) today.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
A provider is anything that returns a card for a path: the vault's own folder, another folder, a web server that speaks plain HTTP and publishes a route description so a client does not guess its layout, a database holding cards as rows. The card's name is the same whichever provider answers, so a program over cards is a program over a web of vaults, and where a card is stored stays out of every reference to it.

What arrives from another provider is untrusted. A remote card's header is Data, as every tree from outside a program is, and it becomes a typed value at a boundary of chapter 11, where the program states what it requires and the rest is refused or kept as Data. A card of a namespace carries the namespace in its provenance, and so does every value derived from it: a hit, a context item, a run.

docs.title: Retrieval over the web
docs.text:
semantic over a namespace is the provider's index answering a question it holds, with its model, metric and approximation reported in the ranking's retrieval, as chapter 23 reports them for a local index. Two namespaces are two rankings, and a program that combines them does so explicitly, by score within a retrieval or by a join across them, because a score is evidence relative to one index and means nothing against another's.

import hmd

here  = cards | semantic("a creature and its maker") | take(3)
there = source("lit").cards | semantic("a creature and its maker") | take(3)
[here, there] | emit | Context("evidence")

Each item of that context says which namespace it came from, which index ranked it and how. Knowledge semantics becomes a way to query the web: a question in words, answered with cards and the evidence for each, rather than with pages to read.

docs.title: Agents reading agents
docs.text:
An agent is a card, so a namespace can serve one, and a document in one vault can run the librarian of another. delegate across a binding is a run whose child ran elsewhere, kept in children with its provenance, and whose trace records the delegation as an event like any other. The rules of chapter 25 do not change at the boundary: a child run is bounded in depth, every request is recorded under its hash, and a tool stays pure wherever it is evaluated.

import ai

review = cards | lexical("influence") | Context("claims") | run(@[[librarian]] | Agent)
second = review | delegate(@[[lit:reviewer]] | Agent, "Check the claims against your shelf.")
second.trace | filter(e => e.kind == "delegate") | map(e => e.data.namespace)

An agent that reads another agent's run reads a value: the prompt it was given, the tools it called, the answer it gave, and where each piece came from. A conversation between agents is a tree of such values, and a program queries it with the steps of chapter 6.

docs.title: A reader who asks
docs.text:
The same card is served to a person in a browser, to a tool that lints it, and to an agent building a context, from one source and in one format. A site that is a vault answers a question the way a document of chapter 26 does: with a run whose evidence is the site's own cards, whose trace says which cards were read, and whose answer carries their names. The reader asks instead of browsing, and what comes back is not a page but a value with its provenance attached, which the reader, or the reader's agent, may query further.

None of this needs a new language. It needs bindings in configuration, providers that answer by path, and the discipline the earlier chapters already hold: every step typed, every effect explicit, every value carrying where it came from.

docs.title: Where to go from here
docs.text: You have met the whole language, in three parts. The language: values and data, collections and functions, modules, questions in the style of SQL, streams, formats, data read and written through endpoints, the types a program declares and the boundary where data becomes typed, and the tools around it. Data flows: the pipeline, its phases, its unit of execution, and the systems it will connect. Knowledge and AI: a vault that is a namespace, its graph, retrieval by meaning, documents that compute themselves, agents whose runs are values, documents that run them, and the web they point at. The reference states each shipped part precisely, and the examples are where the next part is designed.

docs.title: 28. Statistics
docs.text: This chapter is about the module stats: descriptive statistics over a collection of numbers. It covers the centre of the values (the mean, the median and the mode), their spread, their quantiles, the correlation of two columns, and what a statistic is over an input too small to define it. Each statistic applies to a list written by hand and to a column a query reads.

docs.title: The module
docs.text:
stats is not in the prelude. A program writes import stats and calls stats.mean(xs), or binds them all, from stats import *, and calls mean(xs). Without an import, a statistic is an unknown name, and the checker names the import it needs:

[1, 2, 3, 4] | mean

check error[unknown-name]: `mean` is declared in the module `stats`: write `from stats import mean`
 --> <expression>:1:16
  |
1 | [1, 2, 3, 4] | mean
  |                ^^^^

docs.title: The centre
docs.text:
mean is the sum divided by the count, median the middle value of the sorted values, and the mean of the two middle values where the count is even, and mode the most frequent value:

from stats import *
xs = [2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]
{mean: xs | mean, median: xs | median, mode: xs | mode}

{mean: 5.0, median: 4.5, mode: 4}

A statistic of Int or Float values is a Float. A statistic of Int values is computed exactly and rounded to a Float once. A statistic of Decimal values is a Decimal, exact except where a quotient does not terminate, which is rounded half to even to 100 significant digits as Decimal / is. A literal with a decimal point is a Decimal (Decimal), so a list of prices keeps its cents:

from stats import *
prices = [1.10, 2.20, 3.30, 4.45, 5.05]
[prices | mean, prices | median]

[3.22, 3.30]

mode takes values of any Orderable type, not only numbers. Among equally frequent values, the mode is the least by the type's order:

from stats import *
[[3, 1, 3, 1, 2] | mode, ["novel", "essay", "novel", "poetry"] | mode]

[1, "novel"]

docs.title: Spread
docs.text:
variance is the sample variance, the sum of squared deviations from the mean divided by n - 1, and stdev its square root. pvariance is the population variance, the same sum divided by n, and pstdev its square root:

import stats
from stats import *
xs = [2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]
[xs | stats.variance, xs | stdev, xs | pvariance, xs | pstdev]

[4.571428571428571, 2.138089935299395, 4.0, 2.0]

The prelude declares a variance too: the population variance of Int and Float values. With variance imported from stats, a bare variance over those is ambiguous, and the checker asks for the module's name:

from stats import *
[1, 2, 3, 4] | variance
