check error[unknown-name]: `variance` over List<Int> is declared by `collections` and `stats`, so the call is ambiguous; qualify it, `collections.variance(…)`
 --> <expression>:2:16
  |
2 | [1, 2, 3, 4] | variance
  |                ^^^^^^^^

stats.variance is the sample variance and collections.variance the population variance. Over Decimal values only stats declares one, and a bare variance is the sample variance.

docs.title: Quantiles
docs.text:
quantile(q) is the value below which the fraction q of the sorted values lies, by linear interpolation between the two nearest values: the method R and NumPy use by default. quantiles(n) is the n - 1 cut points that divide the sorted values into n groups of equal probability, so quantiles(4) is the three quartiles and quantiles(100) the percentiles:

from stats import *
xs = [2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]
{p90: xs | quantile(0.9), quartiles: xs | quantiles(4)}

{p90: 7.6, quartiles: [4.0, 4.5, 5.5]}

median is quantile(0.5). Over Int and Decimal values a quantile is computed exactly, so the 95th percentile of the prices is a Decimal:

from stats import *
[1.10, 2.20, 3.30, 4.45, 5.05] | quantile(0.95)

4.9300

A q outside 0.0 to 1.0, or an n below 2, is an evaluation error:

from stats import *
[1, 2, 3] | quantile(1.5)

execute failure[invalid-argument]: `quantile` needs a `q` from 0 to 1, and 1.5 is outside it
 --> <expression>:2:22
  |
2 | [1, 2, 3] | quantile(1.5)
  |                      ^^^

docs.title: Correlation
docs.text:
covariance and correlation take a collection of pairs: the first column in each pair's first, the second in its second. zip builds the pairs from two lists. covariance is the sample covariance, and correlation Pearson's coefficient, the covariance divided by the product of the two standard deviations, from -1.0 to 1.0:

from stats import *
pairs = zip([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], [2, 1, 4, 3, 7, 5])
[pairs | covariance, pairs | correlation]

[3.2, 0.7917946548886297]

docs.title: A column of a query
docs.text:
A statistic takes any collection, so it ends a pipeline as sum and size do. The books of the reading-club vault (chapter 21) carry their pages in the header, and a typed view reads them as numbers:

from stats import *
fn pages(c: Card) : Int = match c.metadata.pages { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }
books = cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
lengths = books | map(pages)
{mean: lengths | mean, median: lengths | median, stdev: lengths | stdev, quartiles: lengths | quantiles(4)}

{mean: 251.0, median: 280.0, quartiles: [169.5, 280.0, 307.0], stdev: 105.56040924513319}

A statistic per group is a map over the groups, as each aggregate of chapter 6 was:

from stats import *
fn pages(c: Card) : Int = match c.metadata.pages { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }
cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| group(by = c => c.metadata.genre)
| map(g => {genre: g.key, books: g.items | size, mean: g.items | map(pages) | mean})

{{books: 2, genre: "essay", mean: 208.0}, {books: 4, genre: "novel", mean: 299.0}, {books: 1, genre: "poetry", mean: 145.0}}

Two columns of one query are a column of pairs. Whether longer books are the later ones is the correlation of the year and the pages:

from stats import *
fn pages(c: Card) : Int = match c.metadata.pages { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }
fn year(c: Card) : Int = match c.metadata.year { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }
cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| map(b => Pair(year(b), pages(b)))
| correlation

0.33335874566223495

docs.title: An empty input
docs.text:
A statistic that is undefined over its input is none, so each statistic but quantiles is an Option. The mean, median and mode of nothing are none. The sample variance and standard deviation need two values, so of one value they are none, while the population variance of one value is 0.0. The correlation is none also where one side has no variance:

from stats import *
nothing = [1, 2, 3] | filter(n => n > 5)
[nothing | mean, nothing | median, [4] | stdev, [4] | pvariance, zip([1, 2, 3], [5, 5, 5]) | correlation]

[none, none, none, 0.0, none]

quantiles of nothing is an empty list. Where a program needs a number whatever the input, unwrap_or gives a default (Option); 0.0f is a Float literal:

from stats import *
nothing = [1, 2, 3] | filter(n => n > 5)
nothing | mean | unwrap_or(0.0f)

0.0

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: A statistic describes values a program has. Chapter 29 is about values a program draws: samples, shuffles and random numbers, and the seed that makes them repeatable.

docs.title: 29. Random values
docs.text: This chapter is about the module random: samples, shuffles, choices, random numbers and UUIDs. It covers the two forms each draw has, the seeded one and the unseeded one, and the evaluation seed that makes a program's random output repeatable.

docs.title: The module
docs.text:
random is not in the prelude: a program binds its functions, from random import *, or writes import random and calls random.sample(…). Each draw has two forms. With a seed argument it is pure: its result is a function of the seed, its input and its call site, the same on every run. Without one it is effectful and draws from the evaluation seed, fixed once per evaluation.

The generator is ChaCha12. A seeded draw is predictable by design, so no draw of random is fit for a key, a token or any other secret.

docs.title: Samples, shuffles and choices
docs.text:
sample(n) is n elements drawn without replacement, in the order they have in the input:

from random import *
range(1, 21) | sample(5, seed = 7)

[1, 5, 8, 11, 12]

shuffle is every element in a uniformly random order, and choice one element drawn uniformly:

from random import *
titles = cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book") | map(c => c.title)
{shuffled: titles | shuffle(seed = 7), picked: titles | choice(seed = 7)}

{picked: "The Common Reader", shuffled: ["Leaves of Grass", "Frankenstein", "The Common Reader", "A Room of One's Own", "The Hobbit", "Mrs Dalloway", "Dune"]}

choice is an Option: over an empty input it is none. sample(n) with n at or above the input's size is the whole input, and a negative n is an evaluation error:

from random import *
nothing = [1, 2, 3] | filter(n => n > 5)
[nothing | choice(seed = 1), [1, 2, 3] | choice(seed = 1)]

[none, 3]

A collection without an order, such as a Set, is sorted by its elements before it is sampled, so the sample does not depend on how the set was built.

docs.title: A seed
docs.text:
A seeded draw is a function of its call site, its position in the program text, as well as of its seed. Two calls with one seed at two places are two draws:

from random import *
deck = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
[deck | shuffle(seed = 1), deck | shuffle(seed = 1)]

[["b", "d", "c", "e", "a"], ["b", "c", "a", "e", "d"]]

One call site with one seed gives one result each time it is reached. A seeded draw inside a map repeats; a seed that varies with the element varies the draw:

from random import *
deck = ["a", "b", "c", "d"]
{same: range(0, 3) | map(_ => deck | shuffle(seed = 1)), varied: range(0, 3) | map(i => deck | shuffle(seed = i))}

{same: [["b", "a", "c", "d"], ["b", "a", "c", "d"], ["b", "a", "c", "d"]], varied: [["c", "b", "d", "a"], ["d", "a", "c", "b"], ["a", "c", "b", "d"]]}

Moving a seeded call to another place in the program text changes its result; running the same program again does not.

docs.title: The evaluation seed
docs.text:
An unseeded draw reads the evaluation seed. --seed <int> fixes it; without --seed, the seed comes from the host's entropy. Each unseeded call site draws from a stream derived from the evaluation seed and its position in the program, so two call sites draw independently, and a program run twice with one --seed writes the same values:

from random import *
xs = range(1, 11)
{sample: xs | sample(3), shuffled: xs | shuffle, picked: xs | choice}

{picked: 5, sample: [4, 5, 7], shuffled: [6, 10, 7, 5, 8, 2, 3, 4, 9, 1]}

An evaluation that takes its seed from the host reports it at info, with the --seed that repeats it:

$ hql --report-level info eval 'import random
range(1, 11) | shuffle | size'
10
execute info[effect]: the evaluation seed is -7270767200120302920; `--seed -7270767200120302920` repeats this evaluation
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | import random
  | ^

Without --seed, a block's values differ from run to run, but what holds of every draw holds of each: a sample of n has n elements, and a shuffle holds every element once:

from random import *
[range(0, 1000) | sample(3) | size, (range(0, 29) | shuffle | sort) == range(0, 29)]

[3, true]

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
random_int(low, high) is an Int drawn uniformly from low to high, both included, and random_float() a Float from 0.0 included to 1.0 excluded. Both are effectful and have no seeded form, so --seed is what makes them repeatable:

from random import *
{dice: range(0, 5) | map(_ => random_int(1, 6)), fraction: random_float()}

{dice: [1, 2, 3, 1, 6], fraction: 0.5633124818544215}

high below low is an evaluation error:

from random import *
random_int(6, 1)

execute failure[invalid-argument]: `random_int` needs `high` at or above `low`, and 1 is below 6
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | random_int(6, 1)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: UUIDs
docs.text:
A UUID is written as lowercase hyphenated text. uuid(name, namespace) is the version 5 UUID of a name in a namespace: a function of the two, with no draw. The namespace is a UUID's text, or one of the standard namespaces "dns", "url", "oid" and "x500":

from random import *
uuid("www.example.com", "dns")

"2ed6657d-e927-568b-95e1-2665a8aea6a2"

uuid() is a version 7 UUID. Its first 48 bits are the evaluation instant's Unix milliseconds and the next 42 a counter, so the UUIDs of one evaluation are distinct and sort in the order they were drawn:

from random import *
ids = range(0, 20) | map(_ => uuid())
[ids == sort(ids), size(Set(ids)) == 20]

[true, true]

Its remaining bits come from the evaluation seed. --now fixes the evaluation instant (the evaluation clock) and --seed the seed, and the two together make uuid() repeatable:

from random import *
[uuid(), uuid()]

["01a16cd1-04c0-706c-9aa2-de28c20754f4", "01a16cd1-04c0-706c-9aa2-de2983927b4e"]

docs.title: A stream
docs.text: sample(n) also takes a stream, by reservoir sampling: the step holds n elements, never the stream, and gives its sample when the stream ends. A stream that does not end gives no sample. The stream form is effectful only.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 30 is about the modules that turn values into bytes and back: digests and encodings.

docs.title: 30. Digests and encodings
docs.text: A digest is the fixed-size output of a cryptographic hash function over a sequence of octets: equal input gives an equal digest, and a change to any octet changes it. An encoding writes octets as text-safe characters and reads them back. This chapter covers the two modules that provide them, crypto.digest and encoding, over a String, a Bytes value and a Data tree.

docs.title: The digest module
docs.text:
crypto.digest is not in the prelude. A program writes import crypto.digest and reaches the module as digest, and its receivers, "abc".digest(Sha256); without the import, the name is a check error:

"abc".digest(Sha256)

check error[unknown-name]: `digest` is declared in the module `crypto.digest`: write `import crypto.digest`
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | "abc".digest(Sha256)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

An algorithm is named by a type, as a format is: Md5, Sha1, Sha256, Sha512 and Blake3. s.digest(A) is the digest of a text's UTF-8 octets under A, written as lowercase hexadecimal, two digits per octet:

import crypto.digest
s = "abc"
[s.digest(Md5), s.digest(Sha1), s.digest(Sha256), s.digest(Blake3)]

["900150983cd24fb0d6963f7d28e17f72", "a9993e364706816aba3e25717850c26c9cd0d89d", "ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad", "6437b3ac38465133ffb63b75273a8db548c558465d79db03fd359c6cd5bd9d85"]

The length of the text follows from the algorithm: 32 hex digits for Md5, 40 for Sha1, 64 for Sha256 and Blake3, 128 for Sha512. Md5 and Sha1 are broken for collision resistance: two different inputs with one digest can be constructed. They serve to compare with digests other tools wrote, not to protect anything new.

b.digest(A) takes a Bytes value, the form for octets that are not text. The two forms agree: the digest of Bytes(s) is the digest of s:

import crypto.digest
from encoding import *
Bytes("68656c6c6f", Hex).digest(Sha256) == "hello".digest(Sha256)

true

docs.title: Fingerprints of data
docs.text:
fingerprint(x) is the SHA-256 digest of a Data tree's canonical JSON, the text canonical(x) gives. Canonical JSON follows RFC 8785: keys sorted, no whitespace, a number as its digits without trailing zeros, a time value as its ISO 8601 text and a Bytes leaf as its base64 text:

from crypto.digest import *
canonical({title: "Dune", pages: 412, price: 9.50, on: Date("2026-10-24")})

"{\"on\":\"2026-10-24\",\"pages\":412,\"price\":9.5,\"title\":\"Dune\"}"

Two trees equal under HQL equality have one canonical text, so one fingerprint. Key order, whitespace and 1.10 against 1.1 in the source text change neither:

from crypto.digest import *
a = Data("{\"b\": 1, \"a\": [1.10, \"x\"]}", Json)
b = Data("{ \"a\" : [1.1, \"x\"],\n  \"b\": 1.0 }", Json)
[fingerprint(a), fingerprint(b)]

["5b07d3c10bbccec19fd995c80fb3393b8fd39691dbcc412ac55c0d08262ed5af", "5b07d3c10bbccec19fd995c80fb3393b8fd39691dbcc412ac55c0d08262ed5af"]

A value's type does count: the number 9.50 and the text "9.50" are different leaves, with different fingerprints:

from crypto.digest import *
[fingerprint({price: 9.50}) == fingerprint({price: 9.5}), fingerprint({price: 9.50}) == fingerprint({price: "9.50"})]

[true, false]

fingerprint(x) is canonical(x).digest(Sha256), so a program in another language reproduces it with any RFC 8785 implementation and SHA-256.

docs.title: The encoding module
docs.text:
encoding is not in the prelude either: a program writes import encoding, which reaches its receivers, "hé".encode(Hex). An encoding is named by a type:

Encoding Writes octets as Hex two hexadecimal digits each, lowercase; either case reads Base64 RFC 4648 base64, standard alphabet, padded Base64Url RFC 4648 base64, URL-safe alphabet, unpadded; padding optional on reading Percent RFC 3986 percent-encoding: A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~ as they are, every other octet as %XX

s.encode(E) writes a text's UTF-8 octets in E:

import encoding
["hé".encode(Hex), "??>".encode(Base64), "??>".encode(Base64Url), "a b/é~".encode(Percent)]

["68c3a9", "Pz8+", "Pz8-", "a%20b%2F%C3%A9~"]

s.decode(E) reads the text back as an Option<String>. It is none where the input is not valid in E, and also where the octets it holds are not UTF-8, as /w== in base64 is the single octet 0xff:

import encoding
["68C3A9".decode(Hex), "aGk/".decode(Base64), "6g".decode(Hex), "/w==".decode(Base64)]

["hé", "hi?", none, none]

Percent-decoding reads %20 as a space and leaves + as it is:

import encoding
"a+b%20%C3%A9".decode(Percent)

"a+b é"

docs.title: Between text and Bytes
docs.text:
Where the octets are not text, Bytes holds them. b.encode(E) writes a Bytes value in E, and s.to_bytes(E) reads it back as an Option<Bytes>, with no UTF-8 requirement; Bytes(s, E) reads it as a value and fails on invalid text. The page Bytes shows each:

from encoding import *
b = Bytes("ff00", Hex)
[b.encode(Hex), b.encode(Base64), b.encode(Base64Url)]

["ff00", "/wA=", "_wA"]

import encoding
["/w==".decode(Base64), "/w==".to_bytes(Base64)]

[none, 0xff]

docs.title: A record already seen
docs.text:
A fingerprint is a key that holds outside the program: in a column, a file name, a cache. Records that arrive with their keys in another order, or as another program wrote them, still match the keys of an earlier load. Here loaded holds a 12-digit prefix of each fingerprint an earlier run stored, and only the new record passes:

from crypto.digest import *
loaded = {"106815777291"}
incoming = [{to: "ada", id: 1}, {id: 2, to: "bo"}]
incoming | filter(r => not loaded.contains(fingerprint(r)[0:12]))

[{id: 2, to: "bo"}]

Within one program, distinct already removes records equal under HQL equality, and Deduplication covers duplicates by key. The fingerprint is for the comparison that crosses a run.

docs.title: A file's digest
docs.text:
source(file(p), Text) reads a file whole as one String, as Source shows. Its digest is the one shasum -a 256 prints for the file, so a program checks a download against a published digest:

import crypto.digest
expected = "ade391083e197c4575f5ccb436b35c499665e77202518e6873a02fa6b54cc8e3"
source(file("examples/io/counts.csv"), Text) | map(t => t.digest(Sha256) == expected)

[true]

The reference states every function of the two modules with its signature: crypto.digest and encoding.

docs.title: 31. Keys and cryptography
docs.text: The module crypto holds keys: the algorithms they belong to, the types that hold them, the text formats other tools write them in, and the rules that keep a private key out of every output. This chapter reads, writes and generates keys, signs and verifies with them, computes MACs and hashes passwords, and then describes the operations that are not in the current release: encryption and the key vault. Digests and text encodings, which need no key, are chapter 30, and the octets a key is made of are the Bytes type of chapter 2.

docs.title: Algorithms and key types
docs.text:
crypto is not in the prelude: a program binds its functions, from crypto import *, or writes import crypto and calls crypto.read_private_key(…). An algorithm is named by a type, as a format is, and a key's type carries its algorithm:

Algorithm Kind What it is Ed25519 signing RFC 8032, pure Ed25519 P256 signing ECDSA over NIST P-256 with SHA-256 Rsa signing RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 with SHA-256, 2048 to 8192 bits X25519 agreement RFC 7748; the key of an age recipient Aes256Gcm, ChaCha20Poly1305 cipher a 256-bit shared key HmacSha256, HmacSha512 MAC a shared key of any length

The first four are asymmetric, each key a pair of a public and a private half. The last four are symmetric, one shared key. Four types hold them:

Type What it holds PublicKey<A> the public half of a key of algorithm A PrivateKey<A> the private half KeyPair<A> both halves, as the fields public and private SecretKey<A> a symmetric key of a cipher or a MAC

PrivateKey, KeyPair and SecretKey are secret types, the subject of the section Private keys below.

docs.title: Reading a public key
docs.text:
read_public_key(file, format, algorithm) reads the key a file holds. The key here is the published test key 1 of RFC 8032, kept in the repository's examples:

from crypto import *

key = read_public_key(file("examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pub.pem"), Pem, Ed25519)
key

PublicKey<Ed25519>(kPrK_qmxVWaYVA9wwBF6Iuo3vVzz7TxHCTwXBygrS4k)

A public key prints as its type and its thumbprint: the RFC 7638 JWK thumbprint, the base64url SHA-256 of the key's canonical JWK. thumbprint() gives it as a String. It names a key in one short line, and is the same whichever format the key was read from.

A key format is named by a type:

Format Text Pem RFC 7468 text around DER: SPKI for a public key, PKCS #8 for a private one Jwk the RFC 7517 JSON text of one key OpenSsh an authorized_keys line, or an OpenSSH private key file Age age's Bech32 recipient and identity text, for X25519 only

PublicKey(text, format, algorithm) reads a key from a String. A public key is not a secret, so its text may be written in a program. The same key as an OpenSSH line and as a JWK is one value:

from crypto import *

line = "ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAINdamAGCsQq31Uv+08lkBzoO4XLz2qYjJa8CGmj3B1Ea"
jwk = "{\"kty\": \"OKP\", \"crv\": \"Ed25519\", \"x\": \"11qYAYKxCrfVS_7TyWQHOg7hcvPapiMlrwIaaPcHURo\"}"
a = PublicKey(line, OpenSsh, Ed25519)
b = PublicKey(jwk, Jwk, Ed25519)
[a == b, a.thumbprint()]

[true, "kPrK_qmxVWaYVA9wwBF6Iuo3vVzz7TxHCTwXBygrS4k"]

Public keys compare by their octets, so == holds across formats.

Text that is not a key of the format and the algorithm is an evaluation error. to_public_key gives none instead, for text whose validity is not known in advance:

from crypto import *

"ssh-ed25519 AAAA" | to_public_key(OpenSsh, Ed25519)

none

A key of one algorithm read as another is an evaluation error naming both:

from crypto import *

read_public_key(file("examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pub.pem"), Pem, P256)

execute failure[invalid-argument]: examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pub.pem: the DER text holds an Ed25519 key, and it is read as P256
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | read_public_key(file("examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pub.pem"), Pem, P256)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A format that holds no key of the algorithm at all is a check error, found before anything is read. Age holds X25519 keys alone, and X25519 has no OpenSsh text:

from crypto import *

PublicKey("age1qyqszqgpqyqszqgpqyqszqgp", Age, Ed25519)

check error[type-mismatch]: Age text holds no Ed25519 key: `Age` holds `X25519` keys alone
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | PublicKey("age1qyqszqgpqyqszqgpqyqszqgp", Age, Ed25519)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Writing a public key
docs.text:
to_text(format) writes a public key in a format another tool reads. OpenSsh is an authorized_keys line with no comment, Jwk the canonical JSON of the required members, and Pem 64-column lines with a final line break:

from crypto import *

key = read_public_key(file("examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pub.pem"), Pem, Ed25519)
[key.to_text(OpenSsh), key.to_text(Jwk)]

["ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAINdamAGCsQq31Uv+08lkBzoO4XLz2qYjJa8CGmj3B1Ea", "{\"crv\":\"Ed25519\",\"kty\":\"OKP\",\"x\":\"11qYAYKxCrfVS_7TyWQHOg7hcvPapiMlrwIaaPcHURo\"}"]

to_der() gives the key's SPKI DER as Bytes, and PublicKey(der, algorithm) reads it back:

from crypto import *

key = read_public_key(file("examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pub.pem"), Pem, Ed25519)
der = key.to_der()
[str(der.size()), str(der), str(PublicKey(der, Ed25519) == key)]

["44", "0x302a300506032b6570032100d75a980182b10ab7d54bfed3c964073a0ee172f3daa62325af021a68f707511a", "true"]

The last 32 octets are the Ed25519 key itself; the 12 before them name the algorithm.

docs.title: Private keys
docs.text:
A secret type is a type whose values hold private key material: PrivateKey, KeyPair and SecretKey. Four rules hold for every value of one:

  • it prints redacted;
  • no format writes it;
  • == does not compare it;
  • its text does not appear in a program's source.

read_private_key(file, format, algorithm) reads a private key. It prints as its type and its public key's thumbprint, which names the key and discloses nothing of it:

from crypto import *

key = read_private_key(file("examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pem"), Pem, Ed25519)
[str(key), key.public().thumbprint()]

["PrivateKey<Ed25519>(kPrK_qmxVWaYVA9wwBF6Iuo3vVzz7TxHCTwXBygrS4k)", "kPrK_qmxVWaYVA9wwBF6Iuo3vVzz7TxHCTwXBygrS4k"]

public() gives a private key's public key. On a Unix host, a private key file that its group or others may read gives a warning naming the path and its mode; chmod 600 the file to clear it. The warning is a diagnostic, and the result is unchanged.

A secret reaches no format. Writing one is a check error that names the operation that turns a private key into text:

from crypto import *

pair = generate_key_pair(Ed25519)
pair.private | format(Json)

check error[type-mismatch]: PrivateKey<Ed25519> holds private key material, which no format writes; `export_private` turns a private key into text where a program means to
 --> <expression>:4:16
  |
4 | pair.private | format(Json)
  |                ^^^^^^^^^^^^

A secret type implements no Eq. Two private keys are the same key when their public keys are equal, and that is the comparison to write:

from crypto import *

pair = generate_key_pair(Ed25519)
pair.private == pair.private

check error[type-mismatch]: PrivateKey<Ed25519> is a secret and implements no `Eq`: `==` does not compare key material; compare public keys, or a MAC with `verify_mac`
 --> <expression>:4:1
  |
4 | pair.private == pair.private
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A string literal that holds private key material is a check error. A private key is read from a file, the environment or a key vault, or generated:

import crypto

text = "-----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----"
text

check error[type-mismatch]: this literal holds a PEM private key: private key material never lives in a program's source; read it from a file (`read_private_key`), the environment (`env.var`), a key vault (`keyvault.key`), or generate it
 --> <expression>:3:8
  |
3 | text = "-----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----"
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Exporting a private key
docs.text:
export_private(format) writes a private key's material as a String, the one operation that does. The result is no longer a secret type: it prints, and a format writes it. With passphrase, the text is encrypted: PKCS #8 under scrypt and AES-256-CBC for Pem, bcrypt-pbkdf and AES-256-CTR for OpenSsh. PrivateKey(text, format, algorithm, passphrase = …) reads it back, and to_private_key gives none for a wrong passphrase:

from crypto import *

pair = generate_key_pair(Ed25519)
sealed = pair.private.export_private(OpenSsh, passphrase = "correct horse")
[PrivateKey(sealed, OpenSsh, Ed25519, passphrase = "correct horse").public() == pair.public,
 sealed | to_private_key(OpenSsh, Ed25519, passphrase = "wrong") | is_none]

[true, true]

PrivateKey with a wrong passphrase is an evaluation error that says so:

from crypto import *

pair = generate_key_pair(Ed25519)
sealed = pair.private.export_private(OpenSsh, passphrase = "correct horse")
PrivateKey(sealed, OpenSsh, Ed25519, passphrase = "wrong")

execute failure[invalid-argument]: the passphrase does not decrypt the OpenSsh private key
 --> <expression>:5:1
  |
5 | PrivateKey(sealed, OpenSsh, Ed25519, passphrase = "wrong")
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Generating keys
docs.text:
generate_key_pair(algorithm) gives a new KeyPair from the host's cryptographically secure generator, and is effectful. bits sets the size of an Rsa key, 2048 to 8192 and 3072 by default. A generated key differs on every evaluation, so the programs here show what holds of every one:

from crypto import *

pair = generate_key_pair(X25519)
[pair.public == pair.private.public(),
 pair.public.to_text(Age) | starts_with("age1"),
 str(pair) | starts_with("KeyPair<X25519>(")]

[true, true, true]

An X25519 public key in Age text is an age recipient, age1…, and its private key exported in Age is an age identity, the text the age command line reads with -i.

generate_secret_key(algorithm) gives a new symmetric key: 32 octets for a cipher and for HmacSha256, 64 for HmacSha512. SecretKey(bytes, algorithm) builds one from octets the program already holds. A secret key prints with no thumbprint, since it has no public half:

from crypto import *

[str(generate_secret_key(Aes256Gcm)), str(SecretKey(Bytes("Jefe"), HmacSha256))]

["SecretKey<Aes256Gcm>(redacted)", "SecretKey<HmacSha256>(redacted)"]

A cipher's key is exactly 32 octets, and a MAC's at least one. Another length is an evaluation error naming it:

from crypto import *

SecretKey(Bytes("short"), Aes256Gcm)

execute failure[invalid-argument]: a Aes256Gcm key is 32 octets, and this one is 5
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | SecretKey(Bytes("short"), Aes256Gcm)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Signatures
docs.text:
A signature is Bytes, detached from what it signs. sign(key) signs a String's UTF-8 octets or a Bytes value with a private key of a signing algorithm. Every scheme signs deterministically: one key and one message give one signature. The Ed25519 test key signs the empty message as RFC 8032 says:

from crypto import *
from encoding import *

key = read_private_key(file("examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pem"), Pem, Ed25519)
"" | sign(key) | encode(Hex)

"e5564300c360ac729086e2cc806e828a84877f1eb8e5d974d873e065224901555fb8821590a33bacc61e39701cf9b46bd25bf5f0595bbe24655141438e7a100b"
Algorithm Signature Ed25519 64 octets, R and S P256 64 octets, r and s, as JWS ES256 Rsa the modulus length, PKCS #1 v1.5 over SHA-256, as JWS RS256

verify(signature, key) checks a signature with the public key. A signature of another message, of another key, of the wrong length or malformed gives false, never an error:

from crypto import *

pair = generate_key_pair(Ed25519)
signature = "ship order 1042" | sign(pair.private)
["ship order 1042".verify(signature, pair.public),
 "ship order 1043".verify(signature, pair.public),
 "ship order 1042".verify(signature[0:63], pair.public)]

[true, false, false]

OpenSSL writes a P-256 signature as ASN.1 DER. p256_signature_from_der converts one to the 64 octets verify reads, and gives none for octets that are not one.

docs.title: Signing a tree
docs.text:
sign_data(key) signs a Data tree over its canonical JSON, the RFC 8785 text chapter 30 fingerprints, and verify_data(signature, key) checks one. Two trees equal under HQL equality have one signature, whatever their key order:

from crypto import *

pair = generate_key_pair(Ed25519)
a = Data("{\"name\": \"hql\", \"version\": \"0.4.0\"}", Json)
b = Data("{\"version\": \"0.4.0\", \"name\": \"hql\"}", Json)
a.sign_data(pair.private) == b.sign_data(pair.private)

true

A verifier in another language checks the signature with any RFC 8785 implementation. The examples hold two releases, each a manifest and a base64 signature by the test key. The second manifest has its version changed, and its signature fails:

from crypto import *
from encoding import *

type Release {
    manifest  : Data
    signature : String
}

public = read_public_key(file("examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pub.pem"), Pem, Ed25519)
releases : Seq<Release> = source(file("examples/crypto/releases.jsonl"))
releases
| map(r => r.manifest.verify_data(r.signature.to_bytes(Base64) | unwrap_or(Bytes("")), public))

[true, false]

A String and a Data tree are signed by different names: sign signs a text's octets, and sign_data a tree's canonical JSON, in which a string is written with its quotes.

docs.title: MACs
docs.text:
A MAC is a tag computed under a shared SecretKey of HmacSha256 or HmacSha512: 32 octets for the first, 64 for the second. mac(key) gives the tag. A webhook's secret is the length its sender chose, and a MAC key takes any length from one octet. RFC 4231's test case 2:

from crypto import *
from encoding import *

key = SecretKey(Bytes("Jefe"), HmacSha256)
"what do ya want for nothing?" | mac(key) | encode(Hex)

"5bdcc146bf60754e6a042426089575c75a003f089d2739839dec58b964ec3843"

verify_mac(tag, key) checks a tag, comparing it in time independent of where it first differs. == over two Bytes is not constant-time, and a received tag is checked with verify_mac:

from crypto import *
from encoding import *

key = SecretKey(Bytes("Jefe"), HmacSha256)
tag = Bytes("5bdcc146bf60754e6a042426089575c75a003f089d2739839dec58b964ec3843", Hex)
["what do ya want for nothing?".verify_mac(tag, key),
 "what do ya want for something?".verify_mac(tag, key)]

[true, false]

docs.title: Password hashes
docs.text:
A password hash is an Argon2id PHC string: $argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$, then the salt and the hash. hash_password draws a new 16-octet salt on every call, so it is effectful and two hashes of one password differ. verify_password(hash) gives whether a password is the one the hash was made from, under the parameters the hash names:

from crypto import *

stored = "correct horse battery staple" | hash_password
["correct horse battery staple".verify_password(stored),
 "Tr0ub4dor&3".verify_password(stored),
 stored.starts_with("$argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$")]

[true, false, true]

memory_kib, iterations and parallelism raise the cost. A cost below OWASP's minimum is an evaluation error naming the parameter:

from crypto import *

"correct horse battery staple" | hash_password(memory_kib = 4096)

execute failure[invalid-argument]: `memory_kib` is 19456 to 1048576, and 4096 is outside: a cost below OWASP's minimum is refused
 --> <expression>:3:34
  |
3 | "correct horse battery staple" | hash_password(memory_kib = 4096)
  |                                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

verify_password reads Argon2id, Argon2i and Argon2d hashes. A stored hash of another scheme, such as bcrypt's $2b$, is an evaluation error naming the scheme, not a wrong password.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
Design only

This section describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: these programs do not run against the current binary, and names, types and outputs may change before they ship.

Shared-key encryption is authenticated: encrypt(key) under a SecretKey of Aes256Gcm or ChaCha20Poly1305 gives a new 12-octet nonce, the ciphertext and a 16-octet tag, as one Bytes. decrypt(key) gives the plaintext, or none for octets that are not an encryption of anything under that key:

from crypto import *

key = generate_secret_key(ChaCha20Poly1305)
sealed = "meet at the north gate" | encrypt(key)
[(sealed.decrypt(key) | and_then(to_text)) == some("meet at the north gate"),
 sealed[:-1].decrypt(key) | is_none]

[true, true]

Encryption to a recipient writes an age v1 message to one or more X25519 public keys, and any of their private keys decrypts it. The age command line reads and writes the same octets:

from crypto import *

pair = generate_key_pair(X25519)
sealed = "J45.909" | encrypt_to([pair.public])
sealed | decrypt_with(pair.private) | and_then(to_text)

"J45.909"

An encrypted endpoint encrypts what a format writes. encrypted_to wraps an endpoint that target writes, and decrypted_with one that source reads; orders.jsonl.age is JSON Lines, encrypted:

from crypto import *

pair = generate_key_pair(X25519)
orders = [{id: 1, total: 12.50}, {id: 2, total: 7.25}]
orders | target(encrypted_to(file("orders.jsonl.age"), [pair.public]))
source(decrypted_with(file("orders.jsonl.age"), pair.private)) | map(o => o.id)

[1, 2]

docs.title: The key vault
docs.text:
Design only

This section describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: these programs do not run against the current binary, and names, keys, types and outputs may change before they ship.

A key vault is a store of named keys that .hql/config.toml configures, as it configures an endpoint. Its secrets are named by *_env keys and never written:

[keyvault.team]
kind = "file"
path = "keys.age"
passphrase_env = "HQL_TEAM_VAULT_PASSPHRASE"

The module crypto.keyvault, imported with import crypto.keyvault and reached as keyvault, names a key by the vault's id and the key's name. keyvault.key gives a KeyRef, which holds the two names and no key material. A stored private key signs and decrypts inside the vault and is never a value of the program:

import crypto
import crypto.keyvault

signer = keyvault.key("team", "release-2026", Ed25519)
manifest = {name: "hql", version: "0.4.0"}
signature = keyvault.sign_data(manifest, signer)
manifest.verify_data(signature, keyvault.public_key(signer))

true

keyvault.keys lists a vault's keys by name, algorithm and what each one does:

import crypto.keyvault

keyvault.keys("team") | map(k => {name: k.name, algorithm: k.algorithm, decrypts: k.decrypts})

[{algorithm: "X25519", decrypts: true, name: "backup-2026"}, {algorithm: "Ed25519", decrypts: false, name: "release-2026"}]

A vault is a file store encrypted with age, the operating system's keychain, an ssh_agent, or aws_kms. In an ssh_agent or aws_kms vault the private key never enters the hql process. hql keyvault generates, imports, lists and deletes the keys of a store; a program does none of these.

docs.title: Declarations
docs.text: A declaration is written as a function is, up to the result type, and stops there. This page reads the parts of a declaration that a function with a body does not have, each from a line of the standard library.

docs.title: The receiver
docs.text:
A first parameter named self is the receiver: the value a call is made on. A declaration with a receiver is reached by a receiver call, value.f(), by a pipe, value | f, and by an ordinary call with the receiver first:

[abs(-3), (-3).abs(), -3 | abs]

[3, 3, 3]

A declaration without self takes its first argument the same way, as the value the call is made on, and is not reached by a receiver call.

docs.title: Positional and named parameters
docs.text:
A / in a parameter list ends the parameters a call writes by position only, and a * begins the ones it writes by name only. pow is declared fn pow(self: Int, exponent: Int, /) : Int, so its exponent has no name at a call:

pow(2, 10)

1024

pow(2, exponent = 10)

check error[type-mismatch]: `pow` takes `exponent` by position: write the value without `exponent =`
 --> <expression>:1:19
  |
1 | pow(2, exponent = 10)
  |                   ^^

A parameter after * is the reverse: fn shuffle<T>(self: Seq<T>, *, seed: Int) : List<T> takes seed by name, xs.shuffle(seed = 7), and never by position. / and * are written in declarations only; a function with a body takes its arguments by position.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text: A parameter with = value after its type may be left out of a call. The declaration states the default so that a reader sees it; the Rust function supplies it, since an argument a call does not write is absent when the function runs. Natives shows one.

docs.title: Forms of one name
docs.text:
A name may be declared more than once, each line a form. A call takes the first form its receiver and arguments fit:

fn abs(self: Int) : Int
fn abs(self: Float) : Float
fn abs(self: Decimal) : Decimal
fn abs(self: Duration) : Duration

[abs(-3), abs(-1.5f).int(), abs(-2.50).int()]

[3, 1, 2]

The forms of a name share one Rust function, which reads the value it was given. A function with a body has one form.

docs.title: Purity
docs.text:
A declaration written fn is pure: its result depends on its arguments alone, so the planner may reorder it, run it once for equal arguments, or skip it when nothing reads the result. A declaration written effectful fn runs once, where it is written. The two forms of shuffle differ in exactly this:

fn shuffle<T>(self: Seq<T>, *, seed: Int) : List<T>
effectful fn shuffle<T>(self: Seq<T>) : List<T>

With a seed the result is a function of the seed and the list. Without one the call draws from the evaluation's seed and is effectful.

docs.title: Shape
docs.text:
A word before fn states how a backend may split the input of a call:

Word What it states elementwise fn the result for each element depends on that element alone partition fn the input is regrouped by a key, and the groups complete in any order reduction fn the whole input collapses to one value through a combiner none a barrier: the whole input is needed before any output

count is declared reduction fn count<T>(self: Collection<T>) : Int: a count of a collection is the sum of the counts of its parts.

[1, 2, 3].count()

3

Purity and shape are claims about the Rust function. The declaration states them, the extension marks its function the same way, and the two markings are compared when the package is bound (next page).

docs.title: How the standard library is built
docs.text: The standard library is a package named std. Its modules are HQL files of declarations, and its extension is Rust compiled into the hql binary. A package you write has the same two halves; the one difference is where its Rust is kept (chapter 35).

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
A module's file of declarations is its contract. This is the head of the contract of math, the file lib/std/math/mod.hql:

module math

import core

/// `self` without its sign, at its own type: `abs(-3)` is `3`,
/// `abs(-1.50)` is `1.50`, and `abs(Duration("-PT1H"))` is `PT1H`.
fn abs(self: Int) : Int
fn abs(self: Float) : Float
fn abs(self: Decimal) : Decimal
fn abs(self: Duration) : Duration

/// The square root of `self`: `sqrt(2.0f)` is `1.4142135623730951`.
fn sqrt(self: Float) : Float

The file opens with module and its name, imports the modules whose types it writes, and declares. A /// doc string above a declaration is what help prints for it. The contract is the whole of what a program is checked against: the checker never reads Rust.

docs.title: The implementation
docs.text:
Beside the contract is one Rust function per declared name, and a table that lists them by that name:

pub(crate) static STEPS: &[Operation] = &[
    declared("abs", eval_abs),
    declared("sqrt", eval_sqrt),
    // …
];

fn eval_abs(
    _: &mut dyn EvalCx,
    input: Value,
    _: &[TypedArg],
    span: Range<usize>,
) -> Result<Value, Diagnostic> {
    match number(&input, "abs", &span)? {
        Value::Int(n) => n.checked_abs().map(Value::Int).ok_or(Diagnostic::overflow(span)),
        Value::Float(x) => Ok(Value::Float(x.abs())),
        Value::Decimal(x) => Ok(Value::Decimal(x.abs())),
        _ => unreachable!("number() answers a number"),
    }
}

eval_abs takes the value the call is made on, the call's other arguments, and the place of the call in the source, and gives a value or a diagnostic. It serves all four forms of abs and reads which one it was given from the value. The Rust states no HQL type: the types are the contract's.

docs.title: Binding
docs.text:
Binding joins the two halves, once, before the first program is checked. For each module of each package it pairs every declaration with the function of the same name in that module's table, and it refuses the package where the halves disagree:

Defect What binding reports a declaration with no function the declaration is declared, and the extension implements no such function a function with no declaration the extension implements a name no contract declares effectful fn over a function marked pure, or the reverse the two markings differ a shape word that differs from the function's marking the two markings differ a type the contract writes and no module declares the declaration states no signature

Because binding runs before any program does, a package is never half usable: either every declaration of its modules has its function, or the package is refused whole.

docs.title: Reading the result
docs.text:
hql builtins prints what binding produced: each module, the package and version that provide it, and each declared name with its forms, its purity and its shape.

hql builtins

math (std 0.7.2, prelude)
  abs
    Int | abs() -> Int
    Float | abs() -> Float
    Decimal | abs() -> Decimal
    Duration | abs() -> Duration
    pure, barrier

Int | abs() -> Int reads: on an Int, abs with no further arguments gives an Int. The value before | is the receiver.

docs.title: 32. Functions and declarations
docs.text:
A function is a name, a signature and a body: an expression in HQL that gives the result. A declaration is a name and a signature with no body: the result comes from a function written in Rust. A program calls both the same way, and the checker types a call from the signature alone, so nothing at the call says which of the two it reaches.

This chapter is about the second kind. Every function of the standard library that a program cannot write for itself, from abs to split, is a declaration, and Part V is about adding declarations of your own.

docs.title: A function has a body
docs.text:
Chapter 4 declares functions. The body follows =, and its type is checked against the result the signature states:

fn double(n: Int) : Int = n * 2

double(21)

42

Everything double does is in the program. Removing the Rust that implements hql would leave the function exactly as it is written.

docs.title: A declaration has none
docs.text:
The same signature without = is a declaration. It states what a call takes and gives, and nothing about how:

abs(-3)

3

abs is declared in the standard module math as fn abs(self: Int) : Int. The line has no body, because no HQL expression defines the absolute value of an Int without already having one. The result comes from a Rust function inside the hql binary.

A declaration is one half of a pair. The other half is the Rust function, and the pair is joined by an extension: the unit that implements the declarations of a package's modules. A declaration in a file that no extension implements is checked and binds no name:

fn area(side: Float) : Float

area(2.0f)

check error[unknown-name]: `area` is not bound
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | area(2.0f)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^

The declaration itself is accepted: its types exist and its name is free. The call is refused because a program has no extension, so nothing implements area.

docs.title: Which one to write
docs.text:
A function A declaration Written in HQL HQL for the signature, Rust for the result Lives in a program or a module of a project a module of a package Needs nothing beyond hql a Rust toolchain to build the package Reaches what HQL expresses anything a Rust crate does Changes take effect on the next run after the package is rebuilt

A function is the default. A declaration is for what HQL cannot express or should not repeat: a numeric routine a Rust crate already provides, a file format, a protocol, a computation whose speed matters.

docs.title: The pages of this chapter
docs.text: Page What it covers Declarations the receiver, positional and named parameters, defaults, forms of one name, purity and shape How the standard library is built a standard module's contract, the Rust beside it, and the check that joins them

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 33 follows an import from the module it names to the package that provides it and the file the package's extension is loaded from.

docs.title: 33. Packages and extensions
docs.text: A program names modules and nothing else. This chapter follows one import from the module it names down to the file on disk that runs, and names each unit on the way. Modules and packages introduced the four terms; here they are put to work on a package that is not part of hql.

docs.title: Four units, one path
docs.text:
Unit What it is For import hello module a named file of declarations; what import names hello package what is installed: a module root and the extension implementing it hello extension the Rust functions behind a package's declarations the hello extension library the compiled file an installed extension is loaded from libhql_ext_hello.dylib

The package of this chapter is hello, a small package kept in the hql repository under tests/packages/hello/. Chapter 34 writes it from an empty directory.

docs.title: An import names a module
docs.text:
import hello

hello.greet("Ada")

check error[unknown-name]: no module named `hello` under examples/reading-club/lib
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | import hello
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^

In the reading-club vault nothing provides hello: no package does, and the vault's module root, examples/reading-club/lib, holds no such file. The import is refused. The program is the same in a project where a package does provide it:

import hello

hello.greet("Ada")

"Hello, Ada!"

Neither program names a package. Which package provides hello, and whether one does, is a fact about the environment the program runs in.

docs.title: A module has one provider
docs.text:
When hql starts it gathers the packages of the environment: the two builtin ones, the crates a project lists, the packages installed in the project and those installed in the HQL home, in that order (chapter 36). Each package states the modules it provides. A module has exactly one provider. Two packages that provide one module are both refused: the order in which packages are found picks no winner.

hql builtins names the provider beside each module:

hql --project examples/packages builtins

math (std 0.7.2, prelude)
…
hello (hello 0.1.0, imported where it is used)
  greet
    String | greet() -> String
    pure, barrier

math comes from the package std at the version of hql itself. hello comes from the package hello at the version of its own crate.

docs.title: A package is a contract and an extension
docs.text:
A package holds two things, as std does (chapter 32):

  • a module root, a directory of contracts, one per module it provides;
  • an extension, one Rust function per name those contracts declare.

For a builtin package both are inside the hql binary. For an installed package the module root is a directory of .hql files and the extension is a library beside it:

~/.hql/packages/hello/
├── package.toml              what was built, from what, against which hql
├── modules/
│   └── hello/mod.hql         the contract of module `hello`
└── libhql_ext_hello.dylib    the extension, as a library

The library is .dylib on macOS, .so on Linux and .dll on Windows.

docs.title: What an import does
docs.text:
import hello makes the declarations of the module hello visible to the program, under the name hello. By the time a program is checked the package is already bound: its contract was read, its library was loaded, and each declaration was paired with its function. The import is a matter of names. That is why a call to a function of a package is checked as any call is:

import hello

hello.greet(3)

check error[type-mismatch]: `greet` needs String, not Int
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | hello.greet(3)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The refusal comes from the contract, fn greet(name: String) : String. The Rust function is never called with an Int.

A name of a package used without its import is reported as a missing import, since the environment knows which module declares it:

"hi".shout()

check error[unknown-name]: `shout` is declared in the module `hello`: write `import hello`
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | "hi".shout()
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 34 writes the hello package: its crate, its contract, and the Rust functions behind it.

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
The contract is the HQL half of the package: the file a program is checked against. This is modules/hello/mod.hql, whole:

/// Greetings, provided by the `hello` package.
module hello

import core

/// A greeting and the number of characters in it.
type Greeting { text : String, length : Int }

/// The greeting of a name: `Greeting("Ada")` holds `Hello, Ada!`.
/// `punctuation` replaces the `!`.
fn Greeting(name: String, *, punctuation: String = "!") : Greeting

/// The text greeting a name: `greet("Ada")` is `Hello, Ada!`.
fn greet(name: String) : String

/// `self` in capitals: `"hi".shout()` is `HI`.
fn shout(self: String) : String

/// The text of a greeting in capitals.
fn shout(self: Greeting) : String

/// The sum of `weight` over the elements of `self`.
fn total<T>(self: List<T>, weight: T -> Int) : Int

/// A function that panics, which the call reports as a failure.
fn fail(message: String) : String

docs.title: The head of the file
docs.text:
A contract opens with module and the module's name, which is the name provides lists and the path of the file under the module root. A file whose module line names another module is refused.

import core makes the types of the language's core visible: String, Int, List. A contract is a module like any other, a closure over its own imports (chapter 5), so it imports every module whose types it writes. The prelude does not apply inside a package.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
type Greeting { text : String, length : Int } declares a record type. A type a contract declares belongs to the language once the package is loaded: a program that imports hello reads g.text, and the checker knows it is a String.

import hello

Greeting("Ada")

Greeting(text = "Hello, Ada!", length = 11)

docs.title: A constructor
docs.text: fn Greeting(…) : Greeting is a declaration named as its type is: a constructor. A record type without one is constructed by naming every field. With one, a call of the type's name reaches the package's function, which computes the fields: here length is counted, never passed.

docs.title: Declarations
docs.text:
The remaining lines are declarations (chapter 32):

  • greet takes one String and has no receiver, so it is called hello.greet("Ada").
  • shout has two forms, on a String and on a Greeting, both receiver calls: "hi".shout().
  • total is generic over the element type and takes a function, T -> Int.
  • Greeting takes punctuation by name only, after *, with a default.
import hello

["hi".shout(), Greeting("Ada").shout()]

["HI", "HELLO, ADA!"]

docs.title: Doc strings
docs.text: A /// paragraph directly above a declaration is its doc string. It is the text hql help prints, so it is written for the caller: what the function gives, with one example. Forms of one name written in one paragraph share a doc string.

docs.title: What the contract does not say
docs.text: The contract states no implementation, and the Rust states no types. A change to a signature is a change to this file alone, as long as the Rust function still reads the values the new signature admits. A change to what a function computes leaves this file untouched.

docs.title: 34. Writing an extension
docs.text:
This chapter writes a package from an empty directory: hello, which provides one module of the same name. It has a crate, a contract and five Rust functions, and it is small enough to read whole. The finished package is in the hql repository under tests/packages/hello/, where the tests of hql build and load it.

A package needs a Rust toolchain: cargo, installed with rustup. It needs no knowledge of how hql is built beyond one module of its crate, hql::ext.

docs.title: The parts of a package
docs.text:
hello/
├── Cargo.toml                the crate, and what package it is
├── modules/
│   └── hello/mod.hql         the contract: declarations without bodies
└── src/
    └── lib.rs                the extension: one Rust function per name
Part Written in Says Cargo.toml TOML the crate's name, that its library is loadable, and the package's name and modules modules/ HQL what a program may call, with types and doc strings src/ Rust what each call computes

docs.title: The order of work
docs.text:
1. The crate: a Cargo.toml that makes a crate a package.
  2. The contract: the module file a program is checked against.
  3. Natives: a Rust function per declared name, the table that lists them, and the extension that exports the table.
  4. Values and errors: what a function receives and returns, records of the package's own types, and failures.
  5. Functions and the context: calling a function the program passed in, and what else the running program offers.

With the three files written, one command builds the package and installs it, and a program imports it:

hql package install --path hello

import hello

hello.greet("Ada")

"Hello, Ada!"

While a package is being written, a project names its crate instead, and hql rebuilds it whenever its source is newer than the last build (a local crate). The programs of this chapter run that way.

docs.title: The pages of this chapter
docs.text: Page What it covers The crate Cargo.toml: the crate type, the hql dependency, [package.metadata.hql] The prelude prelude.hql: the modules every unit imports while the package is active The contract the module file, its types, its declarations and their doc strings Natives the signature of a native function, the table of operations, hql::extension! Values and errors Value, records, named arguments and defaults, failures and panics Functions and the context applying a function argument, and EvalCx

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 35 is about what hql package install produced and how the running hql reaches it: a library, a symbol, and the rule that makes the two fit.

docs.title: Functions and the context
docs.text: Some declarations take a function, as map and filter do. The function belongs to the program, so the native cannot run it: it asks the running hql to. Everything a native asks of the running program goes through its first parameter, the context, cx: &mut dyn EvalCx.

docs.title: Applying a function argument
docs.text:
fn total<T>(self: List<T>, weight: T -> Int) : Int sums a function over a list:

fn total(
    cx: &mut dyn EvalCx,
    input: Value,
    arguments: &[TypedArg],
    span: Span,
) -> Result<Value, Diagnostic> {
    let Value::List(elements, _) = input else {
        return Err(ext::failure(span, "expected a `List`"));
    };
    let Some(weight) = ext::positional(arguments, 0) else {
        return Err(ext::failure(span, "`total` takes a function"));
    };
    let mut sum = 0_i64;
    for element in elements.iter() {
        match cx.apply_lambda(weight, element.clone())? {
            Value::Int(weighed) => {
                sum = sum
                    .checked_add(weighed)
                    .ok_or_else(|| ext::failure(span.clone(), "numeric overflow"))?;
            }
            _ => return Err(ext::failure(span, "`weight` gives an `Int`")),
        }
    }
    Ok(Value::Int(sum))
}

cx.apply_lambda(weight, element) applies the function written as the argument weight to one element and gives its result. A failure inside the program's function comes back through ? as the call's failure.

import hello

[[1, 2, 3].total(x => x * 10), ["ab", "cde"].total(word => word.size())]

[60, 5]

The contract's T -> Int is what lets the program write x => x * 10 without a type: the checker gives x the element type of the list, and checks that the body is an Int, before total is ever called.

docs.title: What the context offers
Why everything goes through the context
docs.text:
A package's library holds its own compiled copy of the hql crate (chapter 35). The running program's state, its bindings, its seed, its clock, its diagnostics, lives in the copy inside the hql binary. The library's copy has state of its own, which no program ever set.

The context is a reference into the running copy. A native that calls cx.draw reads the program's seed. A native that reached for the hql crate's random functions directly would read its own copy's, which is unseeded. For that reason hql::ext exposes values, diagnostics and the context, and a native uses nothing else of the crate.

docs.title: Natives
docs.text: A native is a Rust function that implements the declarations of one name. This page writes the simplest one, lists it in a table, and exports the table as the package's extension. All of it is src/lib.rs.

docs.title: One function
docs.text:
fn greet(name: String) : String is implemented by:

use hql::ext::{self, Diagnostic, EvalCx, Operation, Span, TypedArg, Value};

fn greet(
    _cx: &mut dyn EvalCx,
    input: Value,
    _arguments: &[TypedArg],
    span: Span,
) -> Result<Value, Diagnostic> {
    match input {
        Value::Str(name) => Ok(Value::Str(format!("Hello, {name}!").into())),
        _ => Err(ext::failure(span, "expected a `String`")),
    }
}

Every native has this signature.

Parameter What it is cx the running program: what the function may ask of hql while it runs (Functions and the context) input the value the call is made on: the receiver, or the first argument where the declaration has no self arguments the call's other arguments, unevaluated, each with the name it was written with, if any span where the call is in the program's source, for a diagnostic to point at

The result is a Value or a Diagnostic.

By the time greet runs, the call was checked against the contract, so input is a String. The second arm of the match cannot be reached by a program. It is there because Rust requires every case, and a failure is a better answer to an impossible case than a panic.

docs.title: The table
docs.text:
The functions of a module are listed in a table, each under the name its declarations use:

static HELLO: &[Operation] = &[
    hql::native!("Greeting", greeting),
    hql::native!("greet", greet),
    hql::native!("shout", shout),
    hql::native!("total", total),
    hql::native!("fail", fail),
];

hql::native! makes an Operation from a name and a function. A name with several forms, shout, has one entry. The table has an entry for every name the contract declares and no others: a declaration without an entry, or an entry without a declaration, refuses the package.

An operation built this way is pure and a barrier, which is what a declaration written plain fn states. A declaration written effectful fn takes .effectful() on its entry, and one written with a shape word takes .shaped(…):

hql::native!("split", split).effectful(),
hql::native!("double", double).shaped(hql::ext::Shape::Elementwise),

docs.title: The extension
docs.text:
One line states the package and exports it:

hql::extension!(ext::extension(
    "hello",
    env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"),
    &[ext::provided("hello", HELLO)],
));

ext::extension takes the package's name, the crate's version, and one ext::provided per module: the module's name with its table. The names and their order are those of provides in Cargo.toml.

hql::extension! is written once in the crate. It defines the one function hql looks for when it loads the library, hql_extension_v1 (chapter 35).

docs.title: Building and trying it
docs.text:
hql package install --path hello

installed hello 0.1.0 (hello) in /home/ada/.hql/packages/hello

The command runs cargo build --release on the crate, copies the library and the module root into the HQL home, and loads the result. A package that builds and does not bind is reported here, by the defect binding found, and not when a program later imports it.

import hello

hello.greet("Ada")

"Hello, Ada!"

docs.title: The crate
docs.text:
A package is a Cargo crate with three additions: a name that says so, a library type hql can load, and a table naming the package. This is the whole Cargo.toml of hello:

[package]
name = "hql-ext-hello"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]

[dependencies]
hql = "0.7"

[package.metadata.hql]
package = "hello"
provides = ["hello"]
modules = "modules"

docs.title: The name
docs.text: The crate is named hql-ext- and then the package's name. The package name is one lowercase word, and it is also the namespace of the package's modules: hello provides hello and may provide hello.words, and nothing outside that prefix. A package named ml provides ml and ml.metrics.

docs.title: The library type
docs.text:
crate-type states what the compiler produces from the crate.

Type What it is Why it is listed cdylib a dynamic library: one file the operating system can load into a running process this is what hql loads rlib a Rust library other Rust code links against at build time so cargo test can test the crate's own functions

Without cdylib the build leaves no file to load, and hql package install says so. Chapter 35 explains the two kinds.

docs.title: The hql dependency
docs.text:
The crate depends on hql, the same crate the hql binary is built from, and uses one module of it, hql::ext. hql = "0.7" is a range: every 0.7 release. It says which versions the crate's source is written for.

The version the crate is actually built against is not chosen by this line. hql package install builds the crate against the exact version of the hql that runs the command, and refuses a crate whose range excludes that version before it builds anything (the version rule).

docs.title: The package table
docs.text:
[package.metadata.hql] is the part Cargo ignores and hql reads.

Key What it states package the package's name, which is also its extension's name and its directory once installed provides every module the package provides, in the order they are loaded; a module that imports another comes after it modules the module root: the directory holding the contracts, relative to the crate

provides is stated twice more, by the files under the module root and by the extension in src/lib.rs. The three must agree, and a package where they differ is refused when it is loaded.

A module's contract is found under the module root by its name, a dot becoming a directory:

Module File hello modules/hello/mod.hql or modules/hello.hql hello.words modules/hello/words.hql or modules/hello/words/mod.hql

docs.title: The package's prelude
docs.text:
The module root may hold prelude.hql, the package's prelude: a file of import statements, which is not a module. hello's is one line:

import hello

While the package is active in a run, every unit of the run imports the modules the prelude lists. The prelude states when a package is active and what a prelude may hold.

docs.title: The prelude
docs.text:
A package's prelude is the file prelude.hql at its module root: a list of import statements that every unit of a run imports while the package is active. It is not a module: it has no name and cannot be imported. The standard library has one, lib/std/prelude.hql, which is why a program writes trim and map with no import; a package's own works the same way for the package's modules.

hello's prelude is one line:

import hello

docs.title: Loaded and active
docs.text:
Two states of a package are distinct:

State Holds when Effect loaded the package is discovered and its library opens its modules can be imported active a unit of the run imports one of its modules its prelude's imports are added to every unit

Every discovered package is loaded when hql starts. A loaded package that no unit imports adds no name to any program:

hello.greet("Ada")

check error[unknown-name]: `hello` is not bound
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | hello.greet("Ada")
  | ^^^^^

An import of one of the package's modules activates it. Here the import binds the module under the alias h, and the prelude binds it under its own name:

import hello as h

[h.greet("Ada"), hello.greet("Bo")]

["Hello, Ada!", "Hello, Bo!"]

docs.title: What activates a package
docs.text:
A package is active in a run when one of its modules is imported by any of these:

  • an import in the program;
  • an import in a project module the program reaches through its imports;
  • [modules] import in a configuration file, naming a module or the package;
  • --import <module> on the command line.

Activation is per run, not per unit. The units of a run are the program and every project module it reaches. An import in one of them activates the package for all of them, so a project module that writes no import of the package still reads the names its prelude binds once another unit has imported it.

docs.title: What a prelude is for
docs.text:
A prelude names the modules a program of the package cannot do without. A module it does not name is the package's optional part and is imported where it is used. The ml package (chapter 38) provides ml and ml.metrics, and its prelude is:

import ml

A program that imports only ml.metrics activates the package, so ml is bound too, and Dataset and fit_linear are in scope. ml.metrics stays out of a program that does not import it.

docs.title: What a prelude may hold
docs.text:
• Each statement MUST be an import or a from statement. A declaration, a binding or an expression refuses the package.
  • An import MUST NOT be written with as: a prelude imports a module under its own name, its last segment.
  • Each module named MUST exist: a module of the package, or of a builtin package.

A package whose prelude breaks one of these is refused when it is loaded, and an import of one of its modules reports the reason:

check error[unknown-name]: no module named `hello`: .../modules/prelude.hql: a prelude holds imports and nothing else

Two active packages whose preludes import different modules under one last segment are an error of the run, naming both files. A prelude's import that collides with a name the program binds itself is resolved in the program, by importing under another name with as.

docs.title: Declining preludes
docs.text:
prelude = false under [modules] in .hql/config.toml withholds every prelude's imports, std's and each active package's:

[modules]
prelude = false

Every unit of the project then imports each module it uses. The setting does not change which packages are loaded or active.

docs.title: The prelude does not apply inside its package
docs.text: A contract under the package's module root imports every module whose names it writes, core included (The contract). The package's prelude reaches the units of a run, the program and project modules, and no module of a package.

docs.title: Values and errors
docs.text: A native receives HQL values and returns one. This page covers the Rust type that holds them, arguments written by name, records of a type the package declares, and the two ways a call fails.

docs.title: Value
docs.text:
Every HQL value is a hql::ext::Value, an enum with one variant per kind of value. The ones a package meets most:

HQL type Variant Holds Int Value::Int(i64) a 64-bit integer Float Value::Float(f64) a double Bool Value::Bool(bool) String Value::Str(Arc<str>) text List<T> Value::List(Arc<Vec<Value>>, TypeRef) the elements and the element type a record type Value::Record(Arc<Record>) the type and the fields in declaration order Option<T>, present Value::Present(Arc<Value>) the value Option<T>, absent Value::Absent(TypeRef) the type of what is absent a function Value::Function(…) applied through the context, never by hand

A list is built with Value::list(elements, element_type), and the common types are constants: TypeRef::INT, TypeRef::FLOAT, TypeRef::STR.

A native matches on the variant the contract promises. shout is declared on a String and on a Greeting, so its one function reads both:

fn shout(
    _cx: &mut dyn EvalCx,
    input: Value,
    _arguments: &[TypedArg],
    span: Span,
) -> Result<Value, Diagnostic> {
    let said = match &input {
        Value::Record(record) => match record.field("text") {
            Some(held) => text(held, &span)?,
            None => return Err(ext::failure(span, "expected a `Greeting`")),
        },
        other => text(other, &span)?,
    };
    Ok(Value::Str(said.to_uppercase().into()))
}

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
input is evaluated when the function is called. The other arguments are not: each is a TypedArg, the argument's expression with the name it was written with. A function finds the ones it wants and evaluates them:

Function Gives ext::named(arguments, "punctuation") the argument written punctuation = …, if the call wrote it ext::positional(arguments, 0) the first argument written without a name, after the input ext::value_of(cx, argument) the argument's value

An argument with a default that the call leaves out is not in arguments. The function supplies the default the contract states:

let punctuation = match ext::named(arguments, "punctuation") {
    Some(argument) => text(&ext::value_of(cx, argument)?, &span)?,
    None => "!".to_owned(),
};

import hello

g = Greeting("Ada", punctuation = "?")
[g.text, str(g.length)]

["Hello, Ada?", "11"]

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
A value of a record type the contract declares is built with ext::record: the type by its name, then the fields in the order the contract declares them.

Ok(ext::record(
    ext::ty("Greeting", []),
    [
        ("text", Value::Str(said.into())),
        ("length", Value::Int(length)),
    ],
))

ext::ty("Greeting", []) is the type Greeting with no type arguments. The name is the one the contract declares; the contract is where the fields and their types are stated, and the Rust follows it. An optional field, target? : List<Float>, holds a Value::Present or a Value::Absent.

docs.title: Failures
docs.text:
A function that cannot give a result returns a diagnostic. ext::failure(span, message) makes one that points at the call:

let length = i64::try_from(said.chars().count())
    .map_err(|_| ext::failure(span.clone(), "the greeting is too long"))?;

The message is one sentence for the person who wrote the program. It says what was wrong with the value, in the program's terms: row 1 has 2 features; row 0 has 1, not the name of a Rust error.

A failure is an ordinary failure of the program. Under collect, or handled by the steps of chapter 12, it behaves as a failure of a standard function does.

docs.title: Panics
docs.text:
A Rust panic inside a native does not end hql. hql::native! runs each function under a guard that catches a panic and returns it as a failure of the call, naming the function:

import hello

hello.fail("boom")

execute failure[invalid-argument]: the extension function `fail` panicked: boom
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | hello.fail("boom")
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The guard is a net, and a failure is the intended path. A panic reports a defect of the package: an index out of range, an unwrap on nothing. A value a program can pass is refused with ext::failure.

docs.title: 35. How a library is loaded
docs.text:
hql is one program file. An installed package is a second file, built later, on another day, perhaps by another person. This chapter is about how code in the second file comes to run inside the first: what kind of file a library is, the one name hql looks up in it, and the rule that makes the two files fit.

Nothing here is needed to use a package, and little of it to write one. It is what explains the messages a package gives when it is refused, and why hql package rebuild exists.

docs.title: From a crate to a call
docs.text:
There are two moments.

Install, once per package and again after hql is upgraded: hql package install runs cargo on the crate and writes three things into the HQL home, the library, the module root and a record of the build.

Start, every time hql runs: each installed package is read, its library is loaded into the process, and its contract is bound to its extension. Only then is a program checked.

After that a call to a function of the package costs what a call to a standard function costs. The library's function is called directly, through a pointer, with no copying and no other process.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 36 is the commands: installing, listing, rebuilding and removing packages, and the files they keep.

docs.title: Static and dynamic libraries
docs.text: Compiled code reaches a running program in one of two ways: it is put into the program's file when the program is built, or it is read from a file of its own when the program runs. Rust does the first by default. A package is the second.

docs.title: Static linking
docs.text:
A Rust program is made of crates. Cargo compiles each crate once into an rlib, an archive of compiled code, and the linker then copies what the program uses out of every rlib into one executable file.

hql (the crate)   ─┐
regex             ─┤
serde_json        ─┼─ linker ─→  hql   one file, nothing else needed
…every other crate ─┘

This is static linking. The hql binary holds its own code and the code of every crate it depends on. The builtin packages are part of it: the extension of std is Rust inside the hql crate, linked in like the rest. Static linking is why hql installs as a single file.

It is also why a builtin package cannot be added to. The set of crates is fixed when the binary is built. Adding ml to std would mean building hql again with ml's crates in it, for everyone, whether they use it or not.

docs.title: A dynamic library
docs.text:
A dynamic library is compiled code in a file of its own, in a format the operating system can load into a process that is already running: .dylib on macOS, .so on Linux, .dll on Windows. The loading program names a file, and the system maps it into the program's memory. The program then asks for a function in it by name, a symbol, and gets back an address it can call.

In a crate's Cargo.toml, crate-type = ["cdylib"] asks the compiler for this kind of file:

cargo build --release
ls -lh target/release/libhql_ext_hello.dylib
nm -gU target/release/libhql_ext_hello.dylib

-rwxr-xr-x  754K  libhql_ext_hello.dylib
0000000000002ca0 T _hql_extension_v1

nm -gU lists the symbols a library exports. This one exports a single function, hql_extension_v1. Every other function of the crate is inside the file and has no exported name.

docs.title: A library carries its own copy of hql
docs.text:
The hello crate depends on the hql crate. A cdylib is linked the way an executable is: the linker copies in what the crate uses from every crate it depends on. So the library holds its own compiled copy of the parts of hql it uses: Value, Diagnostic, the code that builds a record. That is most of its 754K; the package's own functions are a few hundred lines.

the hql process
├── hql                          the binary
│   ├── the hql crate
│   ├── std's extension
│   └── the running program
└── libhql_ext_hello.dylib       the library
    ├── the hql crate            a second compilation of the same source
    ├── hello's five functions
    └── hql_extension_v1

The library is not linked against the hql binary, and it does not call into it by name. The two files are two separate compilations of the same source that happen to be in one process. Three things follow, and the rest of the chapter is their consequences.

The two copies must be the same compilation. A Value built in the library is read by the binary. Both must agree on what a Value is, byte for byte (the version rule).

Each copy has its own state. A global variable of the hql crate exists twice. The running program's is the binary's. A native therefore reaches the program through the context it is handed and through nothing else (chapter 34).

The library is never unloaded. The binary keeps pointers to the library's functions and tables for as long as it runs, so the library stays in memory until the process ends.

docs.title: What a library is not
docs.text:
A package's library Another process A WebAssembly module Runs in the hql process a process of its own a sandbox inside the process A call costs a function call a message each way a boundary crossing May do anything hql may: files, network, memory what its own process may what the host grants A crash ends hql ends the other process is contained

A package's library is native code with the rights of the hql process. That is what makes it fast and unrestricted, and it is why a package is installed deliberately, from a source you chose (chapter 37).

docs.title: The entry point
docs.text: A library exports one symbol, hql_extension_v1. hql loads the file, looks that name up, and calls it. Everything else about the package is reached from what the call returns.

docs.title: The symbol
docs.text:
hql::extension! writes the function. The line in a package's crate

hql::extension!(ext::extension("hello", env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"), &[…]));

expands to:

#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub extern "C" fn hql_extension_v1() -> hql::ext::Header {
    static EXTENSION: hql::ext::Extension = /* the extension written above */;
    hql::ext::Header::of(&EXTENSION)
}
Part What it does #[unsafe(no_mangle)] keeps the name exactly hql_extension_v1 in the library, so it can be looked up; Rust otherwise rewrites function names extern "C" fixes how the function is called to the platform's C convention, which does not vary between compilers static EXTENSION the extension lives in the library for as long as the library is loaded -> Header the function returns a small fixed-layout value, described next

The v1 in the name is the version of this arrangement. A future hql that changed it would look for another name and would not mistake an old library for a new one.

docs.title: The header
docs.text:
